title: [AMD] Do not insert barriers between mbarrier-synchronized TDM copies
body:
An async copy that carries an mbarrier operand sends an LDS atomic arrive when it completes, so it takes part in mbarrier synchronization exactly like AsyncCopyMbarrierArriveOp, which membarFilter already recognizes. The mbarrier orders those accesses across the whole workgroup, so a ttg.barrier between two such ops synchronizes nothing.

Copies without a barrier operand are deliberately not covered here. Those are ordered by their async wait instead, and an async wait counter is per wave, so it cannot order accesses between waves.

Without this, a TDM collective expressed with mbarrier completion emits more barriers than the async_tdm_wait formulation it replaces, which makes mbarrier unusable as an alternative.

title: [BACKEND] Fix  abstract signature to match its overrides
body:
`BaseBackend.add_stages` was declared as `add_stages(self, stages, options)`,
missing the `language` parameter. Every concrete backend already overrides it
with `language` included, e.g.:
```
  third_party/amd/backend/compiler.py:
      def add_stages(self, stages, options, language):

  third_party/nvidia/backend/compiler.py:
      def add_stages(self, stages, options, language):
```
and the call site in `python/triton/compiler/compiler.py` passes it:
```
  backend.add_stages(stages, options, src.language)
```
so the abstract method's signature was simply stale. This causes static
type checkers (Pyright/Pylance) to flag every backend override as
"incompatible with base class" due to a positional parameter count
mismatch. Add the missing `language: Language` parameter to the abstract
declaration so it matches actual usage and all existing overrides.

title: [AMD] Make the membar async-load filter direction-aware
body:
The AMD membar filter vetoes the barrier between an async load and a
local_load synced via async_wait regardless of which of the two comes
first.

In the RAW direction (async load, then the synced local_load) the veto
is safe. The load's token proves its copy was waited for, and Membar
already emits a barrier right after that wait, so the copy is visible
to every thread before the read. A barrier in front of the load adds
nothing; any copy still in flight at that point is one the kernel chose
not to wait for, and a barrier cannot complete it either.

In the WAR direction (synced local_load, then an async load refilling
the same buffer) the veto is wrong. The wait covers the read, not what
follows it: other threads may still be reading the buffer when the
refill lands, and only a barrier orders that.

Membar passes the pending (earlier) access as op1 and the current access
as op2, so veto only when the synced local_load is op2. Dropping the
rule altogether would instead put a barrier before every synced
local_load that has an unrelated copy in flight, which multi-stage
pipelines routinely do.

title: [CUDA] Skip unsupported cluster sizes in Gluon tests
body:
On a Jetson Thor (SM110), Gluon tests requesting a 16-CTA cluster fail at launch with `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_CLUSTER_SIZE` / "cluster misconfiguration". For example, pytest's `ctas_per_cga2` label is the `[4, 4]` parameter, which requests 16 CTAs rather than 2.

Query cluster occupancy once per device and requested size using a small Triton kernel, then skip affected test parameters when even that low-resource kernel cannot fit a cluster. The probe is only a test prefilter: a real kernel can still have stricter resource limits. Existing 2/4/8-CTA cases continue to run.

Reproduce on a Thor GPU before this change:

```bash
CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 python -m pytest -s --tb=short -q -n 0 \
  'python/test/gluon/test_core.py::test_shared_gather_cga[16-cta-sharded]' \
  --device=cuda
```

Before: `RuntimeError: Triton Error [CUDA]: a kernel launch error has occurred due to cluster misconfiguration`. After: skipped with `Device does not support 16 CTAs per cluster`.

Validation on Thor, based on upstream `main` at test time:

```bash
CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 python -m pytest -s --tb=short -q -n 0 \
  python/test/gluon/test_core.py python/test/gluon/test_lowerings.py \
  -k 'ctas_per_cga2 or (test_mma_scaled_tcgen05_copy and ctas_per_cga5) or (test_shared_gather_cga and 16-cta) or (test_reduce_funky_layout and (src_layout5-0 or src_layout11-1))' \
  --device=cuda
```

Result: `16 passed, 5856 skipped, 0 failed`. Four representative 2/4/8-CTA cases passed.

title: Fix FP4 TMA Alignment
body:
## Summary

Use physical storage width for Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) stride alignment. Packed FP4 uses `uint8` storage; using its logical 4-bit width incorrectly rejects a 16-byte row stride. Preserve gathered row indices for activation scales so values and scales use the same source rows.

Without preserving those indices, the H100 pointer-gather path pairs `X[gather[i]]` with `X_scale[i]`, producing numerical mismatches rather than a TMA error (maximum relative error 0.9443 versus 0.02 allowed in one case).

[NVIDIA specifies `globalStrides` in bytes, with 16-byte alignment for ordinary TMA.](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-driver-api/cuda_driver_api/group__CUDA__TENSOR__MEMORY.html)

## Desired features

- Accept packed FP4 tensors whose physical storage strides satisfy ordinary TMA alignment.
- Keep gathered activation values and their block/tensor scales on the same source rows.

## Validation

Tested on NVIDIA GB300 (copy below) and NVIDIA H100 (gathered-scale path) with Triton 3.8.0. The copy below is byte-exact and uses ordinary UINT8 TMA (`fp4_padded=False`). The old alignment expression returned `False`; the patched helper returned `True`. This copy does not validate padded FP4 or matmul.

Run with `triton_kernels` from the checkout:

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl
from triton_kernels.tensor import FP4, is_tma_compliant, make_tma, wrap_torch_tensor


@triton.jit
def copy_packed(src, out):
    tl.store(out + tl.arange(0, 32), src.load([0, 0]).reshape(32))


storage = torch.arange(32, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda").reshape(2, 16)
packed = wrap_torch_tensor(storage, dtype=FP4)
out = torch.empty_like(storage)
kernel = copy_packed[(1,)](make_tma(packed, [2, 32], "dense"), out)

# checks
assert torch.equal(out, storage)
assert "cp.async.bulk.tensor" in kernel.asm["ptx"]
assert is_tma_compliant(packed)  # Fails before this change.
```

## Lines Changed

| Type | Added | Removed | Net |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Tests | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Core Logic | 3 | 2 | 1 |
| AutoGenerated | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Total | 3 | 2 | 1 |

## Reviewers Guide

- `python/triton_kernels/triton_kernels/tensor.py`: generic stride-alignment check only; no code movements.
- `python/triton_kernels/triton_kernels/matmul_details/_p_matmul.py`: preserve gathered row indices for activation scales; no code movements.

title: [TEST] Fix `make test-nogpu` failure on macOS after #11806
body:
test_gluon_ast_source_without_driver[target0-cubin] fails on platforms where ptxas cannot execute (e.g. macOS), because CUDABackend.hash() and make_cubin() both invoke ptxas as a subprocess.

The bundled ptxas binary is a Linux ELF executable, so running it on macOS raises 'OSError: [Errno 8] Exec format error'.

This was introduced in #11806 ('[Gluon] Expose GluonASTSource for offline compilation') and breaks 'make test-nogpu' on macOS.

Skip the CUDA parametrization when ptxas is not functional. The HIP parametrization still runs and validates the offline-compilation path.

title: [NVIDIA] Canonicalize constant fdiv through an approximate reciprocal
body:
Canonicalize FP32 `arith.divf(a, b)` with constant denominator magnitudes in `[2^-126, 2^126]` to `a * tt.approx_divf(1.0, b)` on NVIDIA. Scalar and splat denominators use one scalar reciprocal; dense constants are checked elementwise. Use `TargetInfoBase` to restrict the rewrite to CUDA and register it in both the standard and Gluon canonicalizers.

The randomized regression compares raw result bits against `div.full.f32` with the same constant denominator. This checks preservation of the original constant-division behavior; PTXAS can use different reciprocal approximations when the denominator is a runtime value.

## Stack

Depends on #11900. This PR targets `codex/approx-fdiv-op` so its diff contains only the constant-division rewrite and its regression coverage.

## Validation

Validated on a Brix GB300 devbox after a native rebuild and source-hash verification:

- All repository pre-commit checks passed.
- 9 focused lit files passed, covering standard and Gluon canonicalization, AMD exclusions, NVIDIA and AMD lowering, and FPSan.
- 22 division GPU cases passed.
- The randomized regression passed all 2,359,296 raw-bit comparisons: 65,536 numerator encodings across 36 signed in-range constant denominators, including both range endpoints.

AMD was validated through IR tests; no AMD GPU runtime was used.

title: fix: add missing negation in WSDataPartition thenYieldArg check
body:
## Summary

Fixes #9559

The `thenYieldArg` branch in `getBackwardSliceToPartition` (line 324) was missing the `!` negation operator, causing inverted error handling compared to all other call sites.

## Bug

```cpp
// BEFORE (line 324) — returns false on SUCCESS (wrong)
if (getBackwardSliceToPartition(thenYieldArg, partitionScheme, currentDim))
    return false;

// The else branch directly below already has the correct pattern:
if (!getBackwardSliceToPartition(elseYieldArg, partitionScheme, currentDim))
    return false;
```

All other call sites in the same function use `if (!getBackwardSliceToPartition(...)) return false;` to propagate failure. This was the only one without the negation, as confirmed by @htyu in the issue thread.

## Change

Single-character fix — add `!` to match the consistent pattern across the file.
Added a lit test with `scf.if` result feeding into a dot to cover this path.

title: [TRITONGPU] Support two-cta mode
body:
Enable two-CTA MMAv5 for descriptor-loaded operands, including cooperating pairs in larger CTA clusters. Synchronize TMA loads and pipeline a TMEM read-release barrier so both CTAs finish reading before an MMA reuses the accumulator. Unsupported producers and narrow shapes fall back to one-CTA MMA; automatic warp specialization is disabled for two-CTA modules.

The TMEM reuse fix supports a single reader in the loop body or a directly nested conditional. Tutorial 09 uses this path for persistent matmul.

Historical performance on GB200: FP16 inputs/output, FP32 accumulation, `M=N=8192`, `A @ B.T`, split epilogue, ConSan off. Two-CTA measurements are from `6b6f7ca6aa`; old main is `d1fc86be1b90`.

title: Support Python 3.15 and build 3.15t wheels
body:
Adds Python 3.15 support so downstream projects that follow CPython releases (PyTorch is already building 3.15 / 3.15t wheels) are not blocked on Triton.

Two changes, for two different reasons.

## 1. `setup.py`: allow 3.15 to install

```diff
 MIN_PYTHON = (3, 10)
-MAX_PYTHON = (3, 14)
+MAX_PYTHON = (3, 15)
```

This is the actual blocker for 3.15-with-GIL. The existing `cp312-abi3` wheel already runs on 3.15 — `TRITON_STABLE_ABI` sets `Py_LIMITED_API=0x030C0000` and tags the wheel `cp312-abi3`, which is forward compatible — but `python_requires` was `>=3.10,<3.15`, so pip refuses to install it on 3.15. Bumping `MAX_PYTHON` makes it `>=3.10,<3.16` and adds the 3.15 classifier.

**No new non-free-threaded wheel is needed**, and none is added here: the abi3 wheel covers 3.12 through 3.15.

## 2. `wheels.yml`: build a free-threaded 3.15t wheel

Free-threaded builds do not support the limited API, so the cp312 abi3 wheel cannot cover `3.15t` — it needs a version-specific wheel, like the existing cp310/cp311 pass:

```yaml
export CIBW_ENABLE="cpython-prerelease"
export CIBW_BUILD="cp315t-manylinux_${{ matrix.config.arch }}"
export CIBW_ENVIRONMENT="MAX_JOBS=4 TRITON_EXT_ENABLED=ON TRITON_BUILD_WITH_CLANG_LLD=1"
python3 -m cibuildwheel . --output-dir wheelhouse
```

Note `TRITON_STABLE_ABI` is deliberately **not** set for this pass.

### Why `cpython-prerelease`

`manylinux_2_28` currently ships **3.15.0rc1** (`build_cpython315` / `build_cpython315_nogil` stages in pypa/manylinux's Dockerfile), and cibuildwheel gates prerelease CPython behind `CIBW_ENABLE=cpython-prerelease`. The flag can be dropped once the image carries 3.15.0 final. cibuildwheel already knows the identifiers:

```
{ identifier = "cp315t-manylinux_x86_64",  version = "3.15", path_str = "/opt/python/cp315-cp315t" }
{ identifier = "cp315t-manylinux_aarch64", version = "3.15", path_str = "/opt/python/cp315-cp315t" }
```

cibuildwheel's docs caution against publishing prerelease-built wheels to **PyPI**; this workflow publishes to the Triton-Nightly Azure feed, which is the intended consumer for pre-GA testing.

## Scope / follow-ups

- Only `3.15t` is added. `3.13t` and `3.14t` are also uncovered by the abi3 wheel today; adding them is the same one-block change if wanted, but I kept this PR to 3.15.
- The workflow only runs on `schedule`, `workflow_dispatch`, and PRs touching `wheels.yml` — so this PR exercises the new build path in CI.

body:

    and using the instructions it generates is not minimal.)

## Why

Fixes #9559.

`getBackwardSliceToPartition` returns `true` when a value can be sliced and `false` when partitioning should fail. The `scf.if` result path handled the else yield with `if (!getBackwardSliceToPartition(...)) return false;`, but the then yield used the opposite polarity. That made a successful then-yield backward slice abort the whole data partition.

This matters when a warp-specialized value flows through an `scf.if` before reaching a partitioned consumer such as `ttng.warp_group_dot`: the then and else yield operands both have to be followed backward before the result can be sliced.

## What changed

- Make the then-yield recursive check use the same success polarity as the else-yield path.
- Add a `ws_data_partition.mlir` regression where a `ttg.local_alloc` result is yielded through both arms of an `scf.if` and then consumed by `ttng.warp_group_dot`.

There was an earlier closed PR for the one-line code change (#9794). This version adds a focused lit regression and avoids carrying unrelated metadata.

## Testing

- `pre-commit run --from-ref upstream/main --to-ref HEAD`
- `pre-commit run --files third_party/nvidia/hopper/lib/Transforms/WarpSpecialization/WSDataPartition.cpp test/Hopper/WarpSpecialization/ws_data_partition.mlir`
- `git diff --check upstream/main..HEAD`

I could not run the lit invocation locally because this Windows checkout does not have `triton-opt` / `FileCheck` binaries available. The added test is intended for the existing CI command:

```bash
triton-opt test/Hopper/WarpSpecialization/ws_data_partition.mlir -split-input-file --nvgpu-test-ws-data-partition=num-warp-groups=3 | FileCheck test/Hopper/WarpSpecialization/ws_data_partition.mlir
```

title: [AMD][mxfp4] ttg::Fp4ToFpOp add support for FP4 upcast to FP32
body:
# [mxfp4] ttg::Fp4ToFpOp add support for FP4 upcast to FP32

 ## Motivation

On AMD CDNA3 architecture, upcasting FP4 to BF16 requires first upcasting to FP32 then truncating to BF16. In W4A16(a operand dtype is BF16) kernel calculation:

1. Scale (FP8) needs to be upcast to BF16 to multiply with BF16 weight (from `gl.fp4_to_fp`) for dequantization
2. CDNA3 does not support BF16 multiplication, so BF16 weight has to be upcast back to FP32 for computation
3. The repeated FP32 <-> BF16 conversions cause significant performance overhead

## Change

Add FP4 -> FP32 upcast support to ttg::Fp4ToFpOp, eliminating redundant type conversions and improving kernel performance on AMD CDNA3.

title: Extend AxisInfo analysis to support DenseElementsAttr
body:
AxisInfo analysis for arith.constant previously handled IntegerAttr, BoolAttr, and SplatElementsAttr, but it did not support DenseElementsAttr.

This caused incomplete analysis for constants represented as dense element attributes, potentially affecting downstream optimizations or transformations that rely on accurate AxisInfo.

This patch adds support for DenseElementsAttr, ensuring that AxisInfo can now correctly interpret both single-value constants and dense constants. This resolves the TODO in AxisInfo.cpp and improves the robustness of the analysis without changing the behavior for existing attribute types.

By handling dense constants, future passes and analyses can rely on more complete information, reducing the risk of incorrect assumptions or missed optimizations.
This resolves the TODO in AxisInfo.cpp.

title: [AMD/HIP] Add 29 missing libdevice functions with direct OCML mappings
body:
I'm a contributor to FlagGems (open-source GPU kernel library built on OpenAI Triton) and hit this gap when porting operators to ROCm. This PR addresses the root cause systematically.

## What does this PR do?

Adds 29 math functions to `third_party/amd/language/hip/libdevice.py` that were available in the CUDA libdevice but missing from the HIP backend. Each function maps directly to an existing `__ocml_*` function in AMD's OCML math library.

Closes #10375
## Motivation

The HIP libdevice exposes only 57/198 functions compared to CUDA, causing:
- Silent failures for cross-platform Triton kernels
- Users needing manual `IS_HIP` workarounds (see #7135 for `round`)
- FlagGems and other op libraries hitting missing functions when targeting ROCm

## Changes

**File modified:** `third_party/amd/language/hip/libdevice.py`

Added 29 functions across 4 categories:

**Transcendental / special math** — `cbrt`, `rcbrt`, `exp10`, `erfcinv`, `tgamma`, `logb`, `sinpi`, `cospi`

**Statistics / probability** — `normcdf`, `normcdfinv`

**Geometry** — `norm3d`, `rnorm3d`, `norm4d`, `rnorm4d`, `rhypot`

**Arithmetic** — `remainder`, `fdim`, `scalbn`, `llround`, `jn`, `yn`

title: Support computation pipelining after SWP refactoring
body:
With the recent SWP refactoring, it is much easier to support arbitrary stage assignments where computations can be separated into different stages. Computation pipelining is basically splitting computations to different stages. Take flash attention as an example:
Currently the two loads are in stage 0 (S0), all other ops are in the last stage (stage 2). The loop body will look like
MMA0(i)
Softmax(i)
MUL(i)
MMA1(i)
LoadV(i+2)
LoadK(i+2)

This patch defines two different pipeline schedule for attention-like kernels:
1> putting first dot in S2, other computations in S3, loadK in stage 0, loadV in stage 1
MMA0(i+1)    
Softmax(i)
MUL(i)
MMA1(i)
loadK(i+3) 
loadV(i+2)
2> putting second dot in S3, other computations in S2, loadK in stage 0, loadV in stage 1
MMA0(i+1)      
MMA1(i)       
Softmax(i+1)   
MUL(i+1)           
loadK(i+3)       
loadV(i+2)

Preliminary performance number on H100 for flash attention:
  (Batch, Heads, SeqLen, Dhead)    triton_tutorial_flash_v2_opt-tflops    triton_tutorial_flash_v2_tma-tflops    triton_tutorial_flash_v2-tflops
--------------------------  --------------------------------  --------------------------------  ----------------------------
             (8, 16, 8192, 128)                                517.528                                504.565                            481.402

The implementation and the frontend is preliminary for discussion.

title: Implementation of Computation Pipelining
body:
Summary:
The idea of computation pipelining comes from FA3 paper. The goal is to divide computation ops into stages and to overlap ops that use cuda core with ops that use tensor core.

Use flash attention with num_stages=3 as an example, currently the two loads are in stage 0 (S0), all other ops are in the last stage (stage 2). The loop body will look like
S2(i)      S2(i+1) S2(i+2)
S0(i+2) S0(i+3) S0(i+4)
With computation pipelining enabled, we can put the load for the first dot in S0, the load for the second dot in S1, the first dot in S2, and the rest in S3. The loop body will look like
S2(i+1) S2(i+2) S2(i+3)
S3(i)     S3(i+1) S3(i+2)
S0(i+3) S0(i+4) S0(i+5)
S1(i+2) S1(i+3) S1(i+4)

Note that the distance between the load and the corresponding usage stays the same (i.e 2 stages from the load of k in S0(i+3) to the use in S2(i+3), 2 stages from the load of v in S1(i+2) to the use in S3(i+2)), number of buffers stays at 3. The live range for output of S2 is increased to span the loop (i.e from S2(i+1) to S3(i+1)).

Details:
SWP_FIRST_DOT: move first dot in numStages - 2 instead of numStages - 1
--> for this to work, we need to support predicate on barrier_wait or use PEEL_EPILOGUE
LOAD_DIFFERENT_STAGE: put two loads in two different stages
FIRST_USE_OF_LOAD: only consider the first use of each load, for example load of k is used by the first dot and indirectly used by the 2nd dot, but we should only consider the use by the first dot to calculate the use distance.

For both createAsyncCopy and createTMAAsyncCopy, update TMAUserToWait so there will be an extra dependency from the view of the load to the barrier_wait op:
TMAUserToWait[viewLoad] = waitOp; // viewLoad will depend on barrierWait
In scheduleDependencies, waitOp will be added to the same stage/cluster as viewLoad.

LOAD_DIFFERENT_STAGE=1 FIRST_LOAD_OF_USE=1 SWP_FIRST_DOT=1 together with a TMA variant of FA (https://github.com/pytorch/benchmark/pull/2379) seems to improve performance for headDim 128 and 256.

This implementation is kind of specific to flash attention, and needs rework. We can make it more general by adding a dependency analyzer that analyzes dependency and resource usages of ttgir ops, decides how to break ops into stages, and feeds the decisions to SWP. Another less general option is to only support num_computation_stage being 2 (i.e separate computation ops into two stages). In this restricted form, lifting the first dot into its own stage seems reasonable.

Open to discussions and reworks.

title: [NVIDIA] Lower warp-specialization barriers with NVVM
body:
## Summary

Use the NVVM dialect for the remaining NVIDIA non-mbarrier barrier path instead of manually constructing an LLVM intrinsic call.

Warp-specialization switch loops currently emit `llvm.nvvm.barrier.cta.sync.all` by name. Emitting `nvvm.barrier` keeps the target operation represented in MLIR, uses the dialect verifier, and delegates LLVM intrinsic selection to NVVM translation.

CTA barriers, warp barriers, and cluster arrive/wait barriers elsewhere already use NVVM dialect operations. This change makes the warp-specialization all-participant named barriers consistent with them.

At Triton's pinned LLVM revision, `nvvm.barrier` translates to the same `llvm.nvvm.barrier.cta.sync.all` intrinsic and NVPTX backend instruction, so the emitted `bar.sync` semantics are unchanged.

title: [AMD][Draft] Implement implicit layout conversion for DotOp to enable direct GMEM to reg loads
body:
### Related RFC
[RFC][AMD] Optimizations for Paged Attention: Proposal with Multiple Features(https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/issues/8281)

### [Feature 2] Implicit Layout Conversion
**Problem**  
We found that partitioning the `seq_len` dimension of matrix K and the `head_dim` dimension of matrix V across different wavefronts yields significant benefits (because loading matrices K and V does not require shared memory).  
However, the AMD backend pass of the Triton compiler **does not support directly loading data from global memory into registers and completing a `DotOp` with `DotOperandEncodingAttr`.** Instead, it requires an intermediate transfer through shared memory using `ConvertLayoutOp`.  
The goal of implicit layout conversion is to **directly load data in a layout that matches matrix multiplication requirements,** eliminating unnecessary conversions.  

**Core Process**  
1. Traverse operations until a `DotOp` is matched.  
2. For both operands of the `DotOp`, trace backward until a `LoadOp` is matched, and determine whether implicit layout conversion is feasible based on the types of operations along the path (essentially, implicit conversion cannot be applied if data copying occurs).  
   - For `ConvertLayoutOp` and `LocalLoadOp`-like operations, check whether data copying occurs. If so, implicit conversion is not allowed.  
   - For other operations, currently only `TransOp`, `ReshapeOp`, `LoadOp`, and `ElementwiseOp` are supported.  
3. Extract the innermost vectorization size (`vecSize`) from the `LayoutAttr` of the matched `LoadOp`, and update the `kWidth` in the `LayoutAttr` of the `DotOp` operands.  
   - Certain constraints must be applied to the value of `vecSize`.  
4. Back-propagate the updated `LayoutAttr` from the `DotOp` operands to all operations along the path to the `LoadOp`.  
5. Forward-propagate the updated `LayoutAttr` to all subsequent operations.  
   - If `ConvertLayoutOp` exists, remove it (Step 4 ensures that all operations along the path have consistent layouts).  
   - Insert `ConvertLayoutOp` before and after each operation to ensure legality; these will be removed later by `RemoveLayoutConversions`.

title: docs: add FP4 rhs_k_pack constraint for sm120 in dot_scaled
body:
## Summary

Add documentation for `rhs_k_pack` parameter in `dot_scaled` to clarify the FP4 constraint on sm120 architecture.

## Details

As reported in #9678 and confirmed by @masahi, FP4 formats (e2m1, used by MXFP4/NVFP4) require `rhs_k_pack=True` (the default) on sm120 (Blackwell desktop GPUs like GB202/GB203). Using `rhs_k_pack=False` with FP4 inputs on sm120 causes a compilation assertion failure in `MMAv2.cpp`:

```
Assertion `repA[2] == repB[1]' failed.
```

On sm100 (data-center Blackwell GPUs like GB100/GB200), `rhs_k_pack=False` is supported for FP4.

This information was not documented, leading to confusing compilation errors for users on sm120 hardware.

Closes #9678

title: [Backend] Recognise reversed mul operands in CombineBroadcastMulReducePattern
body:
CombineBroadcastMulReducePattern folds a broadcast-mul-reduce form into `tt.dot`. After #10545 generalized this combine, the pattern no longer requires explicit `tt.expand_dims` ops: it identifies dot-like operands from broadcasted shapes such as `(M, K, 1) -> (M, K, N)` and `(1, K, N) -> (M, K, N)`.

Since `arith.mulf` is commutative, the two broadcast operands may appear in either order. However, the matcher still assumed that mul operand 0 was the axis-2 broadcast and mul operand 1 was the axis-0 broadcast.

For example, this order is matched:

```mlir
%lhs_b = tt.broadcast %lhs : tensor<32x16x1xf32> -> tensor<32x16x32xf32>
%rhs_b = tt.broadcast %rhs : tensor<1x16x32xf32> -> tensor<32x16x32xf32>
%mul = arith.mulf %lhs_b, %rhs_b : tensor<32x16x32xf32>
%out = "tt.reduce"(%mul) <{axis = 1 : i32}> ...
```

But the equivalent reversed order is missed:

```mlir
%mul = arith.mulf %rhs_b, %lhs_b : tensor<32x16x32xf32>
```

This patch identifies the dot operands from the broadcast axes instead of from the `arith.mulf` operand order. The axis-2 source is still used as the `tt.dot` lhs and the axis-0 source as rhs, so both multiplication orders produce the same `tt.dot`.

This is similar to #10734 in that it removes an unnecessary ordering assumption when matching operands of a commutative operation.

Added 1 lit test in `test/Triton/combine.mlir`, covering the swapped `arith.mulf` operand order in the generalized broadcast-reduce dot combine pattern.

title: [Testing] do_bench: add fixed iteration count option for distributed workloads
body:
Fixes #9683

## Problem

`do_bench` computes `n_warmup` and `n_repeat` by dividing a target duration (e.g. warmup=25ms) by a per-rank timing estimate. In distributed workloads that use collectives such as `all_reduce` or `all_gather`, this produces different iteration counts across ranks due to small timing differences. The rank with more iterations calls the collective one extra time with no matching call on the other side, causing a hang or crash.

## Solution

Add optional `n_warmup` and `n_repeat` parameters so callers can pin the iteration counts directly. When both are provided, the estimation phase is skipped entirely, guaranteeing that every rank executes `fn` the same number of times.

The new parameters default to `None`, preserving the existing time-based behavior for all current callers.

## Example Usage
```python
triton.testing.do_bench(fn, n_warmup=10, n_repeat=50)
```

title: add bailout for estimation and benchmarking in autotuning
body:
Add `bailout_in_estimation/benchmarking` as optional params to `prune_configs_by`

A common pattern for myself is to autotune over a large search space before dialing
in on a subset of that search space for subsequent runs. Usually like:

```
@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config(
            {
                 "BLOCK_SIZE_M": block_size_m,
                 ...
            },
            ...,
         )
         for block_size_m in [16, 32, 64, 128, 256]
         ...
    ],
    ...
)
@triton.jit
def kernel(...):
    ...
```

This large search space usually has a couple bad and very bad choices, sometimes
10x, 100x, or 1000x slower than the best choice. I think it would be useful to be able
to tell the autotuner "if the first run of choice X is Y times slower than the fastest choice
so far, then stop benchmarking".

I think this is most valuable for folks who reserve hardware from cloud providers, as it reduces
the time spent using that hardware to benchmark choices that are really bad so it costs less overall.

I followed the format of `prune_configs_by` that already exists, so the usage would be like:

```
@triton.autotune(
    configs=[...],
    prune_configs_by={
        "bailout_in_estimation": lambda best_timing: lambda: num_iters, this_iter, timings = ...,
        "bailout_in_benchmarking": lambda best_timing: lambda: num_iters, this_iter, timings = ...,
    },
    ...
)
@triton.jit
def kernel(...):
    ...
```

This way the user can define the criteria for which they would like to bailout, depending on
the best timing seen so far across all configs, as well as where in `do_bench` the bailout is (
I thought it made sense in this way, since we maybe want to be more forgiving early on and
less forgiving as we progress through the benchmarking).

This gave me some nice overall reduction in autotuning cost, for the tutorial matmul on two shapes
~50% less time was spent in benchmarking for a search space of ~750 configs. The performance
seemed to be similar enough given noise:

```
with prune_configs_by={
    "bailout_in_estimation": lambda best: lambda num_iters, this_iter, timings: min(
        timings
    )
    > ((max(num_iters - this_iter, 1.5)) * best),
    "bailout_in_benchmarking": lambda best: lambda num_iters,
    this_iter,
    timings: min(timings)
    > ((max(1.5 - ((this_iter / num_iters) * 0.5), 1.1)) * best),
},

matmul-performance-fp16:
        M       N       K      cuBLAS      Triton
0  1024.0  1024.0  1024.0  171.196087  197.379013
1  1152.0  1152.0  1152.0  201.161024  223.773981
```

```
no bailout

matmul-performance-fp16:
         M       N       K      cuBLAS      Triton
0   1024.0  1024.0  1024.0  170.760470  199.136092
1   1152.0  1152.0  1152.0  195.401817  229.140257
```

There is some additional time saved, since if we bailout we don't synchronize on the remaining
events and therefore there is some pipelining of those remaining events executing and the next
config being compiled, but I didn't know a good way to measure this directly.

I also think it would be valuable to allow users to skip configs that would definitely fail
with out of resources. For example, if the user knows that increasing block sizes strictly
increases shared memory usage for their kernel then it would make sense that if a certain
config fails with out of resources then any related configs that are strictly increasing of the
already failing block sizes can be skipped. If this pull request is valuable, I can follow up with
this option as a next change.

Thank you for the consideration!

title: [TRITONGPU] Add k_chunks_hint attr to tune RS-WGMMA K-split count
body:
Hello! We noticed a regression in an internal workload which bisected back to 432880797af65f49c5d22d7fe416955d6d839e9b. https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/432880797af65f49c5d22d7fe416955d6d839e9b/lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/Transforms/Pipeliner/WGMMAPipeline.cpp#L314-L317 Upon further testing we found the heuristic introduced in Triton 3.7 can degrade performance v.s. 3.6 for kernels around the register limit, pushing them into spilling. By allowing the user to opt-in to tuning `k_chunks_hint` and choosing the 3.6-like setting (`k_chunks_hint = 1`), we see a ~1.8x speedup in the engineered microbenchmark below. We have confirmed on other adversarial microbenchmarks that 1-5% wins are possible across a range of `k_chunks_hint` settings, to ensure it should be a dial and not a binary setting between the old and new behaviour. This change has a significant blast radius and is a special case for rs-wgmma so feedback is especially welcome on this draft implementation! We figured since `max_num_imprecise_acc` is a Hopper-only special case that it wouldn't be unreasonable to consider including another dial in `tl.dot()` args if the performance improvement was meaningful. We felt that there could be a follow up PR to improve how these optional hint attrs (`max_num_imprecise_acc`/`k_chunks_hint`) are handled (to minimise the number of lines + files that need to be touched), and are looking for input on this. An example is the presence of these optional Hopper features in `AccelerateAMDMatmul.cpp`.
microbenchmark.py (Click to expand) ``` k_chunks_hint=None took 0.6268 ms k_chunks_hint=1 took 0.3463 ms k_chunks_hint=2 took 0.6283 ms k_chunks_hint=4 took 1.2085 ms ``` ```py import torch import triton import triton.language as tl @triton.jit def spilling_matmul_kernel( a_ptr, b_ptr, c_ptr, M, N, K, M_BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr, N_BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr, K_BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr, K_CHUNKS_HINT: tl.constexpr, ): pid = tl.program_id(axis=0) m_off = pid * M_BLOCK_SIZE + tl.arange(0, M_BLOCK_SIZE) n_off = tl.arange(0, N_BLOCK_SIZE) NUM_K_STEPS = K // K_BLOCK_SIZE acc = tl.zeros((M_BLOCK_SIZE, N_BLOCK_SIZE), dtype=tl.float32) for k_index in tl.range(0, NUM_K_STEPS): k_off = k_index * K_BLOCK_SIZE + tl.arange(0, K_BLOCK_SIZE) a = tl.load(a_ptr + m_off[:, None] * K + k_off[None, :]) b = tl.load(b_ptr + k_off[:, None] * N + n_off[None, :]) a_reg = a.to(tl.float32) * 1.337 + 1.234 acc = tl.dot(a_reg.to(tl.bfloat16), b, acc=acc, k_chunks_hint=K_CHUNKS_HINT) tl.store(c_ptr + m_off[:, None] * N + n_off[None, :], acc) if __name__ == "__main__": torch.set_default_device("cuda") M = 16384 N = 256 K = 2048 M_BLOCK_SIZE = 256 N_BLOCK_SIZE = 256 K_BLOCK_SIZE = 64 torch.manual_seed(0) a = torch.randn((M, K), dtype=torch.bfloat16) b = torch.randn((K, N), dtype=torch.bfloat16) c = torch.empty((M, N), dtype=torch.float32) grid = (M // M_BLOCK_SIZE,) for K_CHUNKS_HINT in [None, 1, 2, 4]: def fn(): spilling_matmul_kernel[grid]( a, b, c, M, N, K, M_BLOCK_SIZE, N_BLOCK_SIZE, K_BLOCK_SIZE, K_CHUNKS_HINT, num_warps=4, num_stages=2, ) ms = triton.testing.do_bench(fn) print(f"k_chunks_hint={K_CHUNKS_HINT} took {ms:.4f} ms") ```

title: [AMD] build AMD CodeGen LLVM @ 9e5edb7ed944
[AMD] Fix partitioned shared and WMMA layouts for CGAs
body:
## Problem

Partitioned shared layouts were composed globally before applying the CGA mapping. This could interleave partition/group bits across CTAs instead of keeping each CTA’s physical partitions local.

Clustered WMMA lowering also derived repetition counts from the full CGA tile, causing block dimensions to produce redundant WMMA instructions. Broadcast CGA layouts could additionally make partitioned subslice lowering fail because their layouts are surjective but not square.

## Solution

- Compose partitioned shared layouts within each CTA, then add the CGA mapping.
- Validate that each per-CTA partition extent is divisible by all logical pieces.
- Use a pseudoinverse when recovering partition selection from broadcast layouts.
- Compute WMMA repetitions from the per-CTA layout and shape.
- Add regression tests for padded/swizzled layouts, physical-base rotation, and scaled/unscaled WMMA lowering.

## Testing

- Full Triton rebuild
- Partitioned-layout C++ unit tests
- 16 partition-related lit tests

All tests pass.

> This change was implemented, reviewed, and validated by GPT.

bug causes it to fail with fusion disabled.

title: [AMD] Allow the tagged barrier lowering on RDNA in CU mode
body:
Includes #11910 

## Why

`BarrierOpConversion` lowers `ttg.barrier` to fences carrying
`!mmra <"amdgpu-synchronize-as":...>`. The tag tells the AMDGPU memory legalizer
which address space the barrier has to synchronize, so it emits only the waits
and cache operations that space needs. Measured on gfx1100:

| `!mmra` | release side | acquire side |
|---|---|---|
| *(none)* | `s_waitcnt lgkmcnt(0)` + `s_waitcnt_vscnt null, 0` | `buffer_gl0_inv` |
| `local` | `s_waitcnt lgkmcnt(0)` | *(nothing)* |
| `global` | `s_waitcnt_vscnt null, 0` | `buffer_gl0_inv` |

#9416 extended this from CDNA to every target `>= gfx9`. #10906 restricted it
back to CDNA, because on RDNA it miscompiled PyTorch's split-cumsum tests.

That restriction is stronger than it needs to be. A `local`-tagged acquire fence
emits no `buffer_gl0_inv` at all, so a thread that did not itself execute a
preceding acquire depends on some *other* wave having invalidated the L0 it
reads through. That holds whenever the whole work-group shares a single L0:
always true on CDNA, and true on RDNA too — except in WGP mode, where a
work-group is spread across two CUs with an L0 each. WGP is LLVM's default and
Triton never overrides it, so today every RDNA kernel is in the unsafe case.

CU mode removes that case. This PR adds a `cu_mode` option and re-enables the
lowering on RDNA when it is set. **The default is unchanged** — RDNA still falls
back to the generic lowering, so #10906 stays fixed and no existing kernel
changes behaviour.

## Effect

gfx1151, Inductor's split-cumsum kernel — `exclusive_scan_decoupled_lookback_64`,
the kernel that regressed in #10906. Same build, same kernel:

| | `.amdhsa_workgroup_processor_mode` | `buffer_gl0_inv` | of those, after `s_barrier` |
|---|---|---|---|
| default | 1 (WGP) | 9 | 8 |
| `cu_mode=True` | 0 (CU) | **1** | **0** |

Results match the eager reference over 20 iterations for float32, float64,
int32 and int64 in both configurations.

For completeness, the failure this guards against, on the pre-#10906 lowering:

| codegen | mode | float64 | int64 | int32 | float32 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pre-#10906 | WGP | 30/30 wrong | 30/30 wrong | 30/30 wrong | ok |
| pre-#10906 | CU | ok | ok | ok | ok |
| post-#10906 | WGP | ok | ok | ok | ok |

float32 is unaffected throughout because the 32-bit lookback packs
`(value, flag)` into one word and uses only *relaxed* atomics — there is no
acquire, so no exec-masked invalidate to miss.

## Tests

- `test/Conversion/amd/barrier_op_to_llvm.mlir` — adds `cu-mode=True` RUN lines
  for gfx1100/gfx1200 expecting the tagged lowering, keeping the existing
  default-mode lines as the #10906 regression guard.
The option's own tests (descriptor bit, target feature, launch argument,
conflicting `llvm_fn_attrs`) live in PR 1.

All 124 `test/Conversion/amd` + `test/TritonGPU/amd` lit tests pass.

title: [AMD] Add a cu_mode option to compile for CU wavefront execution mode
body:
## Why

On gfx10+ a work-group is by default spread across both CUs of a work-group
processor (WGP mode). CU mode confines it to a single CU, which changes what a
work-group shares  one vector L0 cache rather than two.

LLVM exposes this as the `+cumode` subtarget feature, but Triton passes an empty
feature string in `make_amdgcn`, so every RDNA kernel is compiled for WGP mode
with no supported way to ask for the alternative.

This PR adds the option. It is **off by default**, so no existing kernel changes
behaviour.

## Interface

`cu_mode` is a `HIPOptions` field, so it works everywhere backend options
already do:

```python
kernel[grid](..., cu_mode=True)
triton.Config({"BLOCK": 64, "cu_mode": True}, num_warps=4)
triton.compile(src, target=target, options={"cu_mode": True})
```

```bash
TRITON_HIP_CU_MODE=1     # sets the default; also cache-invalidating
```

Effect on the kernel descriptor, gfx1151:

```
default        .amdhsa_workgroup_processor_mode 1
cu_mode=True   .amdhsa_workgroup_processor_mode 0
```
## Tests

`third_party/amd/python/test/test_cu_mode.py` (new), 6 tests:

| test | asserts |
|---|---|
| `sets_workgroup_processor_mode` | descriptor flips `1` → `0` |
| `sets_target_feature` | `+cumode` reaches the LLVM IR |
| `rejects_asan` | `cu_mode` + `TRITON_ENABLE_ASAN` raises |
| `rejects_conflicting_target_features` | conflicting `llvm_fn_attrs` raises |
| `as_launch_argument` | works as a kernel launch flag, and the kernel still computes the right answer |
| `is_accepted_by_autotune_config` | survives `triton.Config.all_kwargs()` |

The module skips itself on targets with no WGP/CU distinction — `gfx9` and
`gfx1250` — via a `pytestmark` gate on `gfx10` / `gfx11` / `gfx120x`. Note the
`gfx120` prefix rather than `gfx12`, so `gfx1250` is excluded; this mirrors
`is_hip_rdna4()` in `python/triton/_internal_testing.py`.

Verified on gfx1151: 6/6 run and pass.

Include Triton-to-GPU conversion, interpreter and FPSan support, plus frontend and backend regression coverage.

Validated the standalone op commit on a Brix GB300 devbox:

- Native rebuild and all repository pre-commit checks passed.

title: [CI] Log ConSan performance without baseline checks
body:
Remove the compile and runtime baseline comparisons from the ConSan microbenchmark while keeping compilation totals, lowering-stage times, and median execution time in CI output. This avoids noisy threshold failures while preserving measurements that help identify whether a performance change affects compilation or execution.

Remove the dedicated step's `continue-on-error` and delete the unused baseline file.

title: [RUNTIME] Parallelize autotuner compilation
body:
## Motivation

Triton currently compiles autotuning candidates lazily in the same serial loop that benchmarks them. Compilation can dominate autotune wall time when a kernel has many independent candidate configs.

This refreshes and supersedes #9612 on current `main`, while addressing the outstanding CPU-affinity feedback and preserving the tuning space when speculative parallel compilation fails.

The public benchmark in #9612 reports that an 18-config matmul on AMD gfx1151 improved from 9.44 s to 3.23 s for autotuning (2.92x) and from 7.26 s to 1.98 s for compile-only warmup (3.67x).

## What changes

- Add `TRITON_AUTOTUNING_COMPILE_WORKERS`:
  - `1` (default): retain the existing serial path.
  - `>1`: compile independent configs in a `ThreadPoolExecutor`.
  - `0`: choose `min(4, available_cpus // 2)`, using `os.process_cpu_count()` when available, then `sched_getaffinity(0)`, then `os.cpu_count()`.
- Add `TRITON_AUTOTUNING_OVERLAP_BENCH`:
  - `0` (default): finish all compilation before sequential benchmarking.
  - `1`: benchmark completed configs sequentially while remaining configs compile.
- Parallelize compile-only `Autotuner.warmup()` and retain config/result order.
- Preserve serial autotuning semantics:
  - GPU benchmarks remain sequential.
  - expected failures from speculative compilation are retried through the normal benchmark path rather than removing the candidate;
  - completion order cannot change tie-breaking order;
  - config pre-hooks receive private shallow copies of mutable compile metadata.

The original implementation and benchmark work came from @dixieclick in #9612; the commit retains co-author credit.

## Testing

- `pre-commit run --from-ref origin/main --to-ref HEAD`
- `TRITON_BACKENDS_IN_TREE=1 PYTHONPATH=python python -m pytest -s --tb=short python/test/unit/runtime/test_autotuner.py -k 'parallel_autotuner_default_knobs or parallel_autotuner_auto_workers or parallel_autotuner_rejects_negative_workers or parallel_autotuner_preserves_config_order or parallel_autotuner_compile_pre_hook or parallel_autotuner_warmup_preserves_config_order'`
  - 8 passed

Closes #4806.
Supersedes #9612 and #5436.

title: Emit scheduling DAG as a (bb, position) edge list from translate_to_mir
body:
Replaces the old `dump_sched_dag` path with a scheduling DAG emitted directly from the MIR that `translate_to_mir` already dumps. The old path ran a second, independently-scheduled compilation and printed `-misched-print-dags` text that keyed instructions by register name, which is fragile across virtual-register
  renumbering. The new path appends a per-region edge list after the `SCHEDULING DAG` marker in the MIR dump:

```
  region <bb>
  node <pos> <def-reg|-> <opcode>
  edge <src-pos> <dst-pos> <Type> <latency> [<reg>]
```

Instruction identity is `(bb, position)`, so the MIR dump and the DAG stay correlatable regardless of how vregs are numbered. Data/Anti/Output/Memory/Barrier edges are kept; Artificial/Cluster are dropped.

`DAGBuilder` is a thin wrapper over LLVM's `ScheduleDAGInstrs`. It runs as a `MachineFunctionPass` so `LiveIntervals` is available; that lets `buildSchedGraph` track lane masks and produce **subregister-precise** dependencies that match LLVM's own scheduler (without LI, subregister defs/uses are over-approximated and the DAG gains spurious WAW/WAR edges).

The DAG is currently built by re-parsing the dumped MIR text. A subsequent commit will build it from the live pipeline `MachineFunction` instead, avoiding the re-parse round-trip and reusing the pipeline's `LiveIntervals`.

title: [DNR][WIP][Gluon] Publish and import GPU-created tensor maps
body:
PR description written by Codex

GPU-selected backing allocations need a reusable tensor map for subsequent kernels. Production code adds Gluon `tma.publish_tensor_descriptor` and `tma.load_tensor_descriptor` for Hopper and Blackwell. Publication updates a driver-encoded template's base, dimensions, and strides, preserving its tile and format, and performs a GPU-scope proxy release. Import acquires the map in every consumer CTA. Callers provide kernel ordering and keep storage alive through consumption.

GSan tracks descriptor generations and per-CTA acquisition separately from ordinary memory ordering. It diagnoses missing releases, missing or stale acquires, and imports before the required PDL wait. Stores and successful atomics invalidate prior publication; synchronized warp-specialization and mbarrier handoffs preserve acquisitions within their CTA. Acquisition state starts fresh each launch, and extra mbarrier proxy storage is allocated only for tensor-map kernels. GSan retains up to 64 map addresses per CTA; general CUDA event/graph integration and outstanding asynchronous-access lifetime tracking remain existing limitations. Packed-FP4 payload checks use byte units, and ConSan tracks publication staging.

Tests and documentation cover pointer tables, FP16/padded FP4, strided ranks, clustered execution, native graph replay, and positive/negative proxy protocols including PDL and warp specialization. After rebuilding, GB300 GSan/allocator suites passed 424 tests, with 3 skips and 2 pre-existing expected failures. Both GSan lit suites and pre-commit on all PR files pass. Earlier native/API checks also passed ConSan, IISan, and Compute Sanitizer.

title: [Gluon] Add linear asynchronous bulk loads to shared memory
body:
PR description written by Codex

Gluon currently needs inline PTX for linear global-to-shared bulk copies, hiding their memory dependencies from the compiler and sanitizers. Add `hopper.bulk.async_load(smem, pointer, num_bytes, barrier, pred=True, multicast=False)`, also exported from Blackwell and Rubin, with native IR and `cp.async.bulk` lowering.

Production changes support partitioned and replicated CTA clusters, multicast, and shared layouts validated through their canonical LinearLayout. Copies preserve physical byte order and use full per-CTA capacity strides between source tiles, including partial copies. The byte count is a positive compile-time multiple of 16 within a contiguous destination view; addresses must be 16-byte aligned, with a separate completion barrier in each CTA. Requires SM90+/PTX8.6+. ConSan tracks transaction counts and shared-memory completion, GSan tracks exact predicated source ranges, and IISan checks source alignment.

Other changes add documentation and regression coverage for layouts, partial copies, predication, 2/4-CTA partitioning and replication, multicast destinations, arrival routing, phase reuse, warp-specialized handoff, and sanitizer diagnostics. After rebuilding, all 24 affected compiler tests and 147 focused frontend/GPU/sanitizer cases passed on GB300, including code generation for SM90/100/103. The three GSan ordering cases also passed with line information disabled.

ConSan conservatively covers the entire destination view. GSan records source reads at issue time; its pre-existing gap in tracking asynchronous global-memory lifetime through completion remains unchanged.

title: [PIPELINE] Keep dependent loads after GDC waits
body:
The loop scheduler can place a load before an in-loop `gdc_wait()`, allowing a PDL consumer to read data before its producer has finished writing it.

Treat GDC waits like CTA barriers when deciding whether to pipeline a loop. Loops containing a wait remain unpipelined; waiting before the loop still allows pipelining.

Fixes #11905.

Implemented with Codex assistance.

title: [ConSan] Synchronize allocation poisoning across CTAs
body:
ConSan's poison writes can race with a peer CTA's first access to an allocation. In particular, a two-CTA MMA can access the peer's TMEM before that CTA finishes poisoning it, corrupting the result with NaNs.

- Conservatively synchronize all CTAs after allocation poisoning whenever `numCTAs > 1`, covering both TMEM initialization and shared-memory initialization. Retain the CTA barrier for single-CTA kernels.
- Remove the explicit cluster-barrier workaround from `test_local_indexed_cross_cta_visibility` in `python/test/gluon/test_consan.py`.
- Move the shared-memory async-proxy fence into `initializeAllocation`. Emit it after the barrier, using `shared::cluster` coverage for multi-CTA kernels and `shared::cta` for single-CTA kernels. This orders the acquired poison stores, including peers' stores, before subsequent async accesses. TMEM initialization continues to use its store wait.

Add lit coverage for two- and four-CTA TMEM initialization, multibuffer allocations, single-CTA and disabled-initialization behavior, and shared-memory initialization on NVIDIA and AMD. Check the proxy fence's coverage and placement for single-CTA TMA, multicast TMA, and CLC.

Validation: compiler rebuild and both ConSan lit files passed; targeted GPU tests passed with 99 passed and 20 skipped; `pre-commit run --from-ref origin/main --to-ref HEAD` passed.

title: [WIP] [AMD][BACKEND] Emit packed scaled_upcast layout for dot decomposition
body:
**This is still work in progress**

## Description

`amdgpu.scaled_upcast` requires a layout which has `groupSize` (min 4) elements along `axis` held by a thread. When doing software emulation for scaled_dot we currently emit a blocked layout invalidating this requirement and rely on RemoveLayoutConversation to fix this for us. 
With https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/11760 this no longer reliably works and this PR emits an legal packed initial layout. We also treat it as a layout anchor to avoid invalidating the layouts with RemoveLayoutConversions.

This also allows us to have a proper verifier to ensure the layouts are compatible and we no longer trigger late asserts when lowering to llvm. The other option would be to implement a software path were we lower via unpacked instructions, but it would silently regress performance if we mess up the layouts, especially in Gluon.

## Known issues
This will break if the axis dimension is too small so we do not have enough unique elements along `axis`. This is a latent bug and would trigger an assert in the lowering before this PR (it's now a verifier fail). This will be fixed in a follow up PR.

title: [DNR][runtime] Prepare autotuner configs for caller-managed async warmup
body:
Autotuner.warmup() currently skips config pre-hooks, so configurations that prepare tensor descriptor block shapes cannot be warmed up correctly. Invoke those hooks after pruning, on the calling thread, before each JIT specialization. Clear temporary arguments even if preparation or compilation fails.

This provides a caller-managed alternative to #11847. Existing AsyncCompileMode submits the compiler work concurrently after the JIT has captured each specialization; no worker threads enter the autotuner's preparation path. Ordinary autotuning is unchanged, and this adds no Torch dependency to the runtime.

```python
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor:
    with triton.AsyncCompileMode(executor, ignore_errors=True):
        kernel.warmup(*args, grid=grid, **kwargs)
kernel[grid](*args, **kwargs)
```

The caller owns the executor and concurrency policy. Leaving the context waits for compilation. Failed candidates are retried by ordinary autotuning, with its existing error handling.

**Hook contract:** explicit warmup invokes config pre-hooks and the existing JIT preparation path. It does not invoke autotuner benchmark pre/post hooks, reset tensors, restore tensor values, or undo hook side effects. The example is appropriate for hooks that prepare compile-time metadata. Callers whose hooks depend on benchmark setup or mutate payloads can continue using ordinary autotuning.

### Regression cases

The new tests use real JIT functions, GPU tensors, and compiler futures. The following cases target problems in the reviewed worker autotuner at `e34ed2d5196d60bed9767a5e346fb3d85824864d`; their GPU outcomes have **not** been run locally.

| Test in `python/test/unit/runtime/test_autotuner.py` | Behavior covered |
| --- | --- |
| `test_async_warmup_descriptor_specialization` | Preserves descriptor aliases across positional/keyword arguments. Both assignment and in-place block-shape updates capture independent specializations. A blocked executor delays compilation until after a further descriptor mutation; static assertions and numerical launches check the captured shapes. Requires Hopper or newer. |
| `test_async_warmup_hooks_on_caller` | Config hooks run in config order on the caller, preserving thread-local state. |
| `test_async_warmup_noncopyable_argument` | A valid pointer wrapper whose `__copy__` raises can warm up and execute. |
| `test_async_warmup_current_device` | Warmup populates the selected device's JIT cache, not worker-default device 0. Requires two CUDA devices. |
| `test_async_warmup_failed_candidate` | Warmup returns futures under the caller's async context; an invalid candidate is ignored during precompilation and rejected by normal autotuning while a valid candidate executes. |
| `test_autotune_no_speculative_hook_side_effects` | Separate config-hook and JIT-hook cases check the exact pre/post sequence and numerical output. Ordinary autotuning must not add unpaired hook calls for speculative compilation. |
| `test_autotune_pre_hook_before_heuristic` | A heuristic sees state established by the autotuner pre-hook during normal execution. |
| `test_warmup_pre_hook_failure_clears_args` | A preparation exception releases temporary argument references. CPU-only body; checked directly against both implementations. |
| `test_warmup_prunes_before_config_hooks` | Serial and async warmup prepare only retained configs, skip benchmark hooks, leave the tuning cache empty, and do not launch the kernel. |

Each case can be run independently, for example:

```bash
pytest -s --tb=short python/test/unit/runtime/test_autotuner.py::test_autotune_no_speculative_hook_side_effects
```

When evaluating the same new tests with #11847's runtime, enable its worker path with `TRITON_AUTOTUNING_COMPILE_WORKERS=2 TRITON_AUTOTUNING_OVERLAP_BENCH=0`.

### Standalone comparison

`python/test/microbenchmark/autotuner_compile.py` compares serial warmup, the pinned #11847 autotuner loaded directly from Git, and caller-managed AsyncCompileMode. All three use the same installed compiler/native extension and this checkout's JIT. Each sample uses a fresh subprocess and empty Triton cache, rotating execution order.

It measures total compile-only wall time for an 18-configuration FP16 matmul sweep, including executor setup and waiting. Imports, device/tensor initialization, JIT binder initialization, and sysconfig initialization are excluded consistently. It reports samples, medians, and optional JSON with revision and device information. No kernels are launched, and no performance result is claimed here.

```bash
git fetch origin pull/11847/head:refs/remotes/origin/pr11847
PYTHONPATH=python python python/test/microbenchmark/autotuner_compile.py \
    --workers 4 --repeats 3 --output /tmp/autotuner-compile.json
```

### Validation

- Ruff 0.9.1, YAPF 0.43.0 formatting check, Python AST parsing, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Benchmark `--help` passed.
- Executed the CPU-only hook-failure test body directly against the real runtime: passes here, fails against the pinned #11847 autotuner. The new-runtime check also confirms Torch was not imported.
- GPU pytest cases and performance benchmark **not run**. Triton was **not rebuilt**.

title: [TensorDescriptor] Allow backends to specialize descriptor arguments
body:
`specialize_tensordesc` returns no specialization key for any backend, so a descriptor is the only kernel argument a backend cannot key on, despite carrying a base pointer plus per-dimension shapes and strides.

Mirror what tensors already have (`supports_native_tensor_specialization` and `get_tensor_specialization`) with `supports_native_tensordesc_specialization` and `get_tensordesc_specialization`, same opt-out semantics.

Both in-tree backends inherit the flag as set, so the key stays `None` and the hook is never called. 
It is meant for backends that do need to key on descriptor properties, including ones shipped out of tree as an extension.

title: [Backend] Add a pass to lower gather to local_alloc + local_gather
body:
(I think this idea has been discussed under #8480)

Add a new pass that lowers a non-warp local gather to an immutable `local_alloc` + `local_gather` , replacing the `emitGatherInShared` path in gather lowering.

In the NVIDIA Triton pipelines, the pass is placed between `reduce_data_duplication` (which similarly lower a `convert_layout` into a `local_alloc` + `local_load`) and `reorder_instructions`. The `local_alloc` can be hoisted out of a loop in the `reorder_instructions` pass, and CSE can remove duplicate `local_alloc` s from the same source. 

The AMD triton pipeline does not hoist but runs CSE. In the Gluon pipelines there's neither, making it a direct rewrite. While I expect these optimisations to be profitable in the average case, I think respecting the conventions in those pipelines is probably the safest, in particular Gluon users have the options to write these optimisations explicitly.

Cross-CTA gathers now gets an explicitly error (upstream behaviour is crash). `local_gather` already supports cross-CTA memory access on NVIDIA backend, so supporting this should be possible, but I’m not sure who should be responsible for the synchronisation.

More files are touched than I'd like, but most are just mechanical changes due to having to move the `isCrossCTAGatherScatter` helper to shared utility and removing dead code on the old `emitGatherInShared` path.

title: [AMD] Disable AMDGPU trackers on gfx950
[BACKEND] Support fp8 <=> fp64 casts by going through fp32
body:
## Background
`x.to(tl.float8e4nv)` on an fp64 tensor (and `fp8.to(tl.float64)`) cannot compile on any target: the frontend emits `tt.fp_to_fp` between fp8 and f64, but neither backend lowers it.
- NVIDIA: `getConversionFunc` has no f64 entries and calls `report_fatal_error("Unsupported rounding mode for conversion.")`, which aborts the Python process.
- AMD: `failed to legalize operation 'tt.fp_to_fp'`.

Inductor emits exactly this for `x_fp64.to(torch.float8_e4m3fn)`.

```python
@triton.jit
def kernel(X, Z):
    offs = tl.arange(0, 128)
    tl.store(Z + offs, tl.load(X + offs).to(tl.float8e4nv))   # X: *fp64
```

## Summary
- NVIDIA and AMD `FpToFp` lowerings: an f64 source is truncated to f32 before the f32 -> fp8 conversion, and an fp8 -> f64 cast converts to f32 and extends. Only RTNE is supported for f64 -> fp8, as before for other rounding modes.
- Interpreter: `_convert_float`'s downcast rounded ties away from zero, dropped the carry when rounding overflowed the mantissa (126.24 -> fp8e4nv gave 64 instead of 128) and rounded subnormal results twice. It now rounds the mantissa once to nearest even, carries into the exponent, and keeps NaN as NaN. Two shifts also needed unsigned shift amounts for 64-bit types, so fp8 <=> fp64 works in the interpreter too.

## Tests
- Lit: `tritongpu_to_llvm_hopper.mlir` and `amd/fp_to_fp.mlir` check the f32 step in both directions (fail before, pass after).
- `test_core.py::test_cast`: fp8 <=> float64 added to the fp8 cast matrix.
- `test_core.py::test_cast_fp64_to_fp8_rounding`: a few doubles covering ties, rounding into the next binade and subnormals, compared bitwise with `torch.Tensor.to`; also runs in the interpreter.
- Interpreter downcasts checked exhaustively over all fp16/bf16 inputs and ~1.3M fp32 values against an exact reference for every fp8/fp16/bf16 target (RTNE and RTZ).
- H200 (sm90): the raw kernel and `torch.compile` (fp64 -> fp8e4nv, fp8 -> fp64) compile and match eager bit-for-bit; `test_core.py -k "test_cast or test_convert_float16_to_float32"` 170 passed, `test_conversions.py` 57 passed. A800 (sm80): fp64 <=> fp8e5 cases pass. The CI interpreter suite passes on Linux.

title: [AMD] Swap floating-point values as integers in buffer atomic xchg
body:
## Background
`tl.atomic_xchg` on an fp64 tensor aborts the process on gfx942, gfx950 and gfx1250:

```
LLVM ERROR: Cannot select: t90: f64,ch = AMDGPUISD::BUFFER_ATOMIC_SWAP<(volatile dereferenceable load store (s64) ...
```

```python
@triton.jit
def kernel(X, Y):
    offs = tl.arange(0, 256)
    old = tl.atomic_xchg(Y + offs, tl.load(X + offs))   # X, Y: *fp64
    tl.store(X + offs, old)
```

`ConvertToBufferOps` turns the atomic into `amdg.buffer_atomic_rmw exch`, which lowers to `llvm.amdgcn.raw.ptr.buffer.atomic.swap` on the value type, and the AMDGPU backend has no f64 buffer swap. fp32 swaps, i64 swaps and fp64 add/max compile fine (#11019 fixed the `swap` intrinsic name, not the type).

## Summary
A swap only moves bits, so `BufferEmitter::emitAtomicRMW` now emits the XCHG intrinsic on the same-width integer type and bitcasts around it (fp32 swaps become i32 swaps, which is equivalent).

The new Python test also showed that the interpreter rejects floating-point `atomic_xchg` (`ValueError: Unsupported data type`) even though the GPU path accepts it; `float` and `double` are added to the interpreter's XCHG types.

## Tests
- `test/Conversion/amd/buffer_load_store.mlir`: f64 and f32 `exch` lower to an integer `buffer.atomic.swap` (the f64 case fails before, passes after). All AMD lit tests pass (`test/Conversion/amd`, `test/TritonGPU/amd`: 124).
- `test_core.py::test_tensor_atomic_xchg`: int32/int64/fp32/fp64 tensor exchange, with and without using the returned values. Passes on H200 and in the interpreter (the float cases failed in the interpreter before).
- Compile-only (to hsaco) matrix of `atomic_xchg`/`atomic_add`/`atomic_max` x fp64/fp32/i64/i32 x acq_rel/relaxed on gfx942/gfx950/gfx1250: 6 fp64 xchg aborts before, all 72 compile after.
- I don't have AMD hardware, so the new Python test has not been run on an AMD GPU; CI should cover it.

title: [Backend] Emit `trunc nuw` when transfering extended data
body:
We sometimes transport extended values through smem or warp shuffles, and truncate them back on the other side. Since these are opaque to llvm, it loses the information that the values were in range when they were written, and so it has to emit masking instructions.

By tagging the trunc with nuw (or nsw for amd, as it uses sext), llvm can often optimize the masking away. In a microbenchmark of repeated int16 layout conversions within a warp, this gives in a 4.5% speedup.

title: [AMD] Emit actionable errors when a direct-to-LDS copy cannot be lowered
body:
## Problem

On CDNA, `ttg.async_copy_global_to_local` and `amdg.buffer_load_to_local` lower
to a direct-to-LDS copy only when `canLoadDirectToLDS` succeeds. When it doesn't,
the failure was surfaced in two unhelpful ways:

- `amdg.buffer_load_to_local` is not marked illegal in the AMD ConvertToLLVM
  target, so a failed lowering silently survived the pass and surfaced
  much later, during LLVM-IR translation, as a bare
  `error: LLVM Translation failed for operation: builtin.unrealized_conversion_cast`
  with no hint at the real cause.
- `ttg.async_copy_global_to_local` failed at legalization but only with the
  generic `failed to legalize operation ... marked illegal`, again with no
  explanation.

In both cases the underlying reason is almost always one of two things, neither
of which the diagnostics named:

1. the source pointer/offsets can't be proven aligned to a supported vector
   width, or
2. a predication mask isn't aligned to the vector boundary. Since a direct-to-LDS
   copy transfers each lane's whole vector in one transaction, every
   vector-width group of mask values must be identical.

This is painful to debug, especially the buffer path, where the error appears
far from where the decision was made.

## What changes

Failures are now reported at legalization where the decision happens, with
a message that states the achievable vector width and distinguishes the two
causes, as well as concrete guidance (raise provable alignment with `tl.multiple_of`,
align the mask to the vector width, or peel the ragged remainder into a separate
load). `amdg.buffer_load_to_local` is made illegal in the AMD ConvertToLLVM
target so an unlowerable one fails here instead of continuing IR translation.
The mask vector-alignment requirement is also documented in the Gluon
`buffer_load_to_shared` / `global_load_to_shared` docstrings.

### Notes

Marking `amdg.buffer_load_to_local` illegal means an unlowerable one is now a
hard error at legalization rather than passing through conversion. Three
existing test cases in `buffer_load_to_local_to_llvm.mlir` previously asserted
that behavior (the op surviving on gfx942, where 128-bit direct-to-LDS is
unsupported). They now assert the early, actionable error instead.

## Tests

- Updated `async_ops_to_llvm_errors.mlir`, `async_ops_to_llvm_invalid.mlir`,
  `invalid_async_ops_to_lllvm.mlir`, and `buffer_load_to_local_to_llvm.mlir`.
- Added `direct_to_lds_mask_errors.mlir` covering the mask-alignment cause for
  both ops.
- `test/Conversion/amd` and `test/TritonGPU/amd` pass.

title: [ConSan] Restore scratch checks with masked-store workaround
body:
## Summary

PTXAS can mis-analyze divergent control-flow joins around predicated stores in ConSan-instrumented CUDA programs. Add a temporary CUDA-only workaround that places a CTA barrier after each source masked store.

With the workaround in place, restore the operation-local compiler-scratch instrumentation that was temporarily disabled by #11533. This restores race detection for compiler-owned scratch while retaining the existing explicit-memory and callee-frame checks.

The pass snapshots stores before ConSan creates its helper functions, so sanitizer-internal masked stores are unchanged. The NVIDIA ConSan hook explicitly owns the temporary workaround, making its removal straightforward once the assembler issue is fixed.

## Validation

- ConSan and AMD lit coverage, including restored compiler-scratch checks
- Focused ConSan-enabled and disabled NVIDIA lowering checks
- Reduced CUDA reproducer: the unpatched compiler stalls, while the workaround completes three consecutive runs with only the expected barriers added after predicated stores

title: [NVIDIA] Lower SM90 and SM100 mbarriers with NVVM
body:
## Summary

Triton currently emits most NVIDIA `mbarrier` operations through inline PTX. This hides their synchronization semantics from MLIR and LLVM and duplicates instruction selection already implemented by LLVM's NVPTX backend.

Lower SM90 and SM100 mbarrier operations through the NVVM dialect instead. This covers initialization, invalidation, arrival, expected transaction arrival, parity waits, synthetic cluster barriers, and the mbarrier initialization fence.

## Details

- Use explicit LLVM control flow to preserve predication and spin-wait behavior because the LLVM NVVM intrinsics are not predicated.
- Represent remote barriers with shared-cluster address-space pointers so LLVM selects the `shared::cluster` forms.
- Preserve the current CTA scope for regular barriers and cluster scope for synthetic warp-specialization cluster barriers.
- Preserve relaxed arrival, explicit counts, and parity semantics.
- Keep the SM80 wait and explicit-count arrival inline PTX paths as compatibility fallbacks. The pinned NVPTX backend only selects the corresponding scoped intrinsics on SM90+.
- Keep the SM110+ multicast-arrive path inline because LLVM does not yet model that variant.
- Update PTX expectations for LLVM's canonical `shared` spelling, which is equivalent to `shared::cta`.

At Triton's pinned LLVM revision, the NVPTX TableGen definitions map these intrinsics directly to the same PTX opcodes and qualifiers. LLVM's `mbarrier*.ll` code-generation tests cover the mappings.

## Testing

- `pre-commit run --from-ref origin/main --to-ref HEAD`
- `make`
- `lit -v test/Conversion` (81/81 passed)
- `pytest -s --tb=short python/test/unit/language/test_compile_only.py::test_compile_only_ws_cluster_barrier_shared_memory python/test/unit/language/test_compile_only.py::test_compile_only_dot`
- Lowered the migrated forms through `llc` and assembled them with CUDA 13.3 `ptxas` for SM90 and SM100a.

title: [AMD] Use operand-major LDS layout for FMA dot operands
body:
## Motivation
For dot ops that go through the FMA path, the LDS layout is inherited from the operand's global-load contiguity. When an operand arrives K-contiguous in global memory (for example, if B is trasnposed), the dot ends up reading it from LDS strided, which serializes the ds_loads. FMA dot operands actually want the operand-major dimension (M for A, N for B) contiguous in LDS so those reads coalesce. 

On RDNA4 specifically I tested a few matmuls (with B transposed) in f32 (so FMA path is exercised):

| dtype | trA | trB | G | M | K | N | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|     f32     |     F        |     T        |     2    |     64     |     400    |     400     |        2.1x     |
|     f32     |     F        |     T        |     1    |     100    |     100    |     19200  |        1.1x     |
|     f32     |     F        |     T        |     12  |     384    |     64     |     384     |        1.1x     |
|     f32     |     F        |     T        |     64  |     768    |     64     |     64      |        1.3x     |
|     f32     |     F        |     T        |     1    |     128    |     2048  |     1000    |        1.2x     |
|     f32     |     F        |     T        |     32  |     256    |     128    |     256     |        1.1x     |
|     f32     |     F        |     T        |     1    |     16     |     2048  |     1000    |        1.5x     |
|     f32     |     F        |     T        |     14  |     4200  |     64     |     14      |        1.2x     |
|     f32     |     F        |     T        |     1    |     64     |     2048  |     1000    |        1.5x     |
|     f32     |     F        |     T        |     1    |     32     |     2048  |     1000    |        1.2x     |

Speedup column represents the speed of this PR with respect to main branch, with an average speedup of 33%.

## Implementation
In `getSharedEncIfAllUsersAreDotEnc`, the shared encoding is selected. When the dot operand's parent layout is #blocked (i.e. the FMA path), we override the inherited sharedOrder with the operand-major order before building the shared encoding. MFMA/WMMA operands are untouched, and the flip is only applied for 2D operands.

title: [WarpSpecialization] Fix optimize-partition-warps crashing on unencoded convert_layout
body:
## What

Fixes #11860 — `triton-opt -tritongpu-optimize-partition-warps` segfaults when a warp-specialize partition holds a `convert_layout` feeding a `trans`.

## Root cause

`relayoutWarps` clears every tensor encoding in the partition and reruns the conversion pipeline on it. Mid-flight, the transpose canonicalizer (`CanonicalizeConvertFromTranspose` in `TritonGPURemoveLayoutConversions`) can meet a target-materialized `convert_layout` whose source type has no encoding; `isConvertTrivial` then called `getDialect()` on the null `Attribute` and crashed.

## Fix

Two parts, both in the warp-specialization/convert canonicalization path:

1. `isConvertTrivial` returns false when either encoding is null. An unencoded operand is not a provably-trivial convert; deferring it lets the re-encoding passes assign layouts instead of crashing on them.
2. `relayoutWarps`/`takeIntoFunction` resolve the module from the partition (`partition->getParentOfType<ModuleOp>()`) rather than from the axis-info analysis. In a multi-module input (lit test files are this) the analysis is bound to the implicit top-level wrapper, which carries no `ttg.target`, so the relayout pipeline errored with "module missing target specification" before re-encoding. Single-module behavior is unchanged.

## Test

- New regression in `test/TritonGPU/optimize-partition-warps.mlir`: the #11860 reproducer (partition-local `convert_layout` -> `trans`). Crashes on the unfixed binary, passes now.
- `lit test/`: 302 passed, 2 unsupported, 0 failed (macOS arm64, no GPU).
- Reproducer from the issue verified standalone: crashes before, clean after.

title: [WS] Relayout the convert_layout ops left in a warp partition
body:
Fixes #11860.

`OptimizePartitionWarps::relayoutWarps` clears the tensor encodings of a partition and reruns `convert-triton-to-tritongpu` and `relayout-tritongpu` on it. TTG ops are legal as a whole in that conversion, so a `ttg.convert_layout` already in the partition came out with unencoded types, and the `remove-layout-conversions` that follows dereferenced the null encoding in `isConvertTrivial`.

`relayout-tritongpu` now treats a `convert_layout` without encodings as illegal and forwards its source: both layouts are picked again by the relayout anyway, and the conversion framework materializes a new `convert_layout` where one is still needed.

The lit test is the reproducer from the issue. Checked on an RTX PRO 6000 (sm_120): the 8 `test_matmul.py::test_op` cases that failed in `TritonGPUOptimizePartitionWarps` pass.
