title: [TritonGPU] Skip thread-locality rewrite when the accumulator is read in-loop
body:
## Summary

`TritonGPUOptimizeThreadLocality` miscompiles a reduction accumulator that is also read inside the loop body (#11836). The collector walk in `OptimizeThreadLocality.cpp` gates on the reduce having one use and the update having one use, but never on the accumulator's region block argument. For a loop that reads the accumulator in its body, e.g. storing a snapshot before the update, the rewrite re-homes the accumulator into a thread-local partial under the optimized view and only merges the running value back after the loop, so every in-loop read observes the partial state instead of the running value. The reported symptom follows exactly: snapshots read zero, the final accumulator stays correct.

The fix adds one gate to the collector walk: the accumulator's region iter arg must have exactly one use (the update), otherwise the reduce is skipped.

## Test plan

New negative lit test `in_loop_accumulator_use` in `test/TritonGPU/optimize-locality.mlir`: a loop that stores the accumulator in its body before the update. Without the gate the pass rewrites the loop signature and emits the `efficient_layout` view ops the checks reject; with the gate the loop, the in-loop store, and the original update survive unchanged.

Verification scope, stated honestly: the mechanism above is established by reading the walk and the rewrite on current main, and the reporter's Python reproducer maps to every accepted gate (innermost axis, load operands, one-use reduce, one-use update feeding `scf.yield`, constant init). I did not execute the lit test locally: this checkout has no `triton-opt` build and producing one needs the full in-tree LLVM build, which is disproportionate for a one-line gate; the lit run is left to CI. No GPU was used at any point.

Closes #11836

title: [AMD] Do not stagger CDNA4 padded layouts over rows that do not exist
body:
`composePaddedLayoutForAsyncCopyCDNA4` aborts the compiler for any dot operand whose contiguous row spans more than a warp of vectors. Downstream in [ROCm/rocmlirTriton](https://github.com/ROCm/rocmlirTriton) this took down a whole CI tuning stage on gfx950: a generated GEMM kernel with a 1x2048 f16 A tile died on `PaddedSharedEncodingAttr::verify` with "Broadcasting in offset dimension is not supported".

The function divides `warpSize` by `contigLanes` in two places. Once `contigLanes > warpSize` that quotient truncates to zero and both guards that depend on it stop working. `requiredRows` collapses to zero, so `xWayConflicts` always reports one and the "too few rows to stagger" path never triggers. The `useBestWrap` condition degenerates to `nonContigDim >= 0`, which is always true.

`wrap` is then forced to 16 even for a tile with a single row. Bases are added for rows 1, 2, 4 and 8 that the tile does not have, the resulting linear layout broadcasts in the offset dimension, and the verifier rejects it. In an assertions build that aborts rather than falling back to a layout that would have worked.

This compares both guards scaled by `contigLanes` instead of dividing `warpSize` by it, and additionally requires at least `bestWrap` rows before staggering over that many.

The added lit test is the failing case reduced to a dot whose A operand is a single row of 2048 f16 elements, which is 256 vectors of 8 against a warp size of 64. It aborts `triton-opt` without this change and passes with it. The failing call chain is `PipelinePass` -> `expandLoops` -> `lowerLoops` -> `lowerLoop` -> `getSharedEncIfAllUsersAreDotEnc` -> `composePaddedLayout` -> `composePaddedLayoutForAsyncCopyCDNA4`.

One caveat worth stating: this fixes one of at least two causes behind that same broadcasting error. Across 70 shape and dtype combinations it takes aborts from 8 down to 3, and the 3 that remain reach the symptom through a different arithmetic path.

Reviewed internally at AMD as part of the downstream fix in https://github.com/ROCm/rocmlirTriton/pull/508.

title: [KERNELS] Don't take the TMA scatter path on sm_12x
body:

`has_tma_gather()` is `cuda_capability_geq(10, 0)`, which is also true on consumer Blackwell (12.x), and `matmul.py` uses it for both `has_gather_tma` and `has_scatter_tma`. sm_12x has TMA gather but no scatter (#11344, and `test_tma_scatter` is skipped for `is_sm12x()`), so a matmul with a scatter index and a persistent output failed in ptxas with `Feature '.tile::scatter4' not supported on .target 'sm_120a'`.

title: Gluon warp if upstream
body:
FA kernels can spend time rescaling register accumulators when their runtime scale is exactly one. A block-wide branch cannot skip work independently for warps owning different rows, and elementwise selection does not express the execution boundary needed to avoid that arithmetic. This adds `gl.warp_if` to request warp-level skipping while preserving the result of unconditional block-level evaluation.

```python
@gluon.jit
def rescale(acc, total, alpha):
    return acc * alpha[:, None], total * alpha

acc, total = gl.warp_if(alpha != 1, (acc, total), rescale, args=(alpha,))
```

A warp executes the complete body when any of its conditions is true; otherwise it retains its inputs. The compiler verifies that false-condition elements are identities. Thus layout changes can change the amount of skipped work, but cannot change the logical result. Conditions can describe rows, columns, or individual elements. No warp-varying source scalar or elementwise select is introduced.

The initial verifier accepts f32/f64 rescaling by the scale tested with `scale != 1`, identity returns, register-only broadcasts/expansions, and their supported canonicalized forms. It rejects effects, memory access, collectives, nested control flow, uninlined calls, incompatible layouts, and identities it cannot prove. All-true constant masks have no identity obligation but retain the body/layout restrictions. AMD flush-to-zero mode is rejected.

AMD and NVIDIA share a ballot/branch/phi lowering. The region remains visible through layout inference and GPU scheduling. LLVM may if-convert small bodies; final instruction selection is not an API guarantee. GSan and ConSan compilation are covered. FPSan validates the original body and evaluates it unconditionally before replacing arithmetic with hashes. Proton scopes can surround the operation; scopes inside its body are rejected.

## Performance evidence

The measurements below were collected before rebasing onto upstream `68c8a8107`.
Post-rebase regression checks and an FA correctness smoke test pass; performance
has not been remeasured on the new base.

On one gfx950 GPU, tutorial FA v4, BF16, B=32, H=8, N=8192, D=128, BM=256, BN=64, eight warps:

| Compiler | Unconditional MFMA efficiency | warp_if MFMA efficiency | Gain |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Stock LLVM | 62.10% | 69.91% | +7.81 pp |
| Tutorial scheduler | 71.59% | 84.62% | +13.03 pp |

These are medians of three interleaved ATT captures per variant. The tutorial metric is `4096 / measured main-loop cycles * 100`, accounting for two resident waves per SIMD, over 62 paired iterations. These measurements establish the use case, not a universal performance benefit.

The tuned measurements use the tutorial scheduler and its supporting hook, which are not included in this PR. The clean upstream branch also passes the full-size FA comparison against unconditional rescaling and an independent FP32 reference, with identical register/shared-memory use and no spills. A final clean-branch run measured 10.277 ms with `warp_if` versus 10.991 ms unconditionally, a 6.95% throughput gain (median of seven rounds of 40 prepared launches).

## Validation

- Rebased onto upstream `68c8a8107db2c040d07e0f9fb52fef846bbcc2a6` and rebuilt with Proton enabled.
- 86 focused tests passed: AMD/NVIDIA source compilation, identity/layout/effect rejection, constant masks, f32/f64 GPU execution, NaNs/subnormals/signed zeros, row/column/element masks, multiple results, loop reconvergence, and sanitizer integration.
- Complete Gluon frontend suite: 552 passed, 184 skipped.
- Complete MLIR suite: 302 passed, 2 expected failures.
- C++ suite: 300 passed.
- Proton instrumentation suite excluding the overhead benchmark: 26 passed, 8 skipped.
- `pre-commit run --from-ref origin/main --to-ref HEAD` passed.
- Post-rebase FA BF16 smoke test (B=1, H=1, N=1024, D=128): 12 launches; independent FP32 reference passed.

The performance motivation and hardware validation in this proposal are scoped to AMD gfx950. NVIDIA compilation and MLIR lowering checks provide additional coverage; NVIDIA runtime validation and performance claims are outside this submission's scope.

title: [LAYOUTS] Fix three crashes when a padded shared encoding is asked for a placement map
body:
## Problem

`PaddedSharedEncodingAttr` composes a linear component with a padding rule, so its `toLinearLayout` is fatal, and so is a `partitioned_shared` wrapping it. Three places still ask for that map although none of them needs an element's address:

* `verifyLayoutsAreEqual`, `areLayoutsEquivalent`: are these two encodings the same?
* `getCopyVecBytes`: how many elements can a copy move consecutively?

## Repro

The first two crashes happen during verification, so any pass, or none, is enough. The module below is invalid, the declared result keeps an order the transposed encoding does not have, and the verifier should say so rather than kill the process:

```mlir
#shared = #ttg.padded_shared<[32:+16] {order = [1, 0], shape = [64, 64]}>
module attributes {"ttg.num-ctas" = 1 : i32, "ttg.num-warps" = 4 : i32, "ttg.threads-per-warp" = 32 : i32} {
  tt.func @t() {
    %a = ttg.local_alloc : () -> !ttg.memdesc<64x64xf16, #shared, #ttg.shared_memory, mutable>
    %t = ttg.memdesc_trans %a {order = array<i32: 1, 0>} : !ttg.memdesc<64x64xf16, #shared, #ttg.shared_memory, mutable> -> !ttg.memdesc<64x64xf16, #shared, #ttg.shared_memory, mutable>
    tt.return
  }
}
// LLVM ERROR: padded shared encoding has no linear layout; use paddedLinearLayout instead
```

The third crash is in the pipeliner and needs no invalid IR at all. Take a valid loop that loads into a padded buffer and feeds a dot, run `--tritongpu-assign-latencies` over it, and the process dies. The same happens under AMD's own pipeline passes, and a plain `tl.dot` matmul compiled for gfx1250 already gets padded encodings for its dot operands.

No test in tree hits any of this today: the first two abort under every core pass on main, the third under the pipeliner ones, and none of them with this branch.

## Fix

Ask for the placement map through one helper that has no answer for such an encoding, and compare it as an attribute instead. Following the error message would be wrong here: `paddedLinearLayout` is the layout before padding, and `[32:+8]` and `[32:+16]` on a 64x64 buffer share it while taking 5112 vs 6128 elements, so comparing that would let one allocation replace another with different padding.

`getCopyVecBytes` does need addresses, so it reads the shared side through `toLinearLayoutIgnoringPadding` and caps the run at the padding interval, which is what `AsyncSharedStoreOp::verify` already does. For every other encoding that function is `toLinearLayout`, so nothing else changes.

## Tests

Both aborting encodings, the pipelined load (still pipelined), that padding is part of equivalence, and that the copy vector is capped by the padding interval.

title: [TRITONGPU] Try reusing existing layout rematerialization before hoisting layout conversion
body:
Fixes #11526 

If `getRematerializableSlice` / `getConvertBackwardSlice` returns an empty slice, it doesn't mean we don't have to rewrite it. Consider this case:

```
#blocked = #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [1, 1], threadsPerWarp = [2, 16], warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], order = [1, 0]}>
#mma = #ttg.nvidia_mma<{versionMajor = 2, versionMinor = 0, warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], instrShape = [16, 8]}>
#dot0 = #ttg.dot_op<{opIdx = 0, parent = #mma, kWidth = 2}>
#dot1 = #ttg.dot_op<{opIdx = 1, parent = #mma, kWidth = 2}>
module attributes {"ttg.num-ctas" = 1 : i32, "ttg.num-warps" = 1 : i32, ttg.target = "cuda:89", "ttg.threads-per-warp" = 32 : i32} {
  tt.func public @hoist_dot_operand_existing_remat(%xp: tensor<16x16x!tt.ptr<f32>, #blocked>, %w: tensor<16x16xf32, #dot1>, %acc: tensor<16x16xf32, #mma>) -> tensor<16x16xf32, #mma> {
    %x = tt.load %xp : tensor<16x16x!tt.ptr<f32>, #blocked>
    %hi = tt.elementwise_inline_asm "cvt.rna.tf32.f32 $0, $1;" {constraints = "=r,r", packed_element = 1 : i32, pure = true} %x : tensor<16x16xf32, #blocked> -> tensor<16x16xf32, #blocked>
    %lo = arith.subf %x, %hi : tensor<16x16xf32, #blocked>
    %a0 = ttg.convert_layout %lo : tensor<16x16xf32, #blocked> -> tensor<16x16xf32, #dot0>
    %d0 = tt.dot %a0, %w, %acc, inputPrecision = tf32 : tensor<16x16xf32, #dot0> * tensor<16x16xf32, #dot1> -> tensor<16x16xf32, #mma>
    %a1 = ttg.convert_layout %hi : tensor<16x16xf32, #blocked> -> tensor<16x16xf32, #dot0>
    %d1 = tt.dot %a1, %w, %d0, inputPrecision = tf32 : tensor<16x16xf32, #dot0> * tensor<16x16xf32, #dot1> -> tensor<16x16xf32, #mma>
    tt.return %d1 : tensor<16x16xf32, #mma>
  }
}
```

After the first `ttg.convert_layout` is hoisted, we have the following:

```
tt.func public @hoist_dot_operand_existing_remat(%arg0: tensor<16x16x!tt.ptr<f32>, #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [1, 1], threadsPerWarp = [2, 16], warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], order = [1, 0]}>>, %arg1: tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.dot_op<{opIdx = 1, parent = #ttg.nvidia_mma<{versionMajor = 2, versionMinor = 0, warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], instrShape = [16, 8]}>, kWidth = 2}>>, %arg2: tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.nvidia_mma<{versionMajor = 2, versionMinor = 0, warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], instrShape = [16, 8]}>>) -> tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.nvidia_mma<{versionMajor = 2, versionMinor = 0, warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], instrShape = [16, 8]}>> {
  %0 = tt.load %arg0 : tensor<16x16x!tt.ptr<f32>, #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [1, 1], threadsPerWarp = [2, 16], warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], order = [1, 0]}>>
  %1 = ttg.convert_layout %0 : tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [1, 1], threadsPerWarp = [2, 16], warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], order = [1, 0]}>> -> tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.dot_op<{opIdx = 0, parent = #ttg.nvidia_mma<{versionMajor = 2, versionMinor = 0, warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], instrShape = [16, 8]}>, kWidth = 2}>>
  %2 = tt.elementwise_inline_asm "cvt.rna.tf32.f32 $0, $1;" {constraints = "=r,r", packed_element = 1 : i32, pure = true} %1 : tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.dot_op<{opIdx = 0, parent = #ttg.nvidia_mma<{versionMajor = 2, versionMinor = 0, warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], instrShape = [16, 8]}>, kWidth = 2}>> -> tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.dot_op<{opIdx = 0, parent = #ttg.nvidia_mma<{versionMajor = 2, versionMinor = 0, warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], instrShape = [16, 8]}>, kWidth = 2}>>
  %3 = tt.elementwise_inline_asm "cvt.rna.tf32.f32 $0, $1;" {constraints = "=r,r", packed_element = 1 : i32, pure = true} %0 : tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [1, 1], threadsPerWarp = [2, 16], warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], order = [1, 0]}>> -> tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [1, 1], threadsPerWarp = [2, 16], warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], order = [1, 0]}>>
  %4 = arith.subf %1, %2 : tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.dot_op<{opIdx = 0, parent = #ttg.nvidia_mma<{versionMajor = 2, versionMinor = 0, warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], instrShape = [16, 8]}>, kWidth = 2}>>
  %5 = arith.subf %0, %3 : tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [1, 1], threadsPerWarp = [2, 16], warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], order = [1, 0]}>>
  %6 = tt.dot %4, %arg1, %arg2, inputPrecision = tf32 : tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.dot_op<{opIdx = 0, parent = #ttg.nvidia_mma<{versionMajor = 2, versionMinor = 0, warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], instrShape = [16, 8]}>, kWidth = 2}>> * tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.dot_op<{opIdx = 1, parent = #ttg.nvidia_mma<{versionMajor = 2, versionMinor = 0, warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], instrShape = [16, 8]}>, kWidth = 2}>> -> tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.nvidia_mma<{versionMajor = 2, versionMinor = 0, warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], instrShape = [16, 8]}>>
  %7 = ttg.convert_layout %3 : tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [1, 1], threadsPerWarp = [2, 16], warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], order = [1, 0]}>> -> tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.dot_op<{opIdx = 0, parent = #ttg.nvidia_mma<{versionMajor = 2, versionMinor = 0, warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], instrShape = [16, 8]}>, kWidth = 2}>>
  %8 = tt.dot %7, %arg1, %6, inputPrecision = tf32 : tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.dot_op<{opIdx = 0, parent = #ttg.nvidia_mma<{versionMajor = 2, versionMinor = 0, warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], instrShape = [16, 8]}>, kWidth = 2}>> * tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.dot_op<{opIdx = 1, parent = #ttg.nvidia_mma<{versionMajor = 2, versionMinor = 0, warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], instrShape = [16, 8]}>, kWidth = 2}>> -> tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.nvidia_mma<{versionMajor = 2, versionMinor = 0, warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], instrShape = [16, 8]}>>
  tt.return %8 : tensor<16x16xf32, #ttg.nvidia_mma<{versionMajor = 2, versionMinor = 0, warpsPerCTA = [1, 1], instrShape = [16, 8]}>>
}
```

And then we try to hoist `%7 = ttg.convert_layout %3`. Because the layout of `%7` is already rematerialized from the first hoisting process, we will return false here without rewriting it. However, what we should do here is to eliminate `%7` and `%3` and let `%8` use `%2` instead which is already in `#ttg.dot_op ` layout. I called `rewriteSlice` because when slice is empty, it doesn't do anything but only replace the rematerialized layout, which is exactly what we want.

title: [NVIDIA] Support register-staged WGMMA operands
body:
## Problem

  An s8 or tf32 `tl.dot` whose operands come from TMA descriptors, inside a
  `tl.range(..., warp_specialize=True)` loop, aborts during compilation on SM90:

  ```text
  NVGPUToLLVMPass.cpp: Assertion `supported && "WGMMA type or shape is not supported"' failed.
  ```

  The s8 and tf32 WGMMA forms exist only for untransposed operands, so operand B
  must reach the instruction in a shared layout with `transposed = true`. For
  operand B, `NVMMASharedEncodingAttr::transposed = true` corresponds to
  `transB = false` in WGMMA lowering.

  `AccelerateMatmul` picks exactly that encoding, but the Hopper
  warp-specialization pass rebuilt the buffer encoding in `createBuffer` from the
  producer's register order. This discarded the operand role and left B with a
  layout that WGMMA could not lower.

  ## Fix

  This PR makes three related changes in `third_party/nvidia/hopper/`:

  1. `createBuffer` reuses the encoding of the `LocalAllocOp` that the new buffer
     replaces instead of deriving it again. Since a TMA descriptor cannot describe
     the required transposed layout, the affected channel is staged through
     registers (`descriptor_load` → `local_store`) rather than filled directly by
     TMA.

  2. Consumer groups are split according to how their buffers are actually filled,
     and each group is classified using the operation that performs the fill rather
     than the channel's source operation. Without this split, the register-staged
     channel inherits the TMA channel's completion mechanism and receives neither a
     `ProducerCommit` nor a `ConsumerWait`.

  3. A `fence_async_shared` is emitted in the producer after the staged
     `local_store` and before signalling completion. This publishes the generic
     shared-memory stores to the async proxy used by WGMMA.

  ## Tests

  `test/Hopper/WarpSpecialization/ws_code_partition.mlir` gains two reduced
  pass-level regression cases:

  - one checks that operand B retains its transposed encoding and is staged through
    registers while operand A continues to use TMA;
  - one checks the complete token protocol: token types,
    `local_store` → `fence_async_shared` → `producer_commit`, followed by
    `consumer_wait` before `warp_group_dot`.

  The protocol test fails on the intermediate implementation that passed all
  compile-side checks but still produced incorrect results on hardware.

  Compiler-side validation after rebasing onto `dd34455fcf`:

  - clean build;
  - targeted `ws_code_partition.mlir`: 1 passed;
  - full lit suite: 299 passed, 2 unsupported, 0 failed;
  - compile-only int8 and TF32 configurations retained `ttg.warp_specialize`, the
    expected WGMMA instructions, and the register-staged barrier protocol.

  Runtime validation of the exact rebased diff was performed on an H100 PCIe
  (SM90), with PyTorch 2.8.0+cu128 and CUDA 12.8:

  - 30/30 numerical cases passed without instrumentation;
  - the same 30/30 cases passed under active ConSan with no assertion;
  - `python/test/unit/language/test_warp_specialization.py`: 145 passed,
    1432 skipped, 0 failed.

  The numerical matrix covered int8 shapes 64/32/32 and 128/64/32, as well as the
  four TF32 shapes from #11586. Each shape was tested with 1, 2, 3, 4, and 7 K
  tiles. The 4- and 7-tile cases exercise reuse of the three-stage buffers and
  barrier phase changes.

  Int8 results were compared exactly against an int32 CPU reference. TF32 results
  were compared against cuBLAS with a tolerance.

  The validation used `num_warps=4`, `num_stages=3`, `num_ctas=1`, and a 2×2
  grid. FP8, multi-CTA, H200/SXM, and performance were not tested.

  ## Related work

  #11728 replaces the assertion with a diagnostic for genuinely unsupported WGMMA
  forms. This PR fixes the valid s8/tf32 warp-specialized path. The two changes
  touch different files and do not depend on landing order.

  While extending `processProducerCommitOp`, this PR also replaces the
  `report_fatal_error` for the remaining unimplemented token load types with an
  MLIR diagnostic and propagates the failure through `doTokenLowering`. This is
  separate from #11728, which handles unsupported WGMMA encodings in
  `NVGPUToLLVM`.

  Fixes #11586

title: [Analysis] Mark the recursion path in CallGraph::doWalk's visited set
body:
Fixes #11726.

## What

`CallGraph::doWalk` checked `visited.count(funcOp)` to report "Cycle detected in call graph" but never inserted into the set, so the check could never fire: a cyclic call graph recursed until the stack gave out instead of reporting the cycle. The matching `visited.erase(funcOp)` on exit shows the insert was always intended.

## Fix

One line: `visited.insert(funcOp)` after the check, marking the current recursion path before descending. Path-scoped semantics, so a diamond (a->b->d, a->c->d) is still walked twice without tripping the guard.

## Tests

New `unittest/Analysis/CallGraphTest.cpp` with two cases, registered as `TestTritonCallGraph` in the analysis CMake:

- `cycleIsDetected`: a->b->a asserts the walk dies with "Cycle detected in call graph" (EXPECT_DEATH);
- `diamondIsNotACycle`: a->b->d, a->c->d completes, proving path-scoped insertion does not false-positive on a DAG.

Built and ran locally on this build: both pass; the death test hangs/crashes without the fix.

title: Catch LLVM diagnostic and raise Python exception
body:
This issue is reported in https://github.com/triton-lang/triton-windows/issues/45 and I think it's worth porting to the upstream Triton.

In `translateLLVMIRToASM`, if LLVM emits a diagnostic with severity error, we should catch it and throw a C++ runtime error, then it will be catched in Python subprocess and raised as an exception that downstream Python code can handle.

Notably, Triton 3.7.x pins LLVM `1f126a6dea50d185c0781743a667390037ae88bd`, which calls `exit(1)` if the diagnostic is unhandled. This explains the behavior reproduced in https://github.com/triton-lang/triton-windows/issues/45 . Now LLVM has removed the `exit(1)`, see https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/pull/194858 , but I think we should still fail early in `translateLLVMIRToASM`.

title: [AMD] Compute the HIP pointer-range bit natively
body:
4 commits included, 2 of them reduce `JitFunction` kernel launch overhead, 1 commit add benchmark script, the other commit `[[RUNTIME] Include default options in the JIT cache key](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/11880/changes/fa19c0511023024ad740a73ae90ea03ac1fe1ca6)` is duplicate of https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/11879, which fix a bug and works as requested refactor for `[AMD] Make use_buffer_ops a compilation option`.

The 2 host launch perf optimization are as following:

[AMD] Make use_buffer_ops a compilation option
AMDGCN_USE_BUFFER_OPS was read during lowering and once per tensor
specialization, while compiled results did not record the choice.

Move it to HIPOptions, resolve its environment default before the
in-memory cache lookup, and gate lowering from the parsed option.
Environment changes and per-kernel overrides now select the correct
compiled kernel. Tensor specialization reports S based only on range.

Measured on MI300X/gfx942 with torch 2.14+rocm7.2:

  measurement                              before      after
  specialize one tensor argument         1.545 us   1.257 us
  launch with 1 tensor argument          13.332 us  13.364 us
  launch with 4 tensor arguments         19.455 us  18.774 us
  launch with 8 tensor arguments         27.118 us  25.376 us
  marginal cost per tensor argument      1.974 us   1.716 us

For comparison, PR https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/11399 measured on Windows/gfx1100:

  measurement                              before      after
  specialize one tensor argument          2.98 us    1.24 us
  launch with 1 tensor argument          14.63 us   12.58 us
  launch with 4 tensor arguments         26.96 us   19.32 us
  launch with 8 tensor arguments         43.79 us   26.89 us
  marginal cost per tensor argument      4.17 us*   2.04 us*

* Derived from its one- and eight-tensor launch figures.

[AMD] Compute the HIP pointer-range bit natively
HIP previously called Python for every tensor argument to compute
the S specialization bit.

Add NONE, ALIGN, and RANGE native-specialization modes. RANGE computes
D/S through the stable Torch C ABI when available, falls back to Python
for subclasses and unsupported objects, and discovers torch if it is
imported after Triton initializes. S reflects the underlying storage and
is emitted only up to INT32_MAX.

Per tensor argument on MI300X/gfx942 with torch 2.14+rocm7.2:

  measurement                               before     after
  native_specialize_impl(HIP, tensor)     1256.6 ns  484.1 ns
  native_specialize_impl(CUDA, tensor)     284.7 ns  257.9 ns

End-to-end HIP launch:

  tensor arguments    before      after
  1                  13.364 us  12.356 us
  4                  18.774 us  15.221 us
  8                  25.376 us  18.771 us
  marginal            1.716 us   0.916 us

title: Fix two dead fast paths on the kernel launch path
body:
Two guards intended to skip per-launch work never fired. Measured on MI300X/gfx942 with torch 2.14+rocm7.2.

1. CompiledKernel.launch_metadata() checked whether launch_enter_hook was None, but the knob defaults to an empty HookChain. Add HookChain.__bool__() and test hook chains for emptiness, including load and unload hooks.

2. fpsan_homomorphic_casts was a live env_bool descriptor, so each launch paid for Python calls and an environment scan. Resolve it once, like the adjacent launch-path knobs, and refresh it through refresh_knobs().

  measurement                           before     after
  launch_metadata()                    0.466 us  0.146 us
  fpsan_homomorphic_casts read         0.230 us  0.044 us

The latter matches runtime.debug at 0.043 us.

End-to-end launch time, using four interleaved A/B rounds of the best of 5 x 20000 measurements:

  tensor arguments    before      after       delta
  1                  12.814 us  11.969 us  -0.846 us
  4                  18.994 us  18.087 us  -0.907 us
  8                  26.992 us  26.238 us  -0.754 us

The saving is independent of argument count. Interleaving both cases in one process avoids build-to-build variance at larger argument counts.

Knob assignment and registered hooks continue to work; the existing test_launch.py::test_metadata test covers registered hooks.

title: [RUNTIME] Include default options in the JIT cache key
body:
The in-memory key is built before parse_options(), so defaults read there were invisible to cache lookup. Changing
TRITON_DEFAULT_FP_FUSION could therefore reuse a kernel compiled with the old value.

Add a backend hook that resolves JIT cache-key defaults before lookup. Represent unset backend values as None and resolve them in __post_init__, so direct compilation follows the same default.

body:

16-bit types have no portable C scalar representation, so callers
provide their raw bit patterns. Keep fp64 as double.

The generated launcher now stores each scalar in an object whose width
matches the kernel parameter copied by the driver.

follow the same encoding inference. Keep register-broadcasting tests

Recognize identical non-injective layouts as no-op conversions so these
explicit conversions do not unnecessarily use shared memory.

title: [BACKEND] Support multi-CTA scans
body:
## Summary

- compute scan block counts and strides from the per-CTA shape
- extend `tt.scan` lowering with a cluster-level prefix step when the scan axis is split across CTAs
- publish each CTA's segment aggregate to shared memory, synchronize the cluster, and read predecessor aggregates through distributed shared memory
- preserve non-scan CTA coordinates for mixed CGA layouts and handle forward, reverse, non-commutative, and multi-operand scans
- track scan scratch as cross-CTA memory and gate the lowering on target distributed-shared-memory support

CTAs split only along non-scan dimensions continue to use the CTA-local path. Cross-CTA scans are enabled for NVIDIA targets with cluster support; unsupported targets receive a diagnostic instead of reaching invalid codegen.

## Testing

- `make`
- `lit -v test/Conversion/scan_multi_cta.mlir test/Conversion/scan_multi_cta_invalid.mlir test/Conversion/scan_to_llvm.mlir test/TritonNvidiaGPU/membar-cluster.mlir`
- `pytest -s --tb=short python/test/unit/language/test_core.py::test_scan_multi_cta`

The Hopper correctness test covers 2, 4, and 8 CTAs; both scan axes; forward and reverse scans; and `cumsum`, a non-commutative first-element combiner, and a two-operand linear recurrence. It passes 9/9 cases on an NVIDIA SM90 GPU.

Measured on an NVIDIA SM90 GPU with FP32 `cumsum`, `num_warps=4`, 50 warmup launches, and seven repetitions of 1,000 launches. Values are median kernel-launch latency in microseconds.

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|

| 32x32, axis 1 (CTA split on non-scan axis) | 11.744 | 11.580 | 11.452 | 11.741 |
| 16x1024, axis 0 (cross-CTA) | 11.465 | 11.578 | 11.637 | 11.819 |

title: fix(language): fold constexpr % with runtime truncation semantics
body:
## Summary

`(-5.0) % 3.0` produces a different result depending on whether it is constant-folded (both operands `constexpr`) or evaluated at runtime — the sign of the remainder flips. Reported in #10920.

The `constexpr.__mod__` path folded with Python's built-in `%`, whose remainder takes the sign of the **divisor** (floored division). The runtime lowering in `semantic.py::mod` emits `frem` for floats and `srem` for signed integers, both of which truncate toward zero, so the remainder takes the sign of the **dividend**. For mixed-sign operands the two disagree:

| expression | folded (before) | runtime | folded (after) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `(-5.0) % 3.0` | `1.0` | `-2.0` | `-2.0` |
| `5.0 % (-3.0)` | `-1.0` | `2.0` | `2.0` |
| `(-5) % 3` | `1` | `-2` | `-2` |

## Fix

Fold `constexpr.__mod__` with the runtime semantics instead: `math.fmod` for floats, and a truncated integer remainder (`abs(a) % abs(b)` carrying the sign of the dividend) otherwise. Same-sign and all-positive operands are unchanged.

## Testing

Added `test_constexpr_mod_matches_runtime_truncation` (host-only, no device needed): it asserts the folded results now match `frem`/`srem` for the mixed-sign cases that previously flipped, and that the already-agreeing cases stay put. I verified the folding logic against the `frem`/`srem` sign rule offline; the runtime side is exercised by CI.

Note: `constexpr.__floordiv__` has the same floored-vs-truncated mismatch and could be a follow-up, but I've kept this scoped to the `%` operator reported in the issue.

Fixes #10920.

title: [AMD] isolate LLVM CodeGen dependencies
body:

title: Vendor CUDA CCCL headers (nv/target) alongside cudart in the NVIDIA backend
body:
## Summary

`triton/backends/nvidia/include/` bundles CUDA headers (via `cuda_cudart`) so downstream consumers
can compile against them without a full CUDA toolkit installed. In newer CUDA releases,
`cuda_fp16.h`/`cuda_bf16.h` (both part of `cuda_cudart` and already vendored here) transitively
`#include <nv/target>` -- a CUDA C++ Core Libraries (CCCL) header. CCCL ships as its own separate
redist component (`cuda_cccl`), which this backend never vendors, so any compile against these
bundled headers with no other CUDA include path available fails:

```
fatal error: nv/target: No such file or directory
```

This bites any downstream user of the bundled `triton/backends/nvidia/include/` headers as their
CUDA include path -- for example a host-side C++ compile step (not a Triton-JIT-compiled kernel)
run in an environment with only pip-installed CUDA wheels and no system toolkit, where these
bundled headers are the only CUDA headers available at all.

## Change

Add `cuda_cccl` to the vendored NVIDIA toolchain packages in `get_nvidia_toolchain_packages()`,
following the exact same pattern already used for the other header-only entries (`cudacrt`,
`cudart`):
- `cmake/nvidia-toolchain-version.json`: pin `cccl` to `13.1.78` -- the `cuda_cccl` version paired
  with the currently pinned `cudart` `13.1.80` in NVIDIA's `redistrib_13.1.0.json` manifest.
  Verified the archive exists for both `linux-x86_64` and `linux-sbsa` and contains
  `include/nv/target` at the expected path.
- `python/build_helpers.py`: new `NvidiaToolchainPackage` entry (`component="cuda_cccl"`,
  `src_path="include"`, `dst_path="include"`), plus the matching `BuildHelperArgs` field and CLI
  override flag (`--triton-cccl-path`), mirroring `cudart_path`/`--triton-cudart-path`.
- `CMakeLists.txt`: `TRITON_CCCL_PATH` cache variable + passthrough, mirroring `TRITON_CUDART_PATH`.
- `python/triton/knobs.py`: `TRITON_CCCL_PATH` env knob, added to `build_knobs.backend_dirs`
  alongside `cudacrt_path`/`cudart_path`.

## Test plan

- [x] Verified the `cuda_cccl-linux-{x86_64,sbsa}-13.1.78-archive.tar.xz` archives exist at
      `developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/redist/cuda_cccl/...` and each contains
      `include/nv/target`.
- [ ] Could not run the full native build in my environment to confirm the downloaded headers land
      at `triton/backends/nvidia/include/nv/target` after a build -- the diff is a structural mirror
      of the already-covered `cudart_path` code path in every location it touches
      (`get_nvidia_toolchain_packages()`, `BuildHelperArgs`, CLI arg parsing, CMake cache var
      plumbing, `knobs.py`), so this should follow the same download/copy/knob-override behavior
      that path already exercises. Flagging for maintainer verification via CI.

title: [RUNTIME] Reopen a missing cache read once in CompiledKernel
body:
A cached file can raise `FileNotFoundError` during content read even after its path was returned. `CompiledKernel` now reopens a metadata, IR or binary file once when that read fails. A second failure propagates; permission errors and other I/O errors are not retried.

Successful reads incur no preliminary open/stat. The retry wraps the actual read, replacing the earlier `get_file()` preflight-open approach, which did not cover the reported failure location. This addresses a bounded recovery case from #11512, not a guarantee for persistent absence or arbitrary filesystem visibility delays. Cache cleanup is separate work in #11517.

|---|---|---|
| First read fails for JSON metadata | Constructor raises | Reopen succeeds |
| First read fails for PTX | Constructor raises | Reopen succeeds |
| First read fails for cubin | Constructor raises | Reopen succeeds |
| Persistent ENOENT | Propagates immediately | Propagates after exactly 2 reads |
| EACCES / EIO | Propagate | Propagate after exactly 1 read |
| Real CUDA-targeted compilation, first cubin read fails | Not rerun as an integration control | Compiles successfully after reopening |

title: [KERNELS] Add valid-row counts for non-persistent batched matmul
body:

title: [Tutorial] Fix FP8 attention V descriptor offsets

The FP8 attention path stores V physically as `[Z, H, HEAD_DIM, N_CTX]`, but the tutorial described it as `[HEAD_DIM, Z * H * N_CTX]`. That flattening crosses non-contiguous logical dimensions, so descriptor loads for every batch/head after the first read the wrong values.

title: [PROTON] Release HIP metric buffers before runtime teardown
body:
PR description written by Codex

HIP graph metric buffers can survive until after HIP teardown and abort process exit in `hipFreeHost`, even after `proton.finalize()`. Call `hipInit(0)` before registering Proton's existing shutdown handler, then release the buffers in the SDK tool finalizer after its tracing and PC-sampling buffer flushes. Keep the buffers across ordinary session finalization so captured graphs remain replayable.

The production diff covers ROCprofiler lifecycle handling and a dynamic HIP initialization wrapper. Tests cover single and sequential sessions, replay after finalize, exit without explicit finalize, and profiling started before Torch/HIP initialization. Native Proton passed all 16 focused tests, seven lifecycle probes, and ten repeated early-start cases on MI355X with ROCm 7.2.3 and SDK 1.3.5, using the existing compiler and Torch binaries. Omitting startup HIP initialization reproduces both early-start exit aborts.

title: [RUNTIME] Preserve cache publication when temporary-directory cleanup is busy
body:
## The problem

Two defects in `FileCacheManager` make a compilation fail on filesystems that
delay the visibility of a freshly published cache entry, as reported in #11512.

**Cleanup failure failed a successful publish.**  `put()` writes into a private
per-writer temp directory, atomically `os.replace`s the file to its final name,
and then removes that directory.  That removal shared the put's failure surface,
so a filesystem refusing the leaf `rmdir` with EBUSY failed a compilation whose
real work had already completed.  Worse, the removal used `os.removedirs`, which
keeps walking up after the leaf and prunes the shared cache key directory and its
ancestors whenever they happen to be empty.

**Read-back trusted `exists()`.**  `get_file()` decided whether an entry was
usable with `os.path.exists()`.  An entry can have been published - the
`os.replace` returned - and still not be readable by this process, because the
directory entry or the data has not become visible yet.  Returning the path on
the strength of `exists` alone turns that into a crash where it should have been
a cache miss followed by recomputation.

## The fix

- `put()` now uses `os.rmdir`, so cleanup stays scoped to this writer's own temp
  directory, and treats EBUSY / ENOTEMPTY / ENOENT from it as the pure cleanup
  no-op it is.  The publish is already atomic and durable at that point; every
  other errno still propagates.
- `get_file()` checks the entry by actually opening it, and reports ENOENT and
  EACCES as a miss.  A real permission problem on the directory, or an error
  that is not about this entry, still propagates - the point is to survive a
  missing read-back, not to hide every failure.

## Testing

- `python/test/unit/runtime/test_cache_cleanup_11512.py` (13 cases): EBUSY on
  the post-publish cleanup leaves the published file readable for text, binary
  and `put_group`; repeated cleanup failures do not poison later puts; cleanup
  never escapes the writer's temp dir; genuine write/publish failures still
  raise; and the concurrent same-key publish workload from the issue
  (4 and 8 processes, barrier-aligned) completes with a trustworthy denominator.
  Fault injection is narrow - only the leaf `rmdir` of this writer's own temp
  dir, only once the published file exists, and only once per put.
- `python/test/unit/runtime/test_cache_readback_11512.py` (7 cases): unreadable
  entry is a miss, EACCES is a miss, a genuinely absent entry is still a miss, a
  readable entry is still returned unchanged, and unrelated errno values (EROFS,
  others) still propagate.

All 20 pass on the patched tree.  As a control, the same tests fail on the
unpatched `cache.py`: the cleanup tests fail on the EBUSY assertions and the
readback tests fail with the uncaught error, which is the reported behaviour.

## Performance

No effect on the success path: the cleanup change replaces one `os.removedirs`
with one `os.rmdir`, and `get_file` opens the entry rather than merely stat-ing
it.  Both are in the compile cache path, not in kernel execution.

Related to #11512

title: [RUNTIME] Preserve cache publication when temporary-directory cleanup is busy

**The removal escaped the writer's directory.**  It used `os.removedirs`, which
continues walking up after the leaf and prunes the shared cache key directory and
its ancestors whenever they happen to be empty.

## The fix

Use `os.rmdir` so cleanup stays scoped to this writer's own temp directory, and
treat EBUSY / ENOTEMPTY / ENOENT from it as the pure cleanup no-op it is - the
publish is already atomic and durable at that point.  Any other errno still
propagates, so genuine failures are not swallowed.

## Testing

`python/test/unit/runtime/test_cache_cleanup_11512.py` (13 cases):

- EBUSY on the post-publish cleanup leaves the published file readable, for
  text, binary and `put_group`;
- cleanup stays inside the writer's own temp directory and never touches the
  shared key directory or the cache root;
- repeated cleanup failures do not poison later puts;
- a failed temp write and a failed publish still raise;
- the concurrent same-key publish workload from the issue (4 and 8 processes,
  barrier-aligned) completes, with a trustworthy denominator;
- the semantics callers rely on (distinct keys, cache hits, text/bytes
  round-trip) are unchanged.

Fault injection is narrow by design: only the leaf `rmdir` of this writer's own
temp directory, only once the published file already exists, and only once per
put.  Every other path reaches the real `os.rmdir`.

All 13 pass on the patched tree; on the unpatched tree the EBUSY and
cleanup-scope cases fail, which is the reported behaviour.

The read-back half of #11512 is a separate change.

Related to #11512

title: [KERNELS] Add masked batched matmul for per-expert valid rows
body:
## What this does

Adds a masked batched matmul path to `triton_kernels` for per-expert valid rows.

The batched path in `matmul_ogs` had no way to say "only the first `k` rows of
expert `e` are real".  Callers decoding MoE with a ragged per-expert token count
had to either pad every expert to the maximum row count or split into per-expert
launches.  This adds the mask so one batched launch covers a ragged batch.

## Motivation

Expert batched matmul in decode is dominated by the largest expert.  Padding
every expert to `max(rows)` wastes MMA work proportional to the imbalance, and
per-expert launches lose the batching.  A validity mask keeps a single launch
while making the wasted rows cheap instead of fully computed.

## Correctness

- `python/triton_kernels/tests/test_masked_batched_matmul.py` covers the mask
  contract: fully-valid, partially-valid and fully-masked experts, mask larger
  and smaller than the tile, and rows past the valid count producing no
  contribution.
- 306/306 kernel cases pass on the 3.6.x tree, and the masked path is bit-exact
  against the unmasked reference on every shape tested.

## Performance

Single-card bf16 on 8x NVIDIA L20 (SM89), CUDA-graph replay, `inner=50 x
outer=7` median, measured against the unmasked batched path across 11 shapes x 6
occupancies.  Median speedup over the 11 shapes:

| valid rows | median speedup vs unmasked batched | min | max |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 100% | 1.012x | 0.990x | 1.053x |
| 75% | 1.051x | 0.976x | 1.330x |
| 50% | 1.979x | 1.000x | 2.102x |
| 25% | 2.137x | 1.000x | 3.389x |
| 10% | 2.140x | 0.990x | 3.389x |
| 1% | 2.142x | 1.000x | 3.389x |

The gain rises as the valid-row fraction drops, because that is what removes
empty tiles from the launch; at full occupancy there is nothing to skip and the
result is parity (median 1.012x, worst 0.990x, i.e. noise).  The `M_capacity=128`
shape is 1.000x at every occupancy because at `M_capacity == block_m` there are
no empty tiles to drop at all.  A fully-empty batch is the limiting case: for
`E16·M512·K4096·N4096` it runs 469x faster than the dense launch (0.0058 ms vs
2.6991 ms).

## Testing

- `python/triton_kernels/tests/test_masked_batched_matmul.py`

## Notes on the target branch

Developed and validated against the 3.6.x line, so it is based on
`release/3.6.x`.  On current `main` this code has moved: `matmul_ogs.py` was
merged into `matmul.py` with a reworked batched path, so this is not a
drop-in for `main`.  Happy to port it there if that is preferred.

title: [GPU] Preserve safe layouts for dependent global store/read-back
body:
## The bug

`tritongpu-coalesce` groups memory accesses by shape and order and then gives the
whole group the widest per-thread element count any member reached.  When one
access reads back a pointer another access in the group writes, the two must
agree on which thread owns which element: there is no barrier between them, so a
disagreement is a data race and the result is wrong and run-dependent (#10924).

For the kernel in the issue - an f32 store whose pointer is read back, with an
f16 load sharing the shape and order in the same block - the coalescer produces

```
tt.store %10, %11 : tensor<8x256x!tt.ptr<f32>, #blocked2>   ; sizePerThread [1,4]
%13 = tt.load %12  : tensor<8x256x!tt.ptr<f32>, #blocked1>   ; sizePerThread [1,8]
```

The 128-bit-per-thread limit on vectorized stores is what splits them: the f16
load legitimately reaches 8 elements per thread, the f32 store is clamped to 4,
and the f32 read-back load kept the group's 8.

## The fix

Detect the aliasing load explicitly - a load whose memory access pointer is one a
store in the same group writes - and clamp it to that store's own width instead
of to the group maximum.  Loads that merely share the shape and order keep the
width they are entitled to, since the group is not keyed on memory.

With the fix both ops come out `#blocked2`:

```
tt.store %10, %11 : tensor<8x256x!tt.ptr<f32>, #blocked2>
%13 = tt.load %12  : tensor<8x256x!tt.ptr<f32>, #blocked2>
```

## Testing

Adds a `tritongpu-coalesce` case to `test/TritonGPU/coalesce.mlir` asserting the
store and its read-back share one layout.  The lit suite passes with the new case
(the only failure in the run is a pre-existing test that requires
`TRITON_BUILD_UT=ON`).

## Performance

No regression: an interleaved A/B on a matched binary pair (only
`CoalesceUtils.cpp` differing) gives identical checksums for matmul, softmax and
stream kernels and timings within noise.

Fixes #10924

title: [AMD] Use hardware OCP FP8 upcasts on RDNA4
body:
# New contributor declaration
- [x] I am not making a trivial change, such as fixing a typo in a comment.

- [x] I have written a PR description following these
  [rules](https://cbea.ms/git-commit/#why-not-how).

- [x] I ran pre-commit over the PR diff (`HEAD^..HEAD`); all applicable hooks passed. The workflow-only YAML expansion hook was skipped because this PR does not touch workflow files.

- Select one of the following.
  - [x] I have added tests.
    - `/test` for `lit` tests
    - `/unittest` for C++ tests
    - `/python/test` for end-to-end tests
  - [ ] This PR does not need a test because `FILL THIS IN`.

- Select one of the following.
  - [ ] I have not added any `lit` tests.
  - [x] The `lit` tests I have added follow these [best practices](https://mlir.llvm.org/getting_started/TestingGuide/#filecheck-best-practices),
    including the "tests should be minimal" section. (Usually running Python code
    and using the instructions it generates is not minimal.)

## Problem

RDNA4 implements `v_cvt_pk_f32_fp8` with OCP E4M3FN semantics, but Triton's AMD lowering currently selects hardware paths only for CDNA4 and GFX1250. On gfx1200/gfx1201, OCP E4M3FN upcasts therefore fall back to the much larger software decoder, including in inner loops that upcast FP8 inputs before arithmetic.

Fixes #11497.

## Solution

Enable the packed hardware conversion specifically for `ISAFamily::RDNA4` and use it for all three supported OCP E4M3FN upcasts:

- FP8 -> FP32 uses the packed FP32 result directly.
- FP8 -> FP16 converts the packed FP32 result to FP16.
- FP8 -> BF16 converts the packed FP32 result to BF16. This leg is exact because E4M3 has three mantissa bits while BF16 has seven.

The RDNA4 gate is separate from `hasFnuzFp8HW`: the same opcode has FNUZ semantics on CDNA3, so extending that existing gate would be incorrect. Existing CDNA3, CDNA4, GFX1250, and software fallback behavior is preserved.

### Avoiding the gfx12 e32 assembler mismatch

Using `ROCDL::CvtPkF32Fp8Op` with `wordSel=false` causes the currently pinned AMD LLVM instruction selector to choose the e32 form for the low word. Triton's pinned AMD assembler then rejects the generated gfx12 assembly:

```text
v_cvt_pk_f32_fp8_e32 v[0:1], v0
                         ^ operands are not valid for this GPU or mode
```

The RDNA4 path avoids inline assembly while retaining the standard ROCDL intrinsic. It shifts the packed low word into the high half and invokes both conversions with `wordSel=true`. LLVM consequently selects the accepted e64 form for both conversions:

```text
v_lshlrev_b32_e32 ..., 16, ...
v_cvt_pk_f32_fp8_e64 ..., ... op_sel:[1,0]
v_cvt_pk_f32_fp8_e64 ..., ... op_sel:[1,0]
```

This costs one shift per four FP8 inputs, but keeps the workaround in typed LLVM/ROCDL IR and leaves the existing CDNA3 path unchanged.

## Tests

- Full incremental build completed successfully.
- `lit -sv build/cmake.linux-x86_64-cpython-3.12/test/Conversion/amd`: 50/50 passed.
- Applicable pre-commit hooks passed, including ruff, yapf, clang-format, and mypy.
- Complete f32, f16, and bf16 kernels compiled and assembled with Triton's pinned AMD LLVM for both gfx1200 and gfx1201.
- On an AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201), standalone Triton kernels generated the shift plus e64 sequence above. Exhaustively testing all 256 E4M3FN byte patterns produced:

```text
f32 runtime mismatches:  0/256
f16 runtime mismatches:  0/256
bf16 runtime mismatches: 0/256
```

The existing exhaustive Python upcast test is now enabled for RDNA4. The PyTorch-based test suite was not run locally because this development environment does not have PyTorch installed; the standalone Triton/HIP hardware test covered the same 256 input encodings for all three destination types.

gfx1200 was validated through lowering, complete kernel compilation, and assembly, but not on hardware.

title: [AMD][gfx950][Gluon] Add cd_regclass to mfma and mfma_scaled
body: `gl.amd.cdna3.mfma` and `gl.amd.cdna4.mfma_scaled` take an optional `cd_regclass`: "a" to keep the MFMA accumulator (C and D) in AGPRs, "v" to keep it in VGPRs. It is recorded as `amdg.cd_regclass` on `tt.dot` / `tt.dot_scaled`, and the MFMA lowering wraps each tile's accumulator in an empty inline asm with a tied "=a,0" / "=v,0" constraint, right before the tile's first MFMA and right after its last. This gives a kernel per-call control over the MFMA form without process-wide LLVM options.

title: [TEST] Give test_int_annotation a buffer its store fits in
body: `test_int_annotation` launches `tl.store(X + v, v)` with `v = 3` on a `torch.empty(1)` buffer, so the kernel's only store lands three elements past the end of the allocation. The test just inspects the TTIR for the `extsi`/`extui` and the device lets the write through, so nothing fails today; it showed up when I ran the suite under a bounds-checked interpreter of the TTIR, where this is the one out-of-bounds write in `test_annotations.py`. Four elements cover the fixed `v = 3` for every `width`.

title: [Frontend] Fix integer-to-bool stores
body:
`tl.store` currently narrows integers directly to the byte storage type for boolean pointers, so values such as 256 become false. Cast to the logical element type first, then handle the boolean storage conversion in a single `int1` branch.

This builds on @guoriyue's fix in #11308 and retains the original commit (`4b594ad9fa89c4fb9b1e3bf955bbaa5d928bed0a`) and authorship. Replace the original runtime tests with one frontend FileCheck test requiring `arith.cmpi ne`.

Fixes #9991 closes #11308

### Validation

- All commit hooks passed, including Ruff, YAPF, mypy, and Python syntax checks.
- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` passed.
- Frontend test execution is blocked: the Brix Git checkout endpoint redirects to Microsoft sign-in, so the remote test copy could not be synchronized.

title: [FRONTEND] Fix int-to-bool conversion in tl.store
body:
Fixes #9991 — `tl.sum` over a bool tensor of 256 `True` values stores `False`.

`TritonSemantic.store` rewrites a `pointer_type<int1>` to `pointer_type<int8>` because i1 is stored as a byte, but it does so **before** coercing the value. The following `cast(val, elt_ty)` therefore sees an `int8` destination rather than a boolean one, never reaches the `is_bool` branch that emits `val != 0`, and emits `arith.trunci i32 -> i8`. 256 truncates to 0.

The `load` path already handles this correctly via an `is_bool` flag; the store path lacked the symmetric handling. Float-to-bool stores were already correct.

```
- %1 = arith.trunci %ret : i32 to i8
+ %3 = arith.cmpi ne, %1, %c0_i32 : i32
+ %4 = arith.extui %3 : i1 to i8
```

**Verification** (sm_120). Before: `n=128 -> True`, `n=256 -> False`, `n=512 -> False`. After: all `True`. Integer narrowing is unchanged: `256 -> 0`, `257 -> 1`, `300 -> 44`, `-1 -> -1`, identical before and after.

**Testing.** Three tests added after `test_store_constant`: int-to-bool with values whose low byte is zero, the issue's reduction scenario at sizes 1–512, and 18 guard cases for legitimate narrowing. Without the fix exactly 5 of the 31 new cases fail — the ones with a zero low byte. 501 existing store/cast/load and 740 reduce/sum/bool tests pass, including under `TRITON_INTERPRET=1`.

title: [TRITONGPU] FuseNestedLoops: a use nested in the logue's last op is not a logue output
body:
`createLogueFrom` calls an op result an output of a prologue or epilogue when the logue's last op properly dominates one of its users. `properlyDominates` defaults to `enclosingOpOk = true`, so when that last op has regions (an `scf.if`, an `scf.while`) a user nested inside it counts too, and a value that never leaves the logue is reported as an output. In the epilogue this gives invalid IR: the `then` region of the epilogue `scf.if` yields the value, the `else` region only yields the iter args that feed the outer yield, and the verifier stops the pipeline with

```
error: 'scf.if' op along control flow edge from Operation scf.yield to Operation scf.if: region branch point has 0 operands, but region successor needs 1 inputs
```

It takes little Python to get there, because the pass sinks a prologue value whose only users are in the epilogue:

```python
for i in tl.range(0, n, flatten=True):
    x = i + n
    for j in range(0, n):
        tl.store(out + tid, tl.load(out + tid) + j)
    if flag:  # a runtime value, not 1
        tl.store(out + tid, tl.load(out + tid) + x)
```

This fails with `PassManager::run failed` on the 3.7.1 and 3.8.0 wheels and on `main` 39c755e51 (RTX 4070), and compiles without `flatten=True`. A differential fuzzer found it, in a nest whose epilogue ended in a `while`. It is not #11612: the inner loop is not hoisted here, the logue outputs are wrong.

The change passes `enclosingOpOk = false`. The new lit case is the reduced nest: it does not verify before the change, and all of `fuse-nested-loops.mlir` passes after it. With the change the kernel above compiles and gives the same result with and without `flatten=True`.

title: [BACKEND] Use CUDA 13 ptxas for Hopper
body: Use CUDA 13 ptxas for Hopper and newer while retaining CUDA 12 ptxas below sm_90. title: [NVIDIA] Work around ptxas 13.4 barrier over-arrival on Rubin
body:
ptxas 13.4 miscompiles the ConSan-instrumented two-CTA Gluon attention kernel on SM107. Its divergent-warp path replaces a predicated count-one mbarrier arrival with VOTEU.ALL plus a uniform USYNCS.ARRIVE.TRANS64.ACT0. The uniform predicate preserves whether any lane should arrive, but ACT0 counts every active lane instead of only predicate-true lanes, overflowing the barrier.

This is now established by direct counts, not just a passing binary patch. A native PTX probe initializes a barrier to 128 and queries mbarrier.pending_count after the measured instruction. One unchanged ACT0 cubin contributes 1, 2, 8, 16, 31, and 32 arrivals for those respective runtime lane counts; changing only the count-mode field to A1T0 contributes one in every case. In the untouched attention binary at gluon_attention+0xebf30, CUDA-GDB shows 16 active lanes, P0 false only in lane 0, and the uniform arrival enabled. Single-stepping raises Warp Barrier Arrival Mismatch. In a separate diagnostic run, replacing only the target barrier state with an independently calibrated count-128 state lets the original instruction execute: it changes the pending count from 128 to 112. The one-byte A1T0 control changes it from 128 to 127. The source barrier expects one arrival.

Use O0 only for ConSan on SM107 with ptxas 13.4. The previous lock-election change is fully reverted; it changed code shape rather than fixing the incorrect arrival count. This is an assembler workaround with a possible performance cost for affected instrumented kernels, not a repair of ptxas itself. The assembler must retain the per-thread predicate or compute the count of predicate-true active lanes. A1T0 is appropriate for this single-issuer site, not a generic binary patch. Other targets, versions, and modes retain their existing behavior.

The identical saved PTX fails at O1 and passes at O0 with ptxas 13.4.46 and 13.4.59. Validated all four attention ConSan variants normally and under synccheck (zero errors), 78 compiler-option/instrumentation checks, and 15 barrier/warp-specialization checks (four skipped), including intentional barrier misuse. The corrected compiler emits exactly the baseline PTX and the independently validated O0 cubin. Added tests cover the workaround's target, version, mode, and explicit optimization-disable guards.

[TEST] Ensure private MLIR functions are tested

Previous these cases are not properly tested due to two causes

1. LLVM (e.g., -O1) optimizes these functions as no-op when there's no side effect.
2. Module-level dataflow analysis skips private functions that do not have any callers so we may derive incorrect results. For example, `tmem_store_wait_unknown` should tag these buffers as unknown instead of uninitialized, though they produced the same waiting effects and thus we didn't catch

title: [release/3.8] [TRITONGPU] FuseNestedLoops: preserve empty inner loops when flattening (#11607, #11688)
body:
Cherry-picks of #11607 (4a57ffb21) and its reland #11688 (59c11c8d8) onto `release/3.8.x`, for #11735.

On 3.8.0 a `tl.range(..., flatten=True)` loop whose inner loop has inverted runtime bounds (lower > upper) runs the inner body once per outer iteration instead of never: main's `test_tl_range_fuse_empty_inner_bounds` gives 352 where 337 is expected on the wheel. #11607 keeps the empty inner loop's guard when flattening and #11688 corrects the emptiness test's signedness.

#11607 applies cleanly; #11688 conflicts only in `fuse-nested-loops.mlir`, where the release file lacks other main-only cases, so its lit hunks were merged onto the release file by hand (the new `@speculate_unsigned_inner_bounds` case is included). Built on `release/3.8.x` with the branch's LLVM on an RTX PRO 6000: the 12 cases of the test pass and the lit file passes.

The same test also fails on the 3.7.1 wheel (sm_89, the same 352), so this is long-standing rather than a regression shipped in 3.8.0. An earlier version of this description said the opposite, which was my misreading of my own results table.

Use constrained LLVM fdiv to preserve rounding and select rcp.rn.f32 for 1/x.

title: [BAKCEND] Avoid reading zero TMEM base
body:
TMEM allocations of 512 columns or more always have base offset zero. Use the constant directly instead of loading the allocation result from shared memory, while retaining the barrier that ensures allocation completes. This removes the second shared-memory barrier, which is only needed to protect the loaded result.

The lowering test covers 512- and 576-column allocations. The focused Conversion/nvgpu_to_llvm.mlir lit test passes.

title: [TEST] Fix histogram checks after redux change
body: Update the one-bin histogram FileCheck expectation to match the redux lowering introduced by #11823 while keeping the two-bin case on shuffle/add. #11820 tested against an earlier main revision, so the changes merged without a textual conflict but left current main expecting shuffle/add for both. The conversion LIT now passes on GB200, gfx90a, and gfx942.

title: [MEMBAR][CORRECTNESS] Preserve mbarrier wait progress before notifications
body:
Ensure all participating warps finish a pending mbarrier wait before a write can notify a peer that advances its phase. Omit the extra rendezvous when the mbarrier or write destinations are confined to the same execution region and CTA.

Stacked on #11481.

title: Fix recursion in long elif chains
body:
## Why

PyTorch Inductor-generated kernels can contain hundreds of if/elif arms. Frontend lowering recursively visits each else arm, which can exceed the Python recursion limit before TTIR is produced.

## What changed

- build an iterative CFG for long dynamic elif chains
- preserve the existing scf.if path for ordinary chains and the existing handling of early returns and loop control flow
- add a frontend regression with 200 elif arms

Fixes #1763

## Testing

- `python -m pytest -s --tb=short python/test/unit/language/test_frontend.py`: 71 passed

title: [MEMBAR] Distribute TMA expectations across producer warps
body:
Distribute TMA expectations across producer warps using the same delayed finalization as software arrivals. Fully scalar groups keep their original counts; mixed groups receive compensating arrivals.

Stacked on #11573.

title: [MEMBAR] Refine TMA and mbarrier synchronization
body:
Use access kinds and physical allocation slices to skip redundant synchronization between mbarrier signals, waits, and completed TMA accesses. Retain barriers for payload hazards and storage reuse.

Stacked on #11697.

title: [MEMBAR] Automatic per-warp mbarrier arrival
body:
This PR adds a few things, but it's less scary than the LOC diff suggests:
- It adds warp scope to `ttg.barrier`, lowered through the existing `targetInfo.warpSync`
- It teaches membar about warp barriers and tracks warp synchronization in each execution region
- We add a new flag `per_warp` flag for `arrive` which means that each warp will arrive on its own (not just warp0).
- We provisionally enable `per_warp` for eligible arrivals, then add a pass to finalise the flags and counts.

The pipeline works as follows:
- At `prepareMBarrierArrivals`, before any `bar.sync` is inserted, we set as `per_warp` any arrive that:
   - Uses an initialized barrier allocation with only init, arrive, wait, invalidate and deallocation uses, allowing views and forwarding that preserve the same allocation
- We run membar
- We then run `OptimizeMBarrierArrivalsPass`
  - It first runs `SynchronizationAnalysis`, which removes redundant warp barriers and identifies arrivals with synced warps, whole-region synchronization on every path, and no pending effects. The pass clears their `per_warp` tags.
  - Then `getDistributionScale` computes the least common multiple of `numWarps / gcd(numWarps, count)` over the remaining per-warp arrivals. The pass multiplies all init and arrive counts for that barrier allocation by this scale.


Stacked on #11557.

title: [NVIDIA] Track TMEM thread ownership and publication
body:
Track pending TMEM loads and stores through their completion and publication boundaries. Use physical access geometry and warp ownership to skip barriers between accesses owned by the same warp, while placing completion waits at actual hazards or publication points.

Stacked on #11556.

title: [NVIDIA] Skip barriers between mbarrier signals and waits
body:
Skip redundant CTA barriers between compatible mbarrier signals and waits, including aliased descriptors and nested control flow. Keep the rendezvous required by incrementing async-copy arrivals.

Stacked on #11555.

title: [NVIDIA] Flush pending TMEM accesses before CFG branches
body:
Complete outstanding TMEM loads and stores before CFG branches so incomplete accesses do not cross control-flow edges.

Stacked on #11693.

title: [NVIDIA] Support padded tcgen05.mma layouts
body:
We allow in `tcgen05.mma` layouts where the logical tensor does not cover
the full tile (i.e., part of it is reserved but undefined).

To do this we do several things:

1. Implement `ensureLayoutNot{Larger,Smaller}Than` for TMEM
2. Simplify and generalise TMEM layout creation in `toLinearLayout`
3. Generalise `getReps` to handle these smaller layouts properly
4. Support padded MMAv5 operands (+ tighten the verifier)
5. [minor] Mark Gluon MMAv5 operations as asynchronous. (the flag was not used, but yeah)

title: [GPU] Count small histograms with warp ballots
body:
Add a new ballot-based histogram
```
Generic:
  zero shared bins → atomic increment per input → read bins

Ballot:
  computeWarpHistogram (ballot + popcount) → reduceWarpHistograms → distributeHistogram
``` 

We heuristically choose ballot based on benchmarks for
```
!hasCrossCTAScratch(op) && bins * warps <= 4 && (bins <= 2 || N <= 128)
```

GB300 measurements across 13 configurations showed lower latency as: **4.5–6.2% for two bins** and **1.3–3.9% for four bins**, with no measured regressions.

title: Fix AOT linker algo ID bounds check
body:
## Summary
- Check AOT linker `algo_id` values against the actual function-pointer array length before indexing.
- Reject negative and out-of-range IDs with `TT_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE` instead of relying on `assert`.
- Add a small generated-C regression that runs with `-DNDEBUG` and covers valid IDs plus `-1` and `2` for a two-algo table.

## Root cause
The generated dispatcher compared `algo_id` with `sizeof(kernel_array)`, which is a byte count, and the guard disappeared in release builds. The existing `*_get_num_algos()` helper already used the element-count expression, so the dispatcher now follows that pattern.

## Testing

- `git diff --check -- python/triton/tools/link.py python/test/unit/tools/test_aot.py`
- Standalone generated-C validation compiled and run with `gcc -std=c99 -DNDEBUG`

Not run locally: `PYTHONPATH=python pytest -s --tb=short python/test/unit/tools/test_aot.py::test_linker_rejects_invalid_algo_id` because this checkout does not have `pytest` installed, and the local Triton package import also needs a built `triton._C` extension.

title: [PIPELINE] Account for later-cluster waits in buffer sizing
body:
Fixes #10977.

Completion waits now retain the same later-cluster stage adjustment used for
ordinary load users when the pipeliner determines shared-buffer depth.

`getDefUseStageDiff()` previously applied this adjustment while scanning all
users, but its separate furthest-wait calculation read the wait's raw stage
again. A wait at stage three in a later cluster was therefore treated as stage
three rather than effective stage four.

For the existing regression fixture:

| Operation | Stage | Cluster | Effective stage |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Load | 0 | 2 | 0 |
| Ordinary use | 2 | 0 | 2 |
| Completion wait | 3 | 3 | 4 |

The old calculation allocated three buffers:

```text
max(ordinary use 2, raw wait 3) = 3
```

This permits the following steady-state alias:

```text
cluster 2: producer(I+3) writes buffer (I+3) mod 3
cluster 3: wait(I) still holds buffer I mod 3

(I+3) mod 3 = I mod 3
```

The calculation now uses one effective-stage helper for both passes, producing
four buffers and preventing the producer from reusing the wait's live slice.

The regression updates the existing direct and transitive wait-dependency
fixtures. Restoring the old wait calculation makes both checks fail with three
buffers instead of four.

## Test plan

- `ninja -j1 triton-opt`
- `lit -v test/TritonGPU/pipeline-lower-loop.mlir`
- `pre-commit run --from-ref origin/main --to-ref HEAD`

title: [Docs] Add Neil Dhar to list of maintainers
Preserve source locations for Python 3.13 inspection
body:
Python 3.13 uses precise definition locations when `inspect` retrieves source. Triton's `specialize` and `aggregate` wrappers preserve the original file or class identity but keep a generated location. As a result, `inspect.getsource` can return only a signature fragment for a specialized function or raise `OSError: source code not available` for an aggregate class.

Preserve the original Python function and class definition locations. The adjusted JIT source-location fields stay as they are, and the class location is copied only when the original class provides it.

## Validation

- CPU source-inspection probes reproduced both failures on Python 3.13.15 and passed with this patch. Python 3.12.13 behavior was unchanged.
- The specialization probe preserved generated source, JIT location metadata, and the cache key. The aggregate probes covered module-level and nested classes and preserved observed metadata, hash inputs, and value construction.
- Both affected files at upstream base `38e38e7dc33822d0446e2db4c4024a2bf6929668` match the source used for validation. Downstream Python 3.13 compatibility CI passed the relevant unquarantined checks using the identical source changes.
- Pre-commit passed for the exact base-to-head diff, including Ruff, YAPF, and mypy.

title: [Membar] Schedule thread synchronization with Membar analysis
body: Track thread ordering separately from shared-memory hazards in Membar and place synchronization at the operations that need it. title: Fix register allocation for padded warp groups
body:
## Summary

- Clamp per-partition register allocations to NVVM's minimum of 24 registers.
- Reuse the same minimum for the default warp group.
- Add an end-to-end regression test from warp-group allocation through NVIDIA lowering.

## Problem

`AllocateWarpGroups::padToMaxWarpGroups` pads smaller `ttg.warp_specialize` operations to the largest worker footprint in the module. Those synthetic no-op partitions request 16 registers. The allocator could copy that value into `actualRegisters`, so `ConvertWarpSpecializeToLLVM` generated `nvvm.setmaxregister ... 16`. NVVM only accepts register targets from 24 through 256.

A valid source-level kernel with sequential handoffs using different worker-warp counts can therefore fail during compilation.

## Fix

Clamp each partition estimate to 24 before computing warp-group budgets. This both keeps the lowered `nvvm.setmaxregister` legal and accounts for the padding warp group's real register consumption when distributing the remaining budget to the default warp group.

## Validation

- New allocation-only regression check.
- New allocation-to-NVVM lowering regression check.
- Existing `allocate_warp_groups.mlir` checks in normal and instrumented modes.
- Existing NVIDIA `warp_specialize_to_llvm.mlir` checks.
- Source-level Gluon reproducer compiled to PTX and cubin and launched on B200.
- `pre-commit run --from-ref origin/main --to-ref HEAD`.

body:
Fixes #10743

Adds a section to the Triton Semantics doc clarifying that overlapping tl.store calls to the same address within one program have undefined behavior. The compiler may reorder, fuse, or eliminate overlapping stores, and results may differ across backends.

Includes the recommended pattern: compute the final value with tl.where and store each address only once.

title: [BACKEND] Pass target information to LLVM optimization
body:
We have been investigating performance regressions on the 3.8 release candidate on internal workloads. Many of these regressions relate to LLVM features. During the investigation Codex pointed me to poor cost modeling choices in LLVM that are likely due to selecting a "generic" rather than architecture specific cost model.

This change adds to proper machine target to the LLVM optimize calls to inform the proper cost models.

Full disclosure, we haven't finished testing if this resolves the regressions we are seeing, but we wanted to open it up to initial feedback regardless.

title: [NVIDIA] Work around SM100 ptxas integer abs miscompile
body:
## Summary

- Canonicalize emitted SM100+ PTX integer-abs idioms from `neg.s32` + `max.s32` to `abs.s32`.
- Avoid an optimized ptxas `VIMNMX3` fusion that drops the negated operand and changes `max(abs(x), y)` into `max(x, y)`.
- Add an SM100 regression covering the failure with a live TCGen5 dot and integer neighborhood mask.

Related issue: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/190973

## Root cause

LLVM emits valid PTX equivalent to:

```ptx
neg.s32 neg_x, x;
max.s32 abs_x, x, neg_x;
max.s32 distance, abs_x, abs_y;
```

In the failing kernel, optimized ptxas fuses this into:

```text
VIMNMX3 R167, R8, R8, R167, !PT
```

The negated source has been coalesced with `R8`. On an input spanning `18 ... 0 ... -13` with the other operand equal to 6, cuda-gdb shows the result become `18 ... 7, 6, 6, ...`, leaving 20 mask lanes live instead of 13.

Emitting `abs.s32` prevents the malformed fusion while preserving the original `neg.s32` definition in case it has other uses.

## Reproducers

- Original end-to-end test: [`pytorch-labs/attention-gym::test_natten_masks`](https://github.com/pytorch-labs/attention-gym/blob/main/test/test_natten.py)
- Trimmed Python/Triton kernel: [`repro.py`](https://gist.github.com/drisspg/4ced47465f083119405a28e6a5833872)
- Standalone CUDA Driver API + original 261 KB PTX: [ptxas compiler repro package](https://gist.github.com/drisspg/4ced47465f083119405a28e6a5833872)

The standalone package requires no Python, PyTorch, Triton, or Inductor at runtime. Its optimized cubin has a maximum count error of 819 across 20 rows; compiling the same PTX with ptxas O0 is exact.

## Testing

- `pytest -q python/test/unit/language/test_core.py::test_integer_abs_ptxas_fusion`
  - Before: fails with maximum count error 819.
  - After: passes on GB200.
- `pytest -q test/test_natten.py::test_natten_masks` in `pytorch-labs/attention-gym`
  - Passes all row-major, tiled, and Morton forward, dQ, dK, and dV comparisons with normal optimized ptxas.

<details>
<summary>Investigation details</summary>

- ptxas O0 passes; O1, O2, and O3 fail with byte-identical input PTX.
- Disabling LLVM SLP avoids the forward symptom but originally leaves dQ wrong, showing that SLP only changes the exposing code shape.
- Compute Sanitizer memcheck, initcheck, racecheck, and synccheck remain clean while the reduced kernel is wrong.
- cuda-gdb traces the first wrong value to the malformed `VIMNMX3`; all subsequent predicate, reduction, shared-memory, accumulation, and store operations preserve that value correctly.
- Rewriting only the steady-loop absolute value fixes 12 iterations; rewriting its separately generated epilogue copy fixes the remaining iteration.
- The failure reproduces with ptxas from CUDA 12.8, 13.0, 13.1, and bundled 13.3.

</details>

title: [GSan] Add write_once allocations
body:
This adds a special "write-once" gsan allocation. The rules here are that they can be written exactly once, and read many times after being written. 

This means we only need to track for read-after-write violations, so we can simplify the shadow cell to a single scalar write clock which is 1/6th of the size of a normal shadow cell. This allows us to track byte-granularity while actually using less shadow memory than 4-byte granularity normal allocations.

Also, this allows for a completely wait-free shadow memory access pattern. This means we don't serialize accesses to those address.

title: Preserve NaNs in AMD TF32 matmuls
body:
Keep signaling NaNs from becoming infinities when CDNA3 prepares FP32 inputs for XF32 matrix instructions.

```text
FP32 input bits       main after truncation    this PR
0x7f800001 (NaN)       0x7f800000 (+inf)        NaN
```

XF32 discards the low 13 mantissa bits. If those are a NaN's only payload bits, truncation erases the distinction between NaN and infinity. Quiet the NaNs first with LLVM's canonicalization intrinsic, which becomes one native instruction per value on CDNA3. This preserves NaNs in `tl.dot(..., input_precision="tf32")`, including cast-first mixed matmuls whose FP8 FNUZ conversion produces a low-payload NaN.

Finite values, including subnormals, are unchanged with the default settings. Explicitly enabling `allow_flush_denorm` permits subnormals to become signed zero. Tests cover both operands, both MFMA instruction sizes, NaNs, infinities, signed zero and subnormals.

Independent fix, based on [main](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/tree/main).

## Benchmarks

AMD gfx942, four warps, two stages. Geometric mean of two process medians, five graph/event samples each. Speed = main time / PR time; ⚪ marks ±5%.

| M=N=K | Block tile | Arithmetic / instruction tile | Main µs | PR µs | Speed | Vector registers/thread, main → PR |
| ---: | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 128 | 32 × 32 × 32 | XF32, 16 × 16 | 2.364 | 2.418 | ⚪ **0.978×** | 50 → 53 |
| 128 | 32 × 32 × 32 | XF32, 32 × 32 | 3.142 | 3.338 | 🔴 **0.941×** | 51 → 60 |
| 512 | 32 × 32 × 32 | XF32, 16 × 16 | 5.708 | 5.770 | ⚪ **0.989×** | 50 → 53 |
| 512 | 32 × 32 × 32 | XF32, 32 × 32 | 8.078 | 8.186 | ⚪ **0.987×** | 51 → 60 |
| 2,048 | 32 × 32 × 32 | XF32, 16 × 16 | 132.993 | 137.041 | ⚪ **0.970×** | 50 → 53 |
| 2,048 | 32 × 32 × 32 | XF32, 32 × 32 | 218.772 | 230.788 | 🔴 **0.948×** | 51 → 60 |
| 2,048 | 64 × 64 × 32 | XF32, 16 × 16 | 83.767 | 88.366 | 🔴 **0.948×** | 76 → 70 |
| 2,048 | 64 × 64 × 32 | XF32, 32 × 32 | 91.278 | 93.196 | ⚪ **0.979×** | 70 → 63 |
| 512 | 32 × 32 × 32 | IEEE FP32 control, 16 × 16 | 8.002 | 7.996 | ⚪ **1.001×** | 50 → 50 |

NaN handling still has a cost; the IEEE control stays within **0.1%**. Shared memory is unchanged: 8 KiB for the 32 × 32 × 32 block and 16 KiB for the 64 × 64 × 32 block. No local/spill bytes, global scratch or additional preallocated-launch tensor allocations.

[Raw measurements, special-value cases and the comparison with the previous implementation](https://gist.github.com/roman-openai/377c73de2633ba1f35206bd37d80264a).

| LoC | Added | Removed | Net |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Tests | +38 | -0 | +38 |
| Non-tests | +7 | -0 | +7 |
| All | +45 | -0 | +45 |

- `python/test/unit/language/`, `test/TritonGPU/amd/`: both operands, special values and both MFMA tile sizes.
