title: [frontend] Validate 16-byte stride alignment in make_tensor_descriptor
body:
### Summary (updated)

TMA needs every non-contiguous descriptor stride to be 16-byte aligned. Host `TensorDescriptor` already checks; device `tl.make_tensor_descriptor` did not, so misaligned strides could silence wrong results on device TMA (#10927, tried on sm100).

Example: bf16 `[M, K]`, `K=511` → row stride 1022 B (not ÷16) → broken tiles + wrong `tl.dot`. 

### Fixes

- Compile-time `ValueError` for **static** misaligned strides (matches host message).
- **Dynamic** strides: still a precondition in normal builds; **`TRITON_INSTRUMENTATION_MODE=iisan`** adds device asserts for non-constexpr strides only (Gluon TMA pattern — no always-on / debug-only assert).

summary of how solved:
```
Case                          normal              iisan
static misaligned stride      compile error       compile error
dynamic misaligned stride     no check            device assert
dynamic aligned stride          unchanged           unchanged
```

### checklist
- [x] I am not making a trivial change, such as fixing a typo in a comment.
- [x] I have written a PR description following these [rules](https://cbea.ms/git-commit/#why-not-how).
- [x] I have run `pre-commit run --from-ref origin/main --to-ref HEAD`.
- [x] I have added tests (`/python/test`).
- [x] I have not added any `lit` tests.

Fixes #10927

<details>
<summary>Env — develop & test</summary>

- Triton: this branch on `triton-lang/triton` main + frontend changes in `semantic.py`
- Tests: `python/test/unit/language/test_tensor_descriptor.py` (static compile error, iisan dynamic stride on Hopper+)
- iisan: `TRITON_INSTRUMENTATION_MODE=iisan`, `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` in subprocess tests

</details>

<details>
<summary>Env — where #10927 shows up</summary>

- **Bug:** device-side descriptor + TMA gather/load × `tl.dot`, misaligned leading stride → wrong output (reported on **Blackwell sm100**)
- **Repro shape:** bf16, leading stride not multiple of 16 bytes (e.g. `K=511`)

</details>

<details>
<summary>Driver / API — host vs device</summary>

- **Host** `TensorDescriptor` / `cuTensorMapEncodeTiled`: invalid stride → **`CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE`** (seen with driver **580.159.03**, CUDA **13.0**)
- **Device** `tl.make_tensor_descriptor`: builds tensormap on-device, **does not** call that encode path → **no driver error**, silent miscompute until this PR (compile error or iisan assert)

</details>

title: [Backend] Emit redux for < 32 elements
body: The redux lowering already includes an implementation to support masked reduxes, but notes that this is never profitable. This PR takes a slightly different approach which makes it profitable. Instead of using the member mask, which results in extra reconvergence instructions being generated, we instead use `select` to replace non-participants with the identity element of the reduction. So say there are 16 elements in each group, then we emit two full-warp reduxes with selects to chose which one is active. We also allow lane broadcasting. For some ops, we have `op(x, x) == x` i.e. min, max, and, or. In these cases we can use the redux without masking off any elements in the larger reduction + broadcasting group. Or, for add and xor we can mask the non-leader elements out but still use the redux result. This leads to a slightly complex matrix of possible combinations of broadcasting and multiple-groups, which have been benchmarked to come up with a concise heuristic. The chosen heuristic is conservative and choses only cases where both latency and throughput improved. GB300 results: H100 results:

title: [BACKEND] Broadcast warp-local atomic results with shuffles
body:
Use layout replication masks to broadcast warp-local atomic results through registers on NVIDIA and AMD. Skip shared-memory allocation and result barriers when no cross-warp or cross-CTA communication is needed.

Remove lots of dead code that was not reachable for pre Hopper archs.

title: [Pipeliner] Only add extra buffer for loads that are already pipelined
body:
Problem

A block-scaled FP8 MoE GEMM got 8-10% slower while emitting fewer instructions and using fewer registers. Not worse codegen -- lost overlap.

What the MLIR showed

`getDefUseStageDiff` bumps the use stage when a load's user lands in a later cluster:

    if (*_useCluster > *defCluster)
      _useStage++; // "extra buffer due to unusual execution order"

"Extra" assumes the load is already pipelined, but the bump fires unconditionally. On a load with real `useStage == defStage` it turns `stageDiff` 0 -> 1, and those mean very different things:

- `stageDiff == 0`: not pipelined, `lowerLoads` skips the load
- `stageDiff == 1`: async copy with `numBuffers == 1`

One buffer can't hold a value across an iteration, so no prologue copy is emitted -- the copy is issued, awaited, and consumed in the same iteration. All the cost of `cp.async`, none of the overlap.

Worse, retiring it needs `cp.async.wait_group 0`, whose counter is global: it waits for every copy in flight, including the real multi-buffered prefetch the loop depends on.

Instrumenting the affected loop made it concrete. `a_scale` and `b_scale` are the same kind of load at the same stage/cluster -- only `b_scale`'s user lands in a later cluster:

    A/B:     def s0/c6 -> user mma s2/c3            stageDiff=3 (3 buffers)
    a_scale: def s3/c0 -> user expand_dims s3/c0    stageDiff=0 (registers)
    b_scale: def s3/c0 -> user convert_layout s3/c2 stageDiff=1 (BUMP, 1 buffer)

Result: buffer depths a=3, b=3, b_scale=1, and the in-loop barrier went from `wait_group 2` to `wait_group 0`, draining the 3-deep prefetch on each of the 56 K-iterations.

Fix

One line -- gate the bump on the load actually being pipelined:

    if (*_useCluster > *defCluster && _useStage > defStage)

This restores leaving such loads in registers. It does not make them pipelined -- forcing `numBuffers = max(stageDiff, 2)` was tested and still produces no prologue copy, because buffer count is downstream of the schedule.

Validation

New lit test `@no_async_copy_for_same_stage_later_cluster`: same stage, later cluster -> no `async_copy_global_to_local`.

    test/TritonGPU, without fix: 136/137 (only the new test fails)
    test/TritonGPU, with fix:    137/137

FP8 W8A8 MoE, E=256 top-k=8, hidden=7168, B200 (before = with bug, after = with fix):

    batch  BLOCK_M  before   after
    1024   32       +1.73%   +0.63%
    1536   64       +8.56%   +1.24%
    2048   64       +10.00%  +1.78%
    4096   64       +9.95%   +2.22%
    8192   64       +9.33%   +1.99%
    16384  64       +7.38%   +0.75%

~78-90% recovered. Batch 1024 / BLOCK_M=32 is a control -- it never hit the bump and is unaffected. Output bit-identical, 0 NaN/Inf. A residual ~1-2% at batch >= 2048 remains, unrelated to this defect.

title: [NVIDIA] Fix float64 precise division lowering
body:
`tl.fdiv(x, y, ieee_rounding=True)` fails to compile on NVIDIA when both operands are float64. For example:

```python
@triton.jit
def kernel(X, Y, Z, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    offsets = tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    x = tl.load(X + offsets)  # float64
    y = tl.load(Y + offsets)  # float64
    tl.store(Z + offsets, tl.fdiv(x, y, ieee_rounding=True))
```

With float64 tensors, compilation fails with:

```text
error: intrinsic call returns double but "llvm.nvvm.div.rn.f" actually returns float
error: LLVM Translation failed for operation: llvm.call_intrinsic
RuntimeError: failed to translate module to LLVM IR
```

The lowering of `tt.precise_divf` unconditionally selects `llvm.nvvm.div.rn.f`, which expects float32 operands and returns float32.

Reuse the existing width-aware division lowering for both `arith.divf` and `tt.precise_divf`. Both operations use `llvm.nvvm.div.rn.d` for float64; their existing float32 intrinsic choices remain unchanged.

Adds a lit test checking the float64 intrinsic selection and a Python regression comparing float64 precise division with PyTorch.

title: [GPU] Expose shared gather/scatter index bounds to LLVM
body:
Emit `llvm.assume` for the in-bounds indices required by shared-memory
gathers and scatters. This lets LLVM remove redundant masks from
shared-memory address calculations.

On a GB300 kernel, this removes five dependent `LOP3.LUT` address masks
and lets `ptxas` remove one branch.

title: [AMD] Cap the MFMA instruction shape by the per-warp share of the tile
body:
`chooseMfmaInstruction()` picks the non-K dimension from `min(M, N)` alone. That asks whether the
matrix instruction fits **inside the tile**. It never asks whether it fits the **per-warp share** of
that tile.

A matrix instruction produces `mDim*nDim` outputs on one wavefront. To spread a tile across `W`
warps in M/N the tile has to decompose into at least `W` instruction-sized blocks, i.e.
`d*d <= M*N/W`. When it does not, the surplus is still computed and then discarded.

On gfx90a a `32x64` tile over 4 warps is a 512-output share, while `v_mfma_f32_32x32x8` produces
1024 outputs on a single wavefront. The pass selects `32x32` anyway.

This forwards `numWarps` — **already computed one line above each call site** and simply not passed
on — into the selector, and adds the share test alongside the existing fits-in-tile test.

**The 16x16 rung deliberately keeps the original test.** 16x16 is the smallest square MFMA, so there
is nothing to fall back to: applying the share test there rejects every candidate for a `16x16`,
`16x32` or `32x16` tile on four warps and leaves `mDim = nDim = 0`, dropping the dot off MFMA
silently. The NVIDIA side floors its cap for the same reason —
`lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/Transforms/Utility.cpp:65-68` computes `maxN = max(shape[1] / nWarps, 8)` for
MMAv3. That caps a single dimension because `m` is fixed at 16 there; the shape chosen here is
square, so the corresponding condition is on area.

`numWarps` defaults to `0`, meaning "not supplied", which degenerates to the previous behaviour for
any caller that does not pass it.

## What actually changes

Measured on gfx90a (MI250X). Baseline and patched were built from the **same build directory** with
only this one `.cpp` swapped between them, counting `v_mfma_*` opcodes in the generated assembly:

| tile | warps | share | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 32x32 | 1 | 1024 | `32x32x8`, 16 instr | unchanged |
| 32x32 | 2 | 512 | `32x32x8`, 24 instr, **2.0x over** | `16x16x16`, 24 instr, 0.5x |
| 32x32 | 4 | 256 | `32x32x8`, 24 instr, **4.0x over** | `16x16x16`, **20 instr**, 1.0x |
| 32x32 | 8 | 128 | `32x32x8`, 24 instr, **8.0x over** | `16x16x16`, 20 instr, **2.0x over** |
| 32x64 | 4 | 512 | `32x32x8`, 32 instr, **2.0x over** | `16x16x16`, **24 instr**, 0.5x |
| 64x64 | 4 | 1024 | `32x32x8`, 24 instr | unchanged |
| 64x64 | 8 | 512 | `32x32x8`, 24 instr, **2.0x over** | `16x16x16`, **40 instr**, 0.5x |
| 128x32 | 8 | 512 | `32x32x8`, 32 instr, **2.0x over** | `16x16x16`, **24 instr**, 0.5x |

Cells where the instruction produces more than the warp's share: **6 of 8 -> 1 of 8**. The survivor
is `32x32` on 8 warps, which the 16x16 floor cannot help — there is no smaller square MFMA.

Over a 20-cell `BLOCK_M x BLOCK_N` sweep at 4 warps, **3 cells change**: `32x32`, `32x64`, `64x32`.
Everything with `min(BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N) <= 16` is untouched.

**The cost is real and visible in the table: `64x64` on 8 warps goes from 24 to 40 MFMA
instructions.** Trading wasted lanes for extra issue slots is not obviously a win at every point,
and this PR does not claim it is. I have gfx90a numbers only. **Triton's perf CI is the right
arbiter and I would like it run on this PR** — that is the main thing I am asking for.

## Usefulness against complexity

CONTRIBUTING says performance work "may be rejected if the trade-off between usefulness and
complexity is deemed unfavorable", so here it is explicitly.

The complexity added is one `int` parameter with a default, one integer expression, and one lambda:
**38 added lines in one file, 18 of which are comment, so 20 lines of code.** No new pass, no IR or
API change, no new option
for users to get wrong. Callers that do not pass `numWarps` keep the old behaviour exactly.

For the usefulness side, the closest existing comparison is **#7467**, which proposed changing
`HIPOptions.matrix_instr_nonkdim` from `0` to `16`. Because a non-zero `enforcedNonKDim`
short-circuits the ladder entirely, that forces `16x16` for **every** shape — **12 of the same 20
cells**, including `64x64` and `128x256`, where `32x32` is the right choice and nothing is wasted.
This PR changes 3 of 20, and only where the shape provably cannot be distributed across the warps.

## Tests

Three `lit` cases in one new file, following the "tests should be minimal" guidance — the cap
(`32x64`, now `16x16`), the boundary (`64x64`, still `32x32`), and the floor (`16x16`, still
`16x16`).

The floor case is a regression test in the sense CONTRIBUTING asks for: an earlier revision of this
patch applied the share test at the 16 rung too, which made `16x16`, `16x32` and `32x16` select
nothing at all. The test fails on that revision and on unpatched `main`.

## Related work

- **#7467** — closed as obsolete rather than rejected, with *"feel free to reopen if still wanting
  to push forward"*. On it, @antiagainst wrote: *"We can probably update the default heuristic as
  Lixun suggested and run the perf CI on this pull request to see the effects."* This is an attempt
  at that heuristic update, scoped to the case where the shape cannot be distributed, and unlike
  #7467 it comes with tests.
- **#11749** (in this PR's base) fixes the same class of problem in `tdmGetWarpDistribution()` —
  warps handed more work than the block holds. Different subsystem, and a lowering failure rather
  than a performance one, but the same question: does the per-warp share fit? Its resolution is also
  to accept under-subscription rather than force every warp to be busy.

I do not have access to MI300/MI350 hardware, so the `mfmaVersion == 4` paths are unverified by me
beyond compiling.

title: [KERNELS] Pad Hopper MX scale K-tail storage
body:
Addresses #10772

## Why

`HopperMXScaleLayout` pads the scale-K dimension to a multiple of 2, but the Hopper matmul kernels read scale storage for a full `BLOCK_K` tile at a time. For MXFP4 weights with `block_k = 128`, that tile reaches 4 scale groups.

For K = 2880, the logical scale-K size is 90 groups. Padding to 90 groups leaves the last tile reaching groups 88:92, so the physical scale storage does not cover the whole tile. Per review feedback, the input layout should guarantee zero-padded storage instead of adding more kernel-side masking.

## What changed

- Pad `HopperMXScaleLayout` scale-K storage to a multiple of 4 groups.
- Add a layout regression covering 90 and 94 scale groups, checking storage shape, zero padding, and roundtrip correctness.
- Update the two existing Hopper scale storage-shape expectations for the wider alignment.

This PR now intentionally makes no kernel changes and no `matmul()` API/shape-contract changes. The reproducer variant that passes an extra logical scale group is better treated as an invalid/pre-padded-input contract question, not part of this PR.

## Downstream validation

vLLM merged [vllm-project/vllm#47910](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47910), which explicitly mirrors this PR by zero-padding the SM90 scale-K dimension from 90 to 92 groups before `convert_layout()`. The downstream PR reports the poisoned-memory GPT-OSS 20B repro improving from 0/100 to 100/100, received two repository-member approvals, and closed vllm-project/vllm#47303.

This is useful validation of the storage-alignment fix, but not a substitute for Triton's own review and CI.

## Tests

title: Fix small-K FP4 scaled dot lowering on SM120
body:
## Background
FP4 scaled dot operations with small K fail to compile on SM120. This PR fixes two issues: selecting native MMA for unsupported K sizes, and assuming that each thread has a multiple of four input bytes during FP4 conversion.

## 1. Fall back to decomposition for K < 64

SM120 native FP4 MMA requires 64 logical K elements, but ScaledBlockedToMMA previously selected this path for smaller tiles. K=16 and K=32 cases fail during LLVM lowering with ```Assertion `Index < Length && "Invalid index!"' failed.```

reproducer:
```python3
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def kernel(A, B, Scale, C):
    m = tl.arange(0, 16)
    n = tl.arange(0, 32)
    k = tl.arange(0, 16)  # 16 packed bytes = 32 FP4 values.
    a = tl.load(A + m[:, None] * 16 + k[None, :])
    b = tl.load(B + k[:, None] * 32 + n[None, :])
    a_scale = tl.load(Scale + m[:, None])
    b_scale = tl.load(Scale + n[:, None])
    c = tl.dot_scaled(a, a_scale, "e2m1", b, b_scale, "e2m1")
    tl.store(C + m[:, None] * 32 + n[None, :], c)

a = torch.full((16, 16), 0x22, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
b = torch.full((16, 32), 0x22, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
scale = torch.full((32, 1), 127, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
output = torch.empty((16, 32), dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
kernel[(1,)](a, b, scale, output, num_warps=4, num_stages=1)
torch.testing.assert_close(output, torch.full_like(output, 32), rtol=0, atol=0)
```

This commit skips the native pattern for K < 64, allowing the existing decomposition path to decode FP4, apply scales, and generate an ordinary dot. Tiles with K >= 64 retain the existing native MMA path.

## 2. Support FP4 upcasting with fewer than four bytes per thread

The conversion code processes four input bytes at a time, but small tiles may give each thread only one or two bytes, causing an assertion failure, like ```assert(xVals.size() % 4 == 0);```


reproducer:
```python3
import torch
from triton.experimental import gluon
from triton.experimental.gluon import language as gl

@gluon.jit
def kernel(X, Y):
    layout: gl.constexpr = gl.BlockedLayout([1], [32], [4], [0])
    offsets = gl.arange(0, 128, layout=layout)
    packed = gl.load(X + offsets)  # 128 threads, one input byte per thread.
    values = gl.fp4_to_fp(packed, gl.bfloat16, axis=0)
    output_offsets = gl.arange(0, 256, layout=values.type.layout)
    gl.store(Y + output_offsets, values)

x = torch.full((128,), 0x32, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
output = torch.empty((256,), dtype=torch.bfloat16, device="cuda")
kernel[(1,)](x, output, num_warps=4)
expected = torch.tensor([1.0, 1.5], dtype=torch.bfloat16, device="cuda").repeat(128)
torch.testing.assert_close(output, expected, rtol=0, atol=0)
```


This commit fills the missing bytes with zeros and keeps only the outputs from the original bytes. Tests cover 1/2/4/8 bytes per thread for FP16 and BF16, plus K=16 NVFP4 matmul.

body:
`tdmGetWarpDistribution()` folded warps left over by its bounded greedy loop into the last dimension. Leftovers only existed once every dimension was saturated, so that fold always overshot and the last dimension ended up with more warps than elements. `getTDMLinearLayout()` then floored its `messageShape` to 0, dropping the "message" in-dim and aborting the lowering. Repros on gfx1250 with a `4xf32` block and `num_warps=8`.

Remove the fallback and leave surplus warps undistributed. Their `warpId` bits already get zero basis rows and are reported as free variables by `getFreeVariableMasks()`, so the lowering predicates those warps off (#10056). By forcing `activeWarps == totalWarps` the fallback kept that path unreachable from this distribution.

Fixes: #11748

title: [TEST] triton_kernels: keep the xdist workers inside an outer CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
body:
`python/triton_kernels/tests/conftest.py` spreads the xdist workers over the GPUs by setting `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` to `n % torch.cuda.device_count()` for worker `gw<n>`. When the caller has already narrowed the visible devices, say `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 pytest -n 8 tests` on a shared two-GPU box, `device_count()` is 1, every worker gets the string `"0"`, and that string now names the physical GPU 0 the caller had excluded. I found this the hard way this morning: all eight workers landed on the GPU somebody else was training on.

This indexes into the caller's list instead, so `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1` keeps the workers on GPU 1 and `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=2,3` alternates them between those two; with the variable unset the behaviour is unchanged. `TRITON_TEST_NUM_GPUS` still short-circuits the whole hook as before.

Checked on an RTX PRO 6000 pair with `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 pytest -n 8 tests`: `nvidia-smi` shows the eight workers on GPU 1 only.

title: [RUNTIME] Avoid overflow in empty grid checks
body:
## Summary

- avoid signed overflow when CUDA and HIP launchers check for an empty grid
- preserve zero-dimension launches as no-ops by checking each dimension directly
- add a runtime regression for a nonzero 3D grid whose product is `2**32`

## Problem

Both launchers determine whether a grid is empty by multiplying the three signed `int` dimensions. That multiplication can overflow. For example, `(16384, 16384, 16)` has only nonzero dimensions, but its product is `2**32`; the old check can evaluate it as zero and silently skip the kernel launch.

This reproduces the failure reported in #7260 and also affects the HIP launcher.

## Fix

Check the dimensions independently instead of multiplying them. This removes the overflow while preserving the existing behavior for grids with a zero dimension.

The regression uses a real compiled kernel, function, and stream. It first verifies a normal launch, then verifies that each zero-dimension grid remains a no-op. For the large nonzero grid, it passes a zero block size so CUDA/HIP rejects the launch before dispatching any programs. The test runs through Triton's timeout-aware `run_in_process` helper and asserts that the native CUDA/HIP launcher error is reached rather than silently skipped.

Fixes #7260.

## Validation

- Exact pre-fix AMD launcher: regression fails because the large nonzero grid returns without an error.
- Patched AMD launcher on Radeon PRO W7900D (`gfx1100`): `python/test/unit/runtime/test_launch.py` passes (`10 passed`).
- `pre-commit run --from-ref upstream/main --to-ref HEAD` passes.
- NVIDIA `driver.c` passes a C syntax check; NVIDIA runtime behavior is left to upstream CI.

title: [BACKEND] Reject tensors without a distributed layout before LLVM lowering
body:
Fixes #11795

## Problem

`triton-opt` segfaults when a tensor without a layout encoding reaches the LLVM lowering passes. In #11795 it is a `ttg.local_load` producing `tensor<32xf32>`; the lowering pattern calls `toLinearLayout` on the result type, which dereferences a null `Attribute` in `LinearLayoutConversions.cpp`. The same root cause is reachable through a `tt.func` argument without an encoding (the poc from #9064, which still crashes on `main` in the type converter). Both `--convert-triton-gpu-to-llvm` and `--convert-triton-amdgpu-to-llvm` are affected.

Minimized repro:

```mlir
#shared = #ttg.swizzled_shared<{vec = 1, perPhase = 1, maxPhase = 1, order = [0]}>
#smem = #ttg.shared_memory
module attributes {"ttg.num-ctas" = 1 : i32, "ttg.num-warps" = 1 : i32} {
  tt.func public @f() {
    %0 = ttg.local_alloc : () -> !ttg.memdesc<32xf32, #shared, #smem, mutable>
    %1 = ttg.local_load %0 : !ttg.memdesc<32xf32, #shared, #smem, mutable> -> tensor<32xf32>
    tt.return
  }
}
```

## Fix

Add `verifyTensorLayouts(ModuleOp)` in `TritonGPUToLLVM/Utility`, which walks the module before conversion and emits an error on the first op whose operand, result, or block argument is a `RankedTensorType` without a `DistributedEncodingTrait` encoding. Both lowering passes call it at the start of `runOnOperation`.

After the change the repro fails cleanly:

```
error: 'ttg.local_load' op requires a distributed layout on tensor type 'tensor<32xf32>'
```

The check is placed at the lowering boundary rather than in the `ttg.local_*` op verifiers: a verifier-level check breaks 12 existing lit tests (`consan.mlir`, `test-membar.mlir`, `test-buffer-region*.mlir`, ...) that intentionally use encoding-less tensors as a shorthand in passes that never lower.

## Testing

- New `test/Conversion/invalid_tensor_layout.mlir` and `test/Conversion/amd/invalid_tensor_layout.mlir` cover the `local_load` case from this issue and the function-argument case from #9064 on both backends.
- `check-triton-lit-tests`: 302 passed, 0 failed, 2 unsupported.
- The original poc from the issue, and the minimized `local_load` / `local_store` / `local_alloc` variants, all produce the new error instead of a segfault; valid IR with a `#ttg.blocked` layout lowers unchanged.

title: [BACKENDS] Validate launcher argument shape before flattening
body:
## Summary

The native AMD and NVIDIA launchers recursively flatten runtime arguments according to compile-time argument annotations. They previously indexed each runtime sequence without first verifying that its length matched the annotations.

When a stale or mismatched compiled kernel is reused for a different signature, or when a nested tuple has the wrong shape, this can read beyond the `PySequence_Fast` item array. The result can be a misleading conversion error, memory corruption, or a process crash.

This was found through an external FlagGems kernel cache on Radeon gfx1201. The cache mismatch originates outside Triton, but the launcher should reject malformed input safely.

## Solution

- Validate the runtime sequence length against its annotations inside `extractArgs`, before indexing.
- Perform the validation at every recursive nesting level, so nested tuple mismatches are covered as well as top-level argument mismatches.
- Apply the same safety check to both AMD and NVIDIA native launchers.
- Raise an actionable `ValueError` with the received and expected counts.
- Add an end-to-end regression test for both top-level and nested tuple mismatches.

Keeping the check in the native recursive extraction path avoids a backend-specific Python guard and covers shapes that a top-level `len(args)` check cannot see. Correct launches are unchanged apart from one length comparison per nesting level.

## Validation

- `make PYTHON=.venv/bin/python`
- Relevant pre-commit hooks passed individually: whitespace, EOF, AST, large files, merge conflicts, private keys, debug statements, Ruff, YAPF, clang-format, and mypy.
- Direct AMD launcher validation passed on gfx1201 for top-level and nested tuple mismatches.
- NVIDIA launcher C source passes syntax compilation locally; CUDA runtime coverage is provided by CI.
- The aggregate `pre-commit run --from-ref ...` command was attempted, but local installation of the repository Go hook is blocked by the machine certificate chain (`CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED`). The applicable hooks above completed successfully.

title: [triton-ext] Coalesce `.extend_with()` into a single top-level function
body:
PR #10775 added `.extend_with()` functions to `libtriton` so that Triton extensions can register themselves dynamically, which allows extensions to be distributed as Python wheels (see [triton-ext#111]). That change, however, left three separate entry points dispersed around the Python tree: `ir.extend_dialects_with()` for dialects,
`ir.builder.extend_with()` for custom operations, and `passes.plugin.extend_with()` for passes. A single plugin `.so` can carry any combination of these, so an extension's `__init__.py` had to call up to three functions to register itself.

This change coalesces those into a single, top-level `libtriton.extend_with("path/to/plugin.so")`. As before, we capture the Python module, but now walk the tree to attach the same callbacks as before in the same places as before. There is one exception: `add_<pass>` now lives in a per-plugin `passes.<plugin_name>` submodule.

This approach, a single function instead of three, is what I landed on after thinking a bit about #10775 ([comment]); unfortunately that was merged before I got to this. I think it will hold up better to changes in the plugin ABI or to Triton's Python API over time: in either case the extension wheels can avoid changes.

Assisted-by: OpenCode/anthropic/claude-opus-4-8

[triton-ext#111]: https://github.com/triton-lang/triton-ext/pull/111
[comment]: https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/10775#issuecomment-5063201753

title: [LANGUAGE] Keep fp16 minimum/maximum in fp16 for scalar literals
body:
## Summary

`tl.minimum` / `tl.maximum` of an fp16 tensor and a Python float scalar literal
promote the result through fp32, unlike the other elementwise ops. On an fp16
tensor `x`, `tl.maximum(x, 0.0)` comes out fp32, and a loop-carried fp16 variable
updated with `tl.minimum(tl.maximum(v, 0.0), 6.0)` fails to compile:

```
Loop-carried variable v has initial type fp16 but is re-assigned to fp32
```

Meanwhile `tl.maximum(x, 0)` (int literal) and `x + 1.0` correctly stay fp16.
Reported in #10730, reproduces on `main`.

## Cause

`minimum` / `maximum` call `_semantic.to_tensor()` on both operands before
`binary_op_type_checking_impl` runs. That turns `0.0` into a 0-d fp32 tensor, so
the "a scalar of equal-or-lower kind does not participate in promotion" rule in
`computation_type_impl` never sees it as a scalar, and the result is promoted to
fp32. The other elementwise ops (`add`, `sub`, `mul`, ...) instead
`_unwrap_if_constexpr` their operands and let the scalar reach
`binary_op_type_checking_impl` as a plain number — which is why `x + 1.0` is fine.

## Fix

Unwrap the operands the same way, and apply the bf16->fp32 promotion (which exists
because the hardware has no bf16 FMAX/FMIN/CMP) only to real tensors, so scalar
literals are passed through as numbers. bf16 tensor operands still promote to fp32.

## Test

`test_fp16_scalar_literal_no_fp32_promotion` checks that `minimum` / `maximum` of
an fp16 tensor and `0.0` stays fp16.

Verified locally on triton 3.7.1 by applying this change (frontend AST->TTIR
compile, no GPU): before it, `tl.maximum(fp16, 0.0)` / `tl.minimum(fp16, 6.0)` and
the loop kernel fail the dtype / loop-carried check; after it they pass, while
`tl.maximum(fp16, 0)`, `x + 1.0`, and bf16 (both scalar and tensor operands ->
fp32) are unchanged.

Fixes #10730.

The AMD stores looked up the register free-variable mask under "reg", but for tensor types those keys come from LinearLayout in-dim names, which use "register". The lookup silently returned 0, so the deduplication branch was dead code: a layout that broadcasts a register emitted one store per duplicate register. 

Rename the fallback key in getAllFreeVarMasks to match, so scalars keep working once the call sites use "register". 

isRedundantThreadPredWarpUniform drops the register term instead of renaming it. The redundant-thread predicate is built only from lane, warp, and block, so register duplication cannot make it lane-varying, and including the term would have forced a branch where direct-to-LDS loads can mask through the shared address.

title: [AMD] Add CDNA5 Gluon stream bandwidth example
body:
# Summary

Add a standalone CDNA5 Gluon stream-bandwidth example.

This PR adds `stream_babel_cdna5.py`, an example for studying memory-bound streaming behavior on CDNA5. It streams fp16 inputs from global memory to LDS through CDNA5 TDM descriptor loads and writes a real output stream back with 128-bit buffer stores, so measured throughput reflects actual global-memory traffic rather than a load that the compiler can drop.

# What Changed

- Added `stream_tdm_kernel`, a single grid-stride kernel parameterized by two `gl.constexpr` values:
  - `NARY` selects the arity: `out = a` (1), `out = a + b` (2), `out = a + b + c` (3). The arithmetic is deliberately trivial so every input stream stays live while the kernel remains memory-bound.
  - `PIPELINED` selects between one LDS buffer per input and double-buffering, where the next tile's TDM loads are issued before consuming the current tile and `async_wait(NARY)` leaves only those loads outstanding.
- Inputs are staged through LDS with `gl.amd.cdna5.tdm.make_tensor_descriptor` / `async_load`. The shared layout pads every half tile to break LDS bank conflicts, capped at 512 fp16 elements because TDM encodes the pad interval as `log2(dwords)` and rejects anything above 8.
- Outputs use `gl.amd.cdna5.buffer_store` with an `offsets < N` mask, so partial tail tiles are handled without a separate epilogue.
- Added `compile_stream_tdm`, which reproduces the `tt.divisibility` specialization the JIT applies at launch. Without it the pointer alignment and mask constancy are unknown, the output store scalarizes to one `b16` per element, and the compiled assembly no longer resembles what actually runs.
- Added tests:
  - `test_compile_stream_tdm` asserts each mode really uses TDM: at least `NARY × buffers` `tensor_load_to_lds` instructions, no `global_load`/`buffer_load` per-lane fallback, and output stores that are exclusively `buffer_store_b128`.
  - `test_stream_copy` checks correctness against a torch reference across partial tiles, uneven per-workgroup iteration counts, and many-workgroup grids.
  - `test_stream_copy_block_sizes` covers block sizes 128 through 4096 with both a full tile and an uneven tail.

# Why

Stream bandwidth on CDNA5 depends on how input tiles reach LDS and on whether the output store stays vectorized. This example isolates those two variables so TDM staging and pipelining depth can be compared directly, and the compile-time tests fail loudly if either regresses into a per-lane load or a scalarized store.

# Usage

Run the unary stream kernel:

```bash
python3 third_party/amd/python/examples/gluon/stream_babel_cdna5.py --nary 1
```

Run a pipelined ternary bandwidth sweep with correctness checking disabled:

```bash
python3 third_party/amd/python/examples/gluon/stream_babel_cdna5.py \
  -n 268435456 --nary 3 --pipelined --no-check \
  --stream-workgroups 1024 --stream-block-size 1024
```

Direct execution also prints a static profile via `cdna5_utils.static_profile`.

# Validation

- `pytest third_party/amd/python/examples/gluon/stream_babel_cdna5.py` (66 passed)
- Local bandwidth runs for unary, binary, and ternary streams, pipelined and non-pipelined

title: [TritonGPU][Gluon] Support logical shared memory indexing
body:
Selecting a row from a pipelined shared-memory tile requires choosing a pipeline buffer and then a row within that tile. `ttg.memdesc_index` previously supported the synthetic buffer dimension but could not represent the logical index that followed, preventing nested selection such as `2x8x64 -> 8x64 -> 64`. A [nested `local_view` use case in TLX](https://github.com/facebookexperimental/triton/pull/2843#discussion_r3827562433) exposed this gap, which also prevented upstream Gluon kernels from expressing the same selection.

This change enables logical indexing in Triton's common GPU compiler and Gluon's existing shared-memory descriptor API, so upstream kernels can write `buffers.index(stage).index(row)`. The selected view retains its physical address mapping, including any swizzle phase introduced by the index. This lets loads and stores access the intended elements and lets alias analysis, synchronization, and ConSan track the same storage used at runtime.

Logical indexing supports `swizzled_shared` and `shared_linear` layouts. It requires a full view within one CTA, power-of-two allocation dimensions, and an invertible layout without padding or partitioning. Further logical indexing and consumers that cannot preserve the selected view's address mapping are rejected.

title: Preserve matmul reduction order for promoted operands
body:
Make matmuls produce the same bits whether inputs are widened inside the kernel or before launch. The fix applies to the `mma.sync` tensor-core instructions used on A100. H100 and GB300 also use `mma.sync` for kernels that do not meet the tile, dtype or launch requirements of their newer instructions (`wgmma` and `tcgen05`, respectively). The small tile in the example below uses `mma.sync` on all three GPUs.

## What goes wrong today

Every finite FP16/BF16 value is exactly representable in FP32. Moving that exact cast outside a matmul can still change its result on main. Triton can still use the original load width to choose how values are grouped into registers. That changes the order in which products are added, even though the dot receives the same FP32 values.

This PR chooses floating-point operand packing from the computation dtype. Casting inside the kernel then uses the same summation order as loading inputs widened before launch. This also covers FP8-to-FP16/BF16 promotion.

## Example: the same inputs produce different bits

The helper below uses a fixed 16 × 32 × 32 tile, four warps, three stages, FP32 output and TF32 input precision. It widens both loaded operands to FP32. The two calls differ only in whether an input was widened before launch.

[Full runnable example](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/roman-openai/b651b26976b47c83727118794b3aec6a/raw/bc3f51b5d4039a390a780991fe741322b4193bc3/bitwise_matmul_example.py).

<details>
<summary>Triton matmul helper</summary>

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def _matmul(A, B, C, M, N, K, SA0, SA1, SB0, SB1,
            BM: tl.constexpr, BN: tl.constexpr, BK: tl.constexpr, COMPUTE: tl.constexpr):
    rows = tl.program_id(0) * BM + tl.arange(0, BM)
    cols = tl.program_id(1) * BN + tl.arange(0, BN)
    offsets = tl.arange(0, BK)
    acc = tl.zeros((BM, BN), tl.float32)
    for block in range(tl.cdiv(K, BK)):
        inner = block * BK + offsets
        a = tl.load(A + rows[:, None] * SA0 + inner[None, :] * SA1,
                    (rows[:, None] < M) & (inner[None, :] < K), other=0.0)
        b = tl.load(B + inner[:, None] * SB0 + cols[None, :] * SB1,
                    (inner[:, None] < K) & (cols[None, :] < N), other=0.0)
        acc = tl.dot(a.to(COMPUTE), b.to(COMPUTE), acc, input_precision="tf32")
    tl.store(C + rows[:, None] * N + cols[None, :], acc,
             (rows[:, None] < M) & (cols[None, :] < N))


def matmul(a, b):
    output = torch.empty((16, 16), device=a.device, dtype=torch.float32)
    _matmul[(1, 1)](a, b, output, 16, 16, 32, *a.stride(), *b.stride(),
                   BM=16, BN=32, BK=32, COMPUTE=tl.float32,
                   num_warps=4, num_stages=3)
    return output
```

</details>

```python
a = torch.ones((16, 32), device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
b = torch.zeros((16, 32), device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32).T
b[0, :], b[1, :], b[8, :] = 2**24, -(2**24), 1

# Both calls run the same kernel, tile, and TF32 mode.
mixed = matmul(a, b)  # Widen loaded values inside the kernel.
cast_first = matmul(a.float(), b.float())  # Widen the same values before launch.

# Main:    mixed is all 0; cast_first is all 1. The assertion fails.
# This PR: both are all 1. The assertion passes.
assert torch.equal(mixed.view(torch.int32), cast_first.view(torch.int32))
```

The exact mathematical result is `1`: the nonzero terms are `2**24`, `-2**24` and `1`. In FP32, adding `1` to `2**24` first rounds it away; cancelling the two large terms first preserves it. The FP16-to-FP32 cast is exact, and these inputs are exact at TF32 precision too. Changing the addition order causes the mismatch.

## Why this helps correctness checks

Cast-first becomes an exact equivalence check for kernels with mixed input dtypes: widen the same stored input values, run the same kernel with the same tile, layouts and precision mode, and compare output bits. Removing summation-order differences caused by storage dtype lets this check catch unintended conversions or arithmetic changes without loosening a tolerance to accommodate a different reduction order.

The reference uses the same arithmetic mode—TF32 in this example. This checks cast placement within the same kernel configuration. An independent accuracy reference remains useful for arithmetic shared by both paths; different kernels or GPUs need not produce identical bits.

## Benchmarks

Speed = [main at the PR base](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/tree/dd34455fcfce44d804a719b3643a3bff59d0d033) latency / PR latency. ⚪ means within ±5%; 🟢 is faster and 🔴 slower outside that band. Each comparison uses the same inputs, tile, launch settings and assembler. FP32 outputs; FP32 compute uses TF32.

Tiles are selected from the fastest tested configurations on main. The 8192-row cases reuse the 4096-row tile; the 128-row cases use 64 × 128 × 32. Timings combine two process medians, five samples each, in main/PR/PR/main order. [Absolute timings, memory, configurations and raw samples](https://gist.github.com/roman-openai/b651b26976b47c83727118794b3aec6a).

The newer tensor-core paths (`tcgen05` and `wgmma`) already agree with cast-first on main; their executable code is unchanged. This PR changes the `mma.sync` fallback, where performance depends on the tile and operand order. All tested PR configurations match cast-first bitwise. Tensor peaks and shared memory are unchanged, with no spills.

title: [NVIDIA] Compute distributed shared addresses unconditionally
body:
Compute distributed shared-memory addresses unconditionally with `NVVM::MapaOp`, keeping the original predicates on the memory accesses.

ptxas implements `MapaOp` with a `PRMT` so predicating it creates an extra `SEL` that just doesn't pay off. We instead emit it unconditionally.

title: [AMD] Support configurable warp-pipeline phase gaps
body:
## Summary

Add configurable phase gaps to AMD Gluon warp pipelines. This allows the two warp groups to be offset by one or two pipeline stages.

## Details

- Add `phase_gap` to `warp_pipeline_stage`.
  - Supported values: `1` and `2` (larger numbers can be supported in theory but no known use case yet).
  - Defaults to `1`.
  - Must be specified on the first stage only.
- Propagate the setting from the stage marker to the pipelined loop.
- Emit matching phase-shift and reconvergence barriers.
- Make LDS dependency analysis aware of the phase offset, including cross-iteration RAW, WAR, and WAW dependencies.
- Preserve boundaries between adjacent pipelines unless both use `phase_gap=1`.
- Avoid duplicate barriers after AMD async waits.
- Avoid redundant LOCAL barriers for async global-to-local producers whose dependencies are covered by explicit waits.

title: [NVIDIA] Use predicate operands for masked async copies
body:
Use the predicate `ignore-src` operand of `cp.async` for masked copies. Pass the inverse of the copy mask directly instead of materializing a source size of either the copy width or zero.

This improves perf of the gluon pipelined-copy tutorial by 9.6%

title: [TEST] Fix test_scaled_dot tolerance for `make test-interpret`
body:
`make test-interpret` consistently fails on:

    test_scaled_dot[128-64-128-False-False-True-e4m3-fp16-4-16-1]
    Greatest absolute difference: 0.001 at index (48, 57) (up to 0.0002 allowed)
    Greatest relative difference: 0.042 at index (48, 57) (up to 0.02 allowed)

Reproduced on AMD x86_64, Intel x86_64, and Apple M4 ARM with bit-exact identical errors.

The interpreter's `create_dot_scaled` computes matmul in float32, while the reference (`dot_scale_ref`) uses `torch.matmul` in fp16 on CPU. The existing `large_tolerance` for interpreter doesn't cover this precision gap.

Relax tolerance to atol=2e-3, rtol=5e-2 for interpreter + CPU + fp16.

title: [AMD]Support GenericLinearLayout in FpToFpOp Conversion
body:
Previously when we do `tensor.to(dtype)` on a tensor with `GenericLinearLayout`, the compiler tries to identify it as a canonical LinearLayout and hit assertion.

It makes us add a specific LDS round-trip to convert layout before doing FP conversion. Concretely, it happens in MoE/GEMM epilogue when we need to convert the data type of accumulator who is in `GenericLinearLayout`. This PR uses common getElemsPerThread function to avoid this issue.

title: [TEST][AMD] Add runtime loop regression for #11378
body:
## Motivation

Add correctness regression coverage for #11378. The affected AMD lowering silently corrupts a guarded runtime loop at `num_warps=1` and can fault at higher warp counts.

The production fix already landed in #10496: changing `BuiltinFuncToLLVM` region simplification from `Aggressive` to `Normal` prevents the lane-0 scalar-store blocks from being merged into a loop re-entry shape. That PR targeted a compile-time regression and did not add runtime correctness coverage for this failure mode.

## What this tests

The test preserves the minimized trigger from #11378:

- a runtime-trip-count loop;
- a reduction and scalar loop-carried accumulator;
- an indexed masked lookup;
- masked ragged stores;
- exact CPU-reference checks for lengths, offsets, and packed output.

It exercises both the dynamic loop and the known-good `tl.static_range` control at `num_warps=1`. Higher warp counts are intentionally excluded because affected compilers can raise a HIP illegal-address fault and poison the test process.

## Validation

On a physical W7900D (`gfx1100`):

- ROCm vendor Triton `3.7.1+git5d6048aa`: dynamic case fails deterministically with 3/6 incorrect counts.
- Latest `main` at `58100bd95`: `2 passed` (dynamic and static cases).
- A controlled release/3.7 build with only #10496 applied changes the original reproducer from 5/5 FAIL to 5/5 PASS and restores the scalar `s_cmp` / `s_cbranch_scc` loop guard.
- `pre-commit run --from-ref upstream/main --to-ref HEAD`: passed.

title: Relax broadcast layouts
body:
There are multiple valid ways to broadcast a tensor with a given source layout. Allow `BroadcastOp` to reflect that the destination layout can be different from the source as long as no instructions have to be generated to do the broadcast.

This is technically already expressible today by setting the source layout to be the desired destination layout, but that is less convenient and may not always be possible in `RemoveLayoutConversions`.

title: Fix operand layouts when absorbing view conversions
body:
In the case of reshape, `canUseResultEncoding` also requires that the reshape's source encoding does not change. However, if the source operand is also part of the backward slice, we could end up rematerialising it with a new layout that might be incompatible with the result encoding that we absorbed.

To fix this, record the desired encoding for the reshape's operand, so that we skip rematerialisation if the value requires a conflicting encoding.

body: Add a disable_runtime_unroll_local option to optimize_module that sets the AMDGPU-specific amdgpu-unroll-runtime-local=false flag to disable runtime unrolling of LDS loops. Enable it for gfx942/gfx950 in the HIP backend.

title: [KERNELS] Support all mixed floating-point matmuls
[OptimizeThreadLocality] Handle multi-use thread locality results
body:
The thread-local reduction rewrite assumed the corresponding scf.for result had one use. This will crash valid kernels that reused it in a build with assert, and will lead to a miscompile without asserts:
```
lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/Transforms/OptimizeThreadLocality.cpp:342: virtual void
  mlir::triton::gpu::(anonymous namespace)::TritonGPUOptimizeThreadLocalityPass::runOnOperation(): 
  Assertion `loopResult.hasOneUse()' failed.
```

For example, we trigger this when `scf`.for produces `result` that is used as both operands in and add operation like so:

```
    %result = scf.for ... iter_args(%acc = %zero)
    ..
    %twice = arith.addf %result, %result
```

This can very easily be triggered from source code with an almost identical pattern.

The rewrite is checking that different values inside the loop have one use, but it forget to check that loopResult.hasOneUse() and thus misses that it can have multiple SSA uses, which all need to be replaced.

title: [LAYOUTS] Dispatch shared-layout lowering through `SharedEncodingTrait`
body:
### Problem

`TritonGPUDialect::toLinearLayout` lowers a shared layout by enumerating the concrete encodings it knows about: `dyn_cast<Swizzled/SharedLinear/NVMMA/AMDRotating/PartitionedShared>`, otherwise `assert(0 && "unknown layout")`, where `PaddedSharedEncodingAttr` already lands.

Yet every one of them already implements `SharedEncodingTrait`, whose distributed counterpart has required `toLinearLayout` for a long time.
Adding a shared layout therefore means editing that switch instead of implementing the interface.

### Change

Dispatch through that existing abstraction:

- shared-layout lowering asks the encoding through `SharedEncodingTrait`

This is the path `DistributedEncodingTrait` and `SharedLinearEncodingAttr` already take - it just stops the call site from naming concrete types.
A layout core doesn't enumerate (a future in-tree encoding, or an out-of-tree one) then lowers without touching the switch.

### Compatibility & tests

No behavior change: the conversion bodies are unchanged and a differential over every in-tree shared encoding is identical before and after. `OutOfTreeSharedEncodingExtensionPoint` drives the seam with a stand-in layout, which without this change reaches the unknown-layout assert.

-------

Same concept as in https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/11025

title: [NVIDIA] Simplify fixed-cluster program IDs
[NVIDIA] Use redux for 64-bit integer min/max reductions
Fix FP8 round-to-nearest conversions on NVIDIA
body:
Fix two NVIDIA paths that round FP8 conversions incorrectly: software E5M2 conversion before Ada, and FP32 conversion on Ada.

```python
# x.to(tl.float8e5, fp_downcast_rounding="rtne")
# FP16/BF16 input on the software path:
# x = 1.125:       main -> 1.25; this PR -> 1.0 (ties to even)

# x.to(tl.float8e4nv, fp_downcast_rounding="rtne")
# FP32 input on Ada:
# x = 1.0625001:   main -> 1.0;  this PR -> 1.125
```

The software path shares one nearest-even FP16 encoder. FP32 first uses round-to-odd, which keeps a bit recording discarded precision so the final round can distinguish an exact tie from either neighbor. BF16 can use the same encoder without changing the E5M2 rounding decision. Finite overflow saturates. Rounding and clamping before extracting the FP8 byte lets the compiler emit fewer shifts.

Ada converts directly from FP32: the old FP16 intermediate lost the bits that distinguish the second example from an exact tie. Tests cover ties and neighbors, subnormals, signed zero, overflow and NaNs.

The fix also enables existing E5M2 conversion, MXFP, reduction-gradient and matmul tests on A100. Remove their obsolete skips while keeping the actual E4M3 hardware requirements.

Independent fix, based on [main](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/tree/main).

## Benchmarks

A100, block size 1,024, four warps, ptxas 12.9. Geometric mean of two process medians, five graph/event samples each. Speed = main time / PR time; ⚪ marks ±5%.

| Cast | Elements | Main µs | PR µs | Relative speed | Registers/thread, main → PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| FP16 → E5M2 | 1,048,576 | 2.290 | 3.151 | 🔴 **0.727×** | 12 → 19 |
| FP16 → E5M2 | 67,108,864 | 117.097 | 127.097 | 🔴 **0.921×** | 12 → 19 |
| BF16 → E5M2 | 1,048,576 | 2.646 | 3.187 | 🔴 **0.830×** | 17 → 23 |

The corrected software path is slower than main. Control casts remain within **0.1%**. Tensor allocations are unchanged; all cases use zero shared, local and global scratch bytes. title: Preserve special values when widening FP8 to BF16
body:
FP8-to-BF16 conversion can turn infinities and NaNs into ordinary numbers. Preserve their meaning on NVIDIA and AMD.

```python
# y = x.to(tl.bfloat16)
# E5M2 +inf (0x7c):     main -> 65536; this PR -> +inf
# AMD E4M3 NaN (0x7f): main -> 480;   this PR -> NaN
```

Use native conversion where available; otherwise NVIDIA widens through FP16, which represents every finite FP8 value exactly, before converting to BF16. AMD also uses exact FP16 widening for E5M2 and restores NaN encodings in its E4M3 software path. Exhaustive tests cover all 256 encodings; existing matmul tests no longer replace these inputs to work around the broken cast.

title: Pipeline converted matmul operands with bounded buffers
body:
Overlap conversion of the next operand tile with the current asynchronous matmul, and include the additional buffers in memory planning.

```text
Before: convert tile 0 → MMA 0 → wait → convert tile 1 → MMA 1
After:  convert tile 0 → MMA 0
                         convert tile 1 → MMA 1
```

Hopper pipelines eligible TMA load → cast/layout-conversion chains. Blackwell buffers eligible private operand stores after checking their ownership and lifetime. Extra buffer slots prevent a later conversion from overwriting an operand still in use. Keep the allocation budget and resource-limit tests with the compiler transformation that needs them.

title: [IR] Canonicalize operations with false predicates
body: Fold constant-false predicates for stores and NVIDIA barrier, TMA, and tensor-memory operations when they suppress all effects. Preserve dependency-carrying waits and operations with independent effects or results, and enable the folds in Gluon canonicalization.

title: [INTERPRETER] Honor round_f32_to_tf32 on host tensor descriptor loads
body:
A host `TensorDescriptor` created with `round_f32_to_tf32=True` makes the TMA unit round every f32 it loads to tf32 (round to nearest even at 10 mantissa bits, Inf and NaN left alone), and `RewriteTensorDescriptorToPointer` inlines the same arithmetic for targets without TMA. The interpreter copies the flag in `_init_args_hst` and then drops it: `_implicit_cvt` builds the `TensorDescHandle` without it and `create_descriptor_load` returns the raw bits, so under `TRITON_INTERPRET=1` such a kernel sees different values than on the device.

This keeps the flag on the handle and rounds in `create_descriptor_load` when it is set and the element type is f32. Gathers reuse that path. In-kernel `tl.make_tensor_descriptor` never rounds, matching the pointer rewrite.

The new test covers a tie that rounds to even, a tie that rounds up, a mantissa that carries out into the exponent, and NaN/Inf. It passes on an RTX PRO 6000 (sm_120) and under the interpreter with this change; without it the interpreter run fails on 13 of 16 elements.

title: [KERNELS] Support FP32 matmul with FP16/BF16
[Proton][AMD] Finalize the ROCprofiler client before process teardown
body:
This reduces flakiness for Proton's rocprofiler-sdk shutdown.

ROCprofiler-SDK can deliver buffered profiling records during process shutdown. Proton previously allowed its profiler state to be destroyed before that delivery was complete, so late callbacks could access freed state.

The resulting failures were timing- and allocator-dependent: affected processes could exit successfully, hang during teardown, report heap corruption, or terminate with `SIGSEGV`/`SIGABRT` after profiling had otherwise completed successfully. Explicit `proton.finalize()` often hid the issue by draining pending records earlier, but process exit without explicit finalization remained unsafe.

This change makes Proton’s lifetime agree with the ROCprofiler-SDK client lifecycle: all callbacks required during terminal SDK shutdown complete while their Proton destinations remain valid. It also adds subprocess coverage for SDK-driven shutdown, using heap perturbation to reliably expose stale- state access that would otherwise depend on allocator reuse and timing.

The included regression test runs profiling in a subprocess, queues GPU work, and deliberately exits without synchronizing the device or calling `proton.finalize()`. This leaves rocprofiler-sdk responsible for completing outstanding work and delivering pending callbacks during its process-exit shutdown sequence, which is where the lifetime bug occurs.

The test also enables glibc’s `MALLOC_PERTURB_` debugging behavior. Without it, freed Proton storage often retains enough of its previous contents for the invalid callback to appear to work, making the bug highly sensitive to allocator reuse and timing. I initially used a simpler test that reproduced the original `SIGSEGV`, but only once across many runs, so it was not reliable enough to demonstrate that the fix changed the behavior rather than merely getting lucky.

With heap perturbation, freed allocations are overwritten with a recognizable byte pattern, making callbacks into destroyed Proton state consistently fail instead of accidentally succeeding. Running the test for 10 subprocesses without the fix in this PR resulted in 10 failures (non-termination during teardown, at least not within a generous timeout). With the fix, 60 out of 60 runs exited successfully (well under timeout).

title: Drop obsolete layout conversions when repartitioning warps
body:
Fix compilation when warp specialization reduces a partition's warp count and that partition contains a layout conversion.

One affected path loads an FP8 tile, widens it to FP32, and stores it in tensor memory. Changing the partition from eight warps to four clears the old layouts, but main leaves a now-meaningless `convert_layout` behind. Compilation then crashes while canonicalizing the layout conversion.

Remove these identity conversions before inferring the four-warp layouts.

Independent fix, based on [main](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/tree/main).

title: [AMD] Swizzle clamping for the direct-to-lds path
body:
<!---
The core Triton is a small number of people, and we receive many PRs (thank
you!).  To help us review your code more quickly, **if you are a new
contributor (less than 3 PRs merged) we ask that you complete the following
tasks and include the filled-out checklist in your PR description.**

Complete the following tasks before sending your PR, and replace `[ ]` with
`[x]` to indicate you have done them.
-->

On targets without direct-to-LDS scatter, the lowering implements a swizzled shared-memory layout by shuffling source pointers between lanes, rather than assigning each lane an arbitrary LDS address. This requires every computed `laneId + swizzleOffset` to remain within `[0, threadsPerWarp)`. However, the shared encoding is derived from the consuming dot operand while lane coverage is determined by the load’s blocked layout. For some combinations, the resulting swizzle spans more chunks than the warp’s lanes cover, causing the shuffle index to cross the warp boundary and select an invalid source pointer.

This PR validates the deduced swizzle against the load’s actual register layout before using it for async copy. If the implied lane permutation leaves the warp, it repeatedly halves the shared encoding’s `maxPhase`, reducing the swizzle’s reach until every shuffle remains in range. Because `maxPhase == 1` disables swizzling, the process always finds a valid encoding while preserving the widest safe swizzle and leaving already-valid encodings unchanged.

title: [AMD] Avoid GIL deadlock during HIP library lookup
body:
## Summary

Loading of AOT cache is thread-unsafe on amd. 
Avoid a ROCm startup deadlock by replacing Triton’s dl_iterate_phdr python
callback with a fully native callback compiled into the existing
triton._C.libtriton.amd extension.

This avoids entering Python while glibc holds its dynamic-loader lock without
introducing a separately runtime-compiled helper.

Another approach would be to add native callback that is compiled in runtime, but this seems a b it cleaner.

## Root cause

Parallel AOT-cache deserialization can create an ABBA deadlock between
Python's GIL and glibc's dynamic linker lock `_dl_load_write_lock`:

- Triton calls `dl_iterate_phdr()` through `ctypes.CDLL`, which releases the
  GIL for the native call. glibc acquires `_dl_load_write_lock` and invokes
  Triton's `ctypes.CFUNCTYPE` callback while still holding it. Entering that
  Python callback requires reacquiring the GIL.

- Concurrently, another Python thread calls `hipModuleLoadData()` through a
  native extension that has not released the GIL. HIP/HSA calls
  `dl_iterate_phdr()` and blocks on `_dl_load_write_lock` while that thread
  still owns the GIL.

This leaves one thread holding `_dl_load_write_lock` and waiting for the GIL,
and the other holding the GIL and waiting for `_dl_load_write_lock` (as shown in gdb and pyspy trace)

This all is observed in vllm workload with amd/Mistral-7B-v0.1-FP8-KV model (vllm loads AOT cache concurrently). Hang is non-deterministic, and I was not able to repro this with vllm workload using Qwen3.5-9B model, but even with mistral it happens not that often, sometimes more than 5 subsequent runs finish normally.

`py-spy --native` captured the same two blocking paths in both tensor-parallel
  workers. For example, TP0 contained:

  ```text
  Thread 7306
    pthread_mutex_lock
    dl_iterate_phdr
    CodeObjectReaderImpl::SetMemory
    load_kernel
    ...
    _load_entry

  Thread 7307
    pthread_cond_timedwait
    ...
    dl_iterate_phdr
    _find_already_mmapped_dylib_on_linux
    ...
    _load_entry

  Main thread
    wait
    result
    result_iterator
    load_all
```
  
  GDB resolved the previously unidentified frames and confirmed the two sides of
  the lock cycle:

```text
  LWP 7307, waiting for the GIL:
    pthread_cond_timedwait
    take_gil
    PyEval_RestoreThread
    PyGILState_Ensure
    closure_fcn
    ffi_closure_unix64
    dl_iterate_phdr

  LWP 7306, waiting for the loader lock:
    pthread_mutex_lock(0x... <_rtld_global+2608>)
    dl_iterate_phdr
    CodeObjectReaderImpl::SetMemory
    ...
    hipModuleLoadData
    load_kernel
```
  GDB also identified _rtld_global+2608 as _dl_load_write_lock and showed that
  it was owned by LWP 7307:

  &_rtld_global._dl_load_write_lock = 0x...2a30

  mutex = {
    __lock = 2,
    __count = 1,
    __owner = 7307,
    ...
  }

The full captures are available in:

- `pyspy_tp0.txt`:  
[pyspy_tp0.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30930227/pyspy_tp0.txt)

- `pyspy_tp1.txt`: 
[pyspy_tp1.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30930229/pyspy_tp1.txt)

- `gdb-tp0.txt`: 
[gdb-tp0.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30930231/gdb-tp0.txt)


## Fix

Preserve the existing dl_iterate_phdr() lookup behavior while moving the
implementation into the existing build-time triton._C.libtriton.amd
extension.

The new implementation:

- invokes an entirely native callback while _dl_load_write_lock is held;
- does not call Python or nanobind from the callback;
- releases the GIL around the complete dl_iterate_phdr() walk;
- reacquires the GIL only after dl_iterate_phdr() has returned and released
the loader lock;
- preserves first-match traversal and basename-substring matching;
- preserves Python filesystem-path decoding;
- returns None when no matching library is loaded;
- retains the existing non-Linux platform check;
- keeps the existing TRITON_LIBHIP_PATH override and filesystem-search
precedence unchanged.

The native callback is the correctness-critical part: it removes the
_dl_load_write_lock -> GIL edge. Releasing the GIL around the walk also
preserves concurrency and avoids acquiring the loader lock while unnecessarily
holding the GIL.

Compiling this function into libtriton instead in runtime avoids:

- invoking a compiler during HIP runtime discovery;
- redundant concurrent helper compilation;
- creating and loading a separate cached extension;
- silently falling back to another HIP runtime when runtime helper compilation
fails.

Tests

python -m pytest \
  third_party/amd/python/test/test_libhip_lookup.py \
  -v

The focused tests verify that:

- an already-loaded shared library is found and returned as a valid path;
- a library that is not loaded returns None.

Runtime validation confirmed that:

- the build-time native binding finds the mapped HIP runtime;
- Triton selects the same mapped HIP runtime used by the process;
- the original concurrent warm-cache vLLM startup workload no longer hangs.

Help of AI agents was used in this investigation, but every line was throughly reviewed by human.

title: Add an opt-in SQLite local cache manager
body:
## Motivation

Fix: https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/issues/11778

Triton's filesystem cache stores IR, assembly, binaries, metadata, and group records as separate files under per-key directories. Kernel specializations and autotuning candidates multiply the number of persistent filesystem objects.

On clusters using quota-managed shared directories on GPFS or Lustre, this can exhaust the file/inode allowance while substantial disk capacity remains.
For example, an allocation at 100,000/100,000 allowed objects can reject a new artifact even if it uses only 20 GiB of a 1 TiB byte quota. These numbers are illustrative. Cache-write failures can interrupt compilation, and jobs sharing the quota compete for the same remaining inodes.

## Implementation

Add `TRITON_CACHE_BACKEND=sqlite`, keeping the filesystem backend as the default.

```text
Existing persistence               SQLite persistence
cache/<key>/kernel.ttir             cache/triton-cache-v1.sqlite3
cache/<key>/kernel.ptx                entries keyed by cache key + filename
cache/<key>/kernel.cubin
cache/<key>/kernel.json             Path-based consumers:
cache/<key>/__grp__kernel.json        database → process-local temporary files
...
```

- Implement the existing `CacheManager` API; returned paths remain usable until normal process exit.
- Persist group member names rather than temporary paths; validate group publication transactionally and retrieve members from one read snapshot.
- Use per-operation connections, rollback journaling, and a busy timeout for concurrent local processes.
- Preserve explicit custom-manager precedence, remote-cache behavior, and file-based dump/override storage.

Database errors are explicit, without silently falling back to per-file storage.
The filename's `v1` identifies the backend schema.

## Usage

```sh
export TRITON_CACHE_BACKEND=sqlite
export TRITON_CACHE_DIR=/path/to/node-local/cache
export TMPDIR=/path/to/node-local/runtime  # Existing writable directory.
python train.py
```

Unset the backend variable or set it to `file` for the existing behavior.
Existing file-cache entries are not migrated. To clear SQLite, stop all users before removing its database and any associated journal.

## Cluster deployment and limitations

The shared-filesystem quota motivates this feature, but **shared writable SQLite on GPFS/Lustre is not a supported deployment**. Use a separate database on each node's local storage. SQLite depends on locking and synchronization guarantees that local tests cannot establish for a network filesystem.

For multi-node reuse: publish a consistent snapshot after stopping writers, or use SQLite's backup API, then copy it into each node's writable cache before use.
Do not copy a live database without its required transactional state.

Clean read-only database lookups are tested, but a full read-only compiler cache is unsupported: misses need writes, and crash recovery can need journal writes.
No automatic shared read-only tier is added.

Temporary inode use remains unbounded; use local `TMPDIR` with sufficient inodes.
Normal exit cleans materializations, but abnormal termination can leave files.
No eviction or size limit is introduced.

## Validation

- 19 focused tests and two existing file/remote-cache tests passed.
- Coverage includes text/binary round trips, isolation, restart reuse, concurrent
  processes, interrupted transactions, read-only lookups, and materialization cleanup.
- Python changes were tested with Triton 3.8.0 binary wheels. The full native source
  build and upstream suite were not run.

Storage-only benchmark: 2,000 synthetic kernels, four artifacts plus one group record each (10,000 logical entries), with separate write and restart-read processes:

| Backend | Persistent objects | Write | Restart read |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| File | 12,000 | 0.70 s | 0.21 s |
| SQLite | 1 | 6.44 s | 1.26 s |

SQLite had 16,003 live temporary objects at the end of the write phase and zero after normal exit. Counts exclude containing directories; transient journals may exist during writes. These measurements demonstrate persistent inode reduction, not an end-to-end speedup: SQLite storage operations are slower in this benchmark.

---

- Related Pytorch Inductor issue: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/196993

As this issue is literally preventing me to properly use triton in an inode constrained context, as a temporary solution I'm using this patch: https://github.com/julien-blanchon/triton-sqlite-patch

title: [NVIDIA] Lower unpredicated global loads and stores through LLVM
body: Emit LLVM loads and stores for unpredicated global accesses with default-equivalent cache policies so LLVM can optimize addressing and integer extensions. Ensure integral L2 cache-policy fractions use PTX floating-point literals.

title: [AMD] Fix two-cluster BlockPingpong LDS race
body:
Fixes https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/issues/11696.

The two-cluster BlockPingpong schedule used a raw `s_barrier` after local loads. This allowed the other warp group to overwrite the shared-memory buffer before outstanding LDS reads completed.

Replace it with the local-memory cluster barrier so the required memory fence is emitted before synchronization.

title: [LANGUAGE] Run tl.zeros/tl.zeros_like in interpreter mode
body:
Fixes #11757.

`tl.zeros` and `tl.zeros_like` were `@jit` helpers in `standard.py`, but the interpreter only patches `@builtin` members of `tl`/`tl.core` (`_patch_builtin`), so calling either inside a kernel under `TRITON_INTERPRET=1` fell straight through to `JITFunction.__call__` and died with "Cannot call @triton.jit'd outside of the scope of a kernel". `tl.full` works because it has always been a builtin.

This converts both to builtins delegating to `core.full` with `_semantic` forwarded, the same passthrough pattern the tensor dunders in `core.py` use. The emitted IR is unchanged: a full-of-zero op either way.

Tests: new `test_zeros_and_zeros_like_run_in_interpreter_mode` covers the issue's repro shape (`tl.zeros` + `tl.zeros_like` inside a kernel under `TRITON_INTERPRET=1`, storing through both). I can't build libtriton on this machine (macOS, no supported target), so the runtime run is on CI; statically, the patched path is `zeros` → patched builtin → `core.full` (also patched) → `interpreter_semantic.full`, and `is_builtin` membership is what `_patch_builtin` keys on. `pre-commit run --from-ref origin/main --to-ref HEAD` passes.
